articles.body:
Putin tells Trump that Russia has no 'aggressive plans' towards Europe
Russian President Vladimir Putin and his counterpart Donald Trump held a “constructive” phone call Tuesday during which the Russian leader emphasised that Moscow had “no aggressive plans towards Europe”, the Kremlin said. The call followed a visit to Moscow by US envoys for talks at ending the war in Ukraine. Read our liveblog to see how the day's events unfolded.
This liveblog is now closed.
Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats as it shifts away from pro-Moscow stance
Hungary ordered 10 members of Russia’s diplomatic mission in Budapest to leave the country over activities deemed unacceptable, the government said Tuesday, signaling a shift away from the previous administration's warm relations with Moscow.
The Russian ambassador was informed that “according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities, 10 members of the Russian mission had engaged in activities in Hungary that are unacceptable for diplomats under the Vienna Convention,” Foreign Minister Anita Orbán said.
That is a reference to an international treaty that governs the conduct of diplomats. Russia said that it planned to respond.
The foreign minister didn't specify the alleged activities or say how long the Russian personnel had to leave Hungary, but stressed that her country seeks to maintain diplomatic contacts with Moscow.
“This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty,” Orbán wrote in a statement. “It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules.”
The Russian foreign ministry, in comments to Russia’s state news agency RIA Novosti, vowed to provide “an appropriate response” to the expulsions. It didn't elaborate.
Trump told Putin he wants swift end to Ukraine war and US-Russia ties restored: Kremlin
US President Donald Trump told Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday in a phone call that he wanted a swift end to the war in Ukraine, something that would allow US-Russia ties to be fully restored, the Kremlin said.
Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov told reporters that the pair had discussed the outcome of US peace negotiators' weekend visit to Moscow and Kyiv - something he said both leaders had rated "with a plus sign" - and said that Putin had told Trump what he believed the United States could do to help end the conflict.
Putin had also given Trump his assessment of what the situation on the battlefield was and had made it clear that Russia had no hostile plans towards Europe, Ushakov said.
"Donald Trump clearly emphasised the desirability of bringing the conflict to an end as soon as possible, which would immediately open up prospects – impressive and far-reaching ones at that – for the full restoration of relations between the US and Russia," said Ushakov.
"In his view, this would have a particular impact on trade and economic ties, promising enormous benefits for both countries. Donald Trump is keen to see a breakthrough achieved during his presidency. Vladimir Vladimirovich Putin supported this approach".
US envoys have 'very good' ideas to end Russia's war on Ukraine, Zelensky says
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Tuesday that US envoys who visited Kyiv presented some “very good, worthwhile ideas” for ending Russia's 4 1/2-year-old war, adding that he hopes to meet with President Donald Trump within two weeks.
But Russia remains determined to accomplish its military goals and it believes it is close to winning, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said. Ukrainian and Western observers believe that Moscow has been unable to make any significant progress on the front line.
Romania detains Russian accused of filming military sites for 'sabotage operation'
Romanian authorities said Tuesday they had detained a Russian citizen accused of filming and photographing military sites in the NATO country bordering Ukraine to prepare for an act of sabotage on the orders of Moscow.
The 40-year-old Russian citizen is accused of gathering military intelligence in the country between February and July 2026, prosecutors said in a statement.
The suspect allegedly photographed NATO equipment at several military bases, including in the capital Bucharest, and the movement of personnel and combat equipment.
"The Romanian Intelligence Service, in cooperation with national and international partners, has foiled a sabotage operation coordinated by the Russian Federation on Romanian territory," the Romanian intelligence service said in a separate statement.
Since Moscow's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, Kyiv's European allies say they have frequently been targeted by "hybrid attacks" linked to Russia.
Putin and Trump held 'constructive' call on potential path to peace in Ukraine, Kremlin says
Russian President Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump had a "constructive and frank" hour-long telephone call during which Trump stressed his wish for the war in Ukraine to end as soon as possible, a Kremlin aide said on Tuesday.
The aide, Yuri Ushakov, told reporters, that the pair had discussed the outcome of US peace negotiators' recent visit to Moscow and Kyiv and said that Putin had told Trump what the US could do to help end the conflict.
Germany sends more Patriot missiles to Ukraine from its national stock
Germany will deliver Patriot air defence missiles to Ukraine from its national stocks, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on Tuesday.
"I decided to deliver urgently needed PAC-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine," Pistorius said at a videoconference of defence ministers from countries supporting Ukraine.
Pistorius said Germany would also step up the provision of air-to-air missiles and would continue to deliver drones and long-range ammunition to Ukraine.
Visitors queue to take a closer look at a Patriot missile launcher during the Armed Forces Day at the Airbase in Laage, Germany, on June 06, 2026. Along with nine other locations, Laage hosts the Armed Forces Day 2026. (Photo by John MACDOUGALL / AFP)
Ukraine contracting 1,000 Patriot missiles from allies, defence chief says
Ukraine is contracting the supply of around 1,000 missiles for U.S.-designed Patriot air-defence systems with the help of allies and through a European Union loan, Kyiv's defence minister said on Tuesday.
Speaking at a meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, Yevhenii Khmara also said that the majority of the missiles would only be shipped in the coming years, and called for more urgent aid.
Pentagon warns of 'protracted conflict' between Russia and Ukraine
The world must be prepared for a protracted conflict between Russia and Ukraine, a senior Pentagon official said Tuesday, even as he said President Donald Trump's administration was pushing for a lasting peace.
"We must be prepared for a protracted conflict and for Ukraine's requirements to persist in the months and years ahead, and we must also be prepared for other plausible contingencies as well," Pentagon policy chief Elbridge Colby said at a videoconference of defense officials from countries supporting Ukraine.
NATO chief urges allies to 'dig deeper' to back Ukraine
Ukraine's allies have no choice but to boost their support to the country in its fight against Russia, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte said on Tuesday.
"Nations must dig deeper, we do not have a choice," Rutte said at a videoconference of defence ministers from countries supporting Ukraine.
"Our collective support will enable Ukraine to seize the opportunities it is creating now across all fronts and to defend itself in the skies," Rutte said.
Ukraine denounces 'horrific' Russian missile,drone assault shortly after US envoy's departure
Ukraine criticised Russia on Tuesday for launching a major missile and drone attack that killed at least two people shortly after a weekend visit by US envoys to both countries' capitals, where they tried to restart stalled talks on ending the war.
In Ukraine, teens try to heal from trauma of war at summer camp
The psychological impact on the Ukrainian population of nearly five years of full-scale Russian onslaught is hard to overstate. Children and teenagers are particularly at risk of trauma. With support from foreign philanthropists, one Ukrainian NGO is trying to help at least a few teenagers cope better, via summer camps that mix therapy and fun. Our correspondent Gulliver Cragg reports.
Romanian intelligence service says it prevented Russian sabotage operation
Romania's SRI intelligence service prevented a sabotage operation coordinated by Russia on Romanian territory, it said on Tuesday.
Moscow vows 'painful' response to Hungary expelling 10 Russian diplomats
Moscow pledged Tuesday a "harsh and painful" response to Hungary's move to expel 10 Russian diplomats over what Budapest called their "unacceptable" activity in the country.
"The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful," foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova told the TASS state news agency.
Lavrov says Russia and Saudi Arabia will coordinate their approaches within OPEC+
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that Russia and Saudi Arabia would work closely together within the framework of OPEC+ group of leading oil producers.
Kremlin says Russia's victory in war with Ukraine is "very near"
Russia is confident that victory in the conflict with Ukraine is "very near," Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday while speaking to Indian journalists.
"Yes, we are confident, and we are sure that victory is very near," Peskov said.
Russia pounds Kyiv after pause for visit of US envoys
Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of US peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across the Ukrainian capital. France 24’s correspondent in Kyiv Emmanuelle Chaze has the latest.
Zelensky hopes to meet Trump this month to discuss missile defence
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said Tuesday he hoped to meet Donald Trump later in September to discuss a package of air defence support for Kyiv, where Russia has intensified its missile and drone strikes over the summer.
The Ukrainian leader told journalists he was "counting on a meeting" with the US president after 20 September, at which he would try to secure US supplies to help intercept Russian ballistic missiles.
Russia does not seek 'de-dollarisation', open to payment methods, Kremlin says
Russia does not seek "de-dollarisation" and is open to every acceptable method of payment, Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said on Tuesday, in a virtual interaction with Indian reporters days before the BRICS leaders' summit in New Delhi.
Some countries are using their national currency as a political tool, he added, without naming any country.
Two killed in Ukrainian attack on Russian-annexed Crimea, Moscow-appointed governor says
Two people have been killed and one has been wounded in a Ukrainian attack on the Crimean peninsula, which was annexed by Russia in 2014, Sergei Aksyonov, the Moscow-appointed regional governor, said.
(FRANCE 24 with AFP, AP and Reuters)

articles.title: Russia resumes strikes on military targets in Kiev (VIDEOS)
articles.body:
Russia resumes strikes on military targets in Kiev (VIDEOS)
Russian forces have struck drone and missile production facilities and logistics centers in the Ukrainian capital, Kiev, the Defense Ministry in Moscow has said.
The raid comes as a three-day break in attacks on military-related targets in the Ukrainian capital, announced by Russian President Vladimir Putin ahead of trips to Moscow and Kiev by US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, expired.
The large-scale overnight strike involved ground-, air-, and sea-based precision weapons as well as long-range attack drones, the ministry said in a statement on Tuesday.
Ukrainian defense industry facilities involved in the production and storage of drones and cruise missiles were hit during the attack, the statement read.
They included the Kiev Radio Plant where components for reconnaissance and strike UAVs were produced, including long-range models used to attack civilian targets within Russia, it said.
An industrial facility belonging to weapons maker Fire Point was also hit during the bombardment, the ministry said, adding that the site had made warheads for attack drones and Flamingo cruise missiles.
Russian forces launched another large-scale overnight attack across Ukraine, using a combination of ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles and jet-powered Shahed drones.
The attack hit multiple parts of the country, with the heaviest damage reported in and around… pic.twitter.com/dcDfYH3PeG
Ukrainian leader Vladimir Zelensky actively promotes Fire Point and its products internationally, despite the firm being linked to his longtime business associate Timur Mindich, who fled Ukraine after becoming a key figure in a $100 million corruption scandal last year.
The Russian military also targeted another plant engaged in the manufacture of parts for US-designed AI-assisted Hornet medium-range strike UAVs, according to the statement.
🇺🇦 In the Kiev region, several facilities, warehouses, residential buildings, and cars were damaged as a result of last night's attack, according to Timur Tkachenko, head of the Kiev Regional State Administration.
In the Borispol district, a warehouse, an enterprise, and seven… pic.twitter.com/tFggFMkNpX
Missiles and drones struck transport, logistics, and distribution centers for military cargo in the Ukrainian capital and Kiev Region, the ministry said.
The Vaslikov airbase of the Ukrainian armed forces and a radio-electronic surveillance facility of the country’s security service, the SBU, in Markhalyovka outside Kiev were also hit as part of the raid.
According to the ministry, Russian forces also destroyed several targets in Odessa Region, including facilities in the port of Chenomorsk, used for unloading military cargo.
Earlier, Ukrainian Telegram channels reported air raid sirens and explosions in and outside Kiev as well as in other parts of the country, including in Odessa and Sumy regions.
Kiev Mayor Vitaly Klitschko announced that the Ukrainian capital was under a ballistic missile attack, urging residents to remain in shelters. According to Klitschko, six people were wounded in the city, with three of them requiring hospitalization.
Putin had ordered the Russian military to pause strikes on targets in the Ukrainian capital until Tuesday ahead of Saturday’s talks with Witkoff and Kushner in Moscow.
The meeting at the Kremlin dedicated to the settlement of the Ukraine conflict lasted over three hours. Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov later said it was indicative of an “atmosphere of trust” between Moscow and Washington.
Trump’s envoys later met with Vladimir Zelensky in Kiev on Sunday, with the Ukrainian leader joking about the hiatus in Russian strikes that Witkoff and Kushner “worked even better than the Patriot systems” and asked them to visit more often.
Witkoff said he “felt good” about the discussions in Moscow and Kiev, expressing hope that trilateral talks between the sides could be announced “in short order.”
Moscow maintains that its long-range missile and drone strikes against Ukraine are a response to Kiev’s daily drone incursions targeting civilian infrastructure and residential areas inside Russia. According to Russian officials, Zelensky’s government is resorting to terrorist attacks in an attempt to compensate for setbacks on the battlefield, where Russian forces continue their steady advance.
The Defense Ministry in Moscow maintains that it does not attack civilians, with its strikes being directed solely at military targets and infrastructure supporting Ukrainian forces.

articles.title: Ukraine war latest: Russia's deadline to capture Donbas slips yet again
articles.body:
Key developments on Sept. 8:
- Russia's deadline to capture Donbas slips again as military asks for more time, Ukraine says
- Germany 'ready to provide missiles for Patriots,' Zelensky says
- Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 5, injuring 29, as brief truce ends in missile fire
- Ukrainian drones ignite blaze at Russia's Saratov Oil Refinery, locals report
- Russian drone violates Moldovan and Romanian airspace, crashes in Moldova
Russia has again postponed its deadline to fully capture Ukraine's Donbas, now setting March 31, 2027, as the target date, Deputy Presidential Office head Pavlo Palisa said on Sept. 7.
The new deadline comes as Moscow continues to demand that Ukraine withdraw from the Donbas, which includes the partially occupied Donetsk and Luhansk oblasts, as part of the U.S.-led peace process, rejecting a ceasefire without such concessions.
Russia's political leadership wants to capture the Donbas by the end of 2026, while the military is seeking to extend the deadline to March 31, 2027, Palisa wrote on social media following a military briefing for U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner.
"Russians have failed to achieve any operational success in Donetsk Oblast," Palisa said. "They have already postponed the deadlines for reaching the oblast's administrative borders 15 times."
Ukraine still controls 21% to 22% of Donetsk Oblast, meaning slightly more than one-fifth of the region remains outside Russian control.
Moscow is effectively demanding that Kyiv surrender territory in a peace deal that Russian forces have failed to capture militarily.
Kyiv privately told the Trump administration that Russia may be unable to capture the remaining Ukrainian-controlled parts of Donetsk Oblast even in 2027, according to a document previously seen by the Kyiv Independent.
Russia's territorial advances have slowed to less than 100 square kilometers (around 40 square miles) per month. At that pace, the document says, Moscow's stated objectives in Donetsk Oblast could be pushed "potentially" beyond 2027.

Germany 'ready to provide missiles for Patriots,' Zelensky says
Germany is 'ready to provide' additional supplies of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 8.
"These are exactly the kinds of decisions that bring peace closer: when you reduce the aggressor’s ability to destroy lives," Zelensky said in a post on social media. No timescale was given for the arrival of the additional interceptors.
"Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority and it requires us to act resolutely and immediately," German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said in comments at the Sept. 8 meeting of the Ramstein Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further step up its continuous provision of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide greater quantities to Ukraine," Pistorius said, also committing to deliver additional IRIS-T air defense systems to Ukraine.
read also
Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 5, injuring 29, as brief truce ends in missile fire
A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least five people, injured 29 others, and sparked a series of huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged in the attack, signaling a violent end to the brief respite for the capital during a diplomatic visit by U.S. envoys over the weekend.
"It's like The Hunger Games, it's just about survival," Dariia Kolisnyk, a resident of a building damaged by a missile in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, told the Kyiv Independent.
"You just go to bed, wondering whether you'll wake up or not. That's life in Kyiv."
The strike follows Russia and Ukraine's agreement to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for three days. While the precise expiration time of the truce was hazy, there is no doubt about its end.
The blasts followed warnings from Ukraine's Air Force that Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones were bound for Kyiv. Monitoring channels reported that at least 12 ballistic missiles have targeted the city in the span of about an hour.
The Air Force later reported that Russian forces launched 32 cruise missiles, 166 Shahed-type drones of which "more than half" were jet-powered, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles. Two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones were intercepted, it said.
It added that missile and drone strikes were recorded at 29 locations.
As of 6:20 p.m. local time, three people had been killed and another 29 injured in Russian attacks, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that as of 5 p.m. local time, 23 people had been injured, 14 of whom were hospitalized. Three people are in serious condition.
The death toll had also risen from three to five, the mayor added.
read also
Ukrainian drones ignite blaze at Russia's Saratov Oil Refinery, locals report
Ukrainian drones reportedly struck the Saratov Oil Refinery in Russia overnight on Sept. 8, according to footage shared by locals on social media and analyzed by monitoring groups.
Saratov is located approximately 460 kilometers (285 miles) east of the Ukrainian border with Russia, near Luhansk Oblast in eastern Ukraine.
Residents of Saratov reported explosions and a fire at the refinery overnight, posting photos and videos of the attack. Independent Russian outlet Astra analyzed the footage and concluded based on geolocation that the Saratov Oil Refinery had been hit and was burning.
Russian drone violates Moldovan and Romanian airspace, crashes in Moldova
A suspected Russian Shahed-type drone violated Moldovan and Romanian airspace on Sept. 8, forcing airspace closures, emergency alerts, and the scrambling of NATO fighter jets.
The Moldovan military detected an "unmanned aerial vehicle" at 4:20 p.m. local time, the Moldovan Defense Ministry said in a statement, identifying it as a "Shahed-type" drone that entered the country's airspace from the "direction of… Ukraine."
The military monitored the drone until it left Moldovan airspace at 4:37 p.m., heading in the direction of Golaiesti in Romania.
Spanish F/A-18 fighter jets, deployed as part of a NATO air-policing mission, were scrambled from Mihail Kogalniceanu Air Base as the drone entered Romanian airspace.

articles.title: Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop
articles.body:
Russia attacked Kyiv overnight into 8 September with ballistic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles and jet-powered drones, killing two people and injuring ten, Ukrainian local authorities and the Air Force reported. Ukraine's foreign minister says Moscow launched it the moment the US peace envoys left the capital, and the country's president says the weapons were combined deliberately to cause the greatest possible harm to life. Strikes the same night reached six other regions.
The strike came as the pause expired
US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner made their first visit to Kyiv on 6 September. Ukraine halted strikes on Moscow for three days around the trip, while the Kremlin said its pause on Kyiv ran only to Monday. Nothing else stopped, and Ukraine logged impacts at 11 sites while the delegation was in Moscow.
Russia launched another massive attack on Kyiv the moment the envoys left, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people, Ukraine's Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said.
"[Russian President Putin's] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy. Strike after strike on residential buildings brings him no closer to winning this war—it is nothing but senseless terror," the minister wrote.
Russian forces resumed strikes on the capital after a three-day break tied to the American visit, RFE/RL's Belarus service reported.
What Russia launched
The attack ran from 18:00 on 7 September through the night, the Ukrainian Air Force reported, without giving the total number of launched ballistics.
Russia fired Oniks anti-ship missiles, ballistic Iskander-M, S-400, and KN-23 missiles, and 32 Kh-101 cruise missiles from four of its regions and occupied Crimea, along with 166 Shahed-type drones, more than half of them jet-powered, and decoys launched from two Russian regions and occupied territory. Air defense downed or suppressed 175 targets by 08:30: two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones. Kyiv Oblast and Odesa Oblast were the main axes.
"It was a hard attack, which the Russians deliberately tried to calculate for the greatest possible harm to life," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine put its own peace proposals on the table as two US envoys reached Kyiv for the first time
Results against cruise missiles were very good, he said, while ballistics remain especially hard, and Ukraine proves that need for interceptors to its partners every day. He said he had already discussed it with the Americans and Europeans and would meet states and companies the same day about supplies and about Ukraine's FREYJA anti-ballistic system.
Ukraine has 67 companies working on interceptors, three to five with real results.
Two dead and 13 rescued in the capital
First explosions in Kyiv came at 03:30. Fires and damage reached at least 16 locations in five districts, the Kyiv Military Administration reported. Warehouses, garages, and cars burned, fire spread from a garage to a business center, and a strike on a 26-story non-residential building wrecked structures at the 23rd floor, the State Emergency Service said. Ten people were freed from a blocked five-story block, the service said, and rescuers saved 13 in all, according to Zelenskyy. Morning drone attacks added a warehouse fire, the city said, and the night's damage forced it to reroute a series of bus, tram, and trolleybus lines.
Beyond Kyiv
Two Russian drones hit the locomotive of the Kyiv–Sumy train in the morning, which a monitoring team had stopped in time to evacuate passengers and crew without casualties, Ukrainian Railways board chairman Oleksandr Pertsovskyi said.
Outside Odesa the strike damaged pavilions at the 7th Kilometer market, the country's largest wholesale market for non-food goods, and hospitalized its 58-year-old guard, oblast head Oleh Kiper said.
In Kharkiv two people were injured, one of them a 17-year-old, and Russian forces most often target energy sites, according to oblast head Oleh Syniehubov, who said they struck settlements across the oblast almost 800 times last week alone.
Zelenskyy said Kyiv Oblast's critical infrastructure, Zaporizhzhia, and Dnipropetrovsk Oblast were also hit.

articles.title: Ukrainian woman designing a ballistic missile to put Moscow in reach
articles.body:
Millennial woman designing Ukraine's own ballistic missile says it will soon put Moscow in reach
Kyiv — Ukraine's most important weapons manufacturer wears mismatched earrings and a black knit dress.
"The good thing about being the boss is that you get to set the dress code," Iryna Terekh, the 34-year-old CEO of Fire Point, one of Ukraine's largest drone makers, told CBS News, grinning as she took a seat next to a model of one of the company's latest designs.
With her high heels, bright smile, and entourage of millennial assistants and executives, Terekh stands out in her factory, where throngs of middle-aged men lug drone parts, wield power tools and chain-smoke cigarettes. But she is hardly an exception in a country forced to reinvent itself since Russia launched its invasion in February 2022.
"When the full-scale invasion started, a lot of people had to review what could be their personal impact," she said. "You never really know what kind of knowledge and what kind of experience could be transformed and pivoted into something new."
Terekh's experience was in design and management.
Trained as an architect in the northern Ukrainian city of Irpin, she started building patios and outdoor furniture while also developing a successful high-performance concrete company.
In the early months of 2022, Russian forces occupied Irpin, destroying roughly 70% of the city.
"I understood how vulnerable we are to the complete barbarian behavior of our enemy," Terekh told CBS News. "And if there are any competences that I could put on the table for the sake of fighting this war, then I have to do this."
After escaping Russian occupation, Terekh began looking for a way to help. In the fall of 2022, Russia started attacking Ukrainian cities with Iranian-made, long-range Shahed exploding drones. It also started manufacturing its own versions, known as Gerans.
Terekh and Ukrainian businessman Denys Shtilerman, whom she had worked with designing outdoor urban spaces before the war, decided to build their own long-range attack drones to help Ukraine strike back.
Shtilerman had a background in defense engineering, but most other initial members of the team, including Terekh, came from civilian backgrounds. Yehor Skalyha, their third co-founder, was a film producer.
At first, the company aimed to build 20 of its FP-1 drones per month. By 2024, they were regularly being used to strike Russian airfields, ammunition depots and oil refineries. But over the last two years, the company's ambitions, and its arsenal, have grown.
Fire Point now makes 300 to 400 long-range attack drones per day, and it has added more advanced weapons to its production lines.
In June, a Fire Point cruise missile completed a mission of over 1,000 miles, which she claimed as the longest-range strike ever carried out by a cruise missile in combat history.
Terekh also made the bold claim that Ukraine has launched twice as many deep strikes into Russia as Russia has into Ukraine in 2026 — with 60% of the Ukrainian attacks using Fire Point weapons.
She said her company is now just months away from deploying Ukraine's first domestically designed and manufactured ballistic missile. Unlike cruise missiles, which stay lower to the ground, ballistic missiles follow an arc trajectory that takes them much higher, making them harder to intercept.
Fire Point is among many Ukrainian startups that have helped to shift the country from being solely a recipient of military aid to an engine of defense technology innovation.
Many other companies have similar, unlikely stories of their beginnings. The founder of Sine Engineering, which has attracted American investment in its communications and navigation technology, ran a business making standing desks before the war. Yaroslav Azhnyuk, founder of the Fourth Law, which makes autonomous guidance systems for drones, previously founded Petcube, a pet tech startup backed by the American business accelerator Y Combinator.
Terekh believes these companies, with their founders' diverse backgrounds outside the defense sector and their shared ability to pivot to new endeavors, have been key to their successes.
"This works in Ukraine because we have very low bureaucracy, because we have direct communication with the army, and because we have companies that react," she said.
The country's innovative approach to defense manufacturing and procurement has also attracted the attention of its allies.
In 2025, the U.S. military announced its own program to copy Iran's Shahed drones, known as "LUCAS," which deployed its first relatively cheap long-range drones in the Middle East in February.
The U.S. and Ukrainian governments are expected to sign a new defense agreement soon that would expand Ukrainian military technology exports to the U.S. and joint ventures with American companies.
Terekh said Fire Point's primary focus remains on Ukraine's defense, but she welcomed the idea of one day playing a role in a new, wider Western security architecture.
"We need to ensure that Ukraine will stop just being a breadbasket for the world," she said, referring to the country's longtime primary export of grains. "Now we have something to offer which is much more valuable, and the defense industry is a huge driver for this."

articles.title: Defence Intelligence reveals 155 Russian companies producing components for Russian weapons

Defence Intelligence reveals 155 Russian companies producing components for Russian weapons
Defence Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has released data on 155 companies belonging to the Russian Ruselectronics holding company that manufacture components for Russian weapons, including ballistic missiles, aircraft, UAVs and electronic warfare systems. Some of these companies are not subject to any sanctions imposed by Ukraine's partner countries.
Source: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
Quote: "DIU has released data on 155 companies that are part of or managed by the Ruselectronics holding company, fully owned by Russia's state-owned corporation Rostec, in the Aggressor's Military-Industrial Complex section of the War&Sanctions portal."
Details: DIU noted that the holding company brings together companies and research organisations specialising in the development and production of radio and electronic components and technologies, communications equipment and systems, automated control systems, robotic systems, microwave electronics, computing equipment and telecommunications equipment.
Ruselectronics products are used in almost all types of Russian weapons, including ballistic and cruise missiles, drones, electronic warfare systems, military equipment and radar and communications systems for tactical, operational and strategic aviation, among others.
The holding company includes, in particular, companies involved in the production of 9M723 ballistic missiles for the Iskander-M tactical missile system and 3M22 Zircon missiles:
- Girikond Research Institute JSC, a manufacturer of precision potentiometers for Zircon missiles
- NICEVT JSC, which supplies flight data processing units for Iskander missiles
- NPP Integral-V JSC, a manufacturer of pulse and heating transformers used in Iskander missiles.
The latter company is currently not subject to sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition, as is the case with almost half of all the holding company's businesses identified by DIU.
"However, the inclusion of Girikond and NICEVT on the sanctions lists of most partner countries has had little impact on the overall production volumes of these missiles. This does not mean that sanctions are ineffective, but rather demonstrates the need to improve mechanisms for monitoring compliance with them and strengthen accountability for violations," DIU noted.
DIU also stressed that components, equipment, software and critical raw materials must not fall into the hands of intermediaries and buyers who cannot confirm that the end recipient is a company with no links to Russia's military-industrial complex.

British and French defense companies will participate in establishing local manufacturing for the air-launched precision weapons, which France operates as the SCALP-EG. articles.title: Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 3, injuring 16, as brief truce ends in missile fire
articles.body:
Russia pounds Kyiv in overnight attack, killing 5, injuring 29, as brief truce ends in missile fire
Smoke rising following a Russian missile strike in Kyiv, Ukraine, early on Sept. 8, 2026. (Eugene Kotenko / AFP via Getty Images)
Editor's Note: This is a developing story and is being updated.
Key developments so far:
- Russia launched a large-scale drone and missile attack at Kyiv and the surrounding region overnight on Sept. 8, killing five people and injuring 29.
- The strike signals a definitive end to the aerial truce the Kremlin declared while Kyiv hosted U.S. officials for peace talks.
- The attack damaged residential buildings, a school, warehouses, and vehicles.
- A We-Ukraine TV channel building was struck during a live broadcast, injuring five people.
- Civilian infrastructure in Kyiv Oblast was also targeted, and one civilian injured.
- Air raid alerts sounded throughout the day as Russian jet-powered drones continued to target the capital.
A mass Russian missile and drone attack on Kyiv overnight on Sept. 8 killed at least five people, injured 29 others, and sparked a series of huge fires that filled the morning air across the city with smoke.
Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged in the attack, signaling a violent end to the brief respite for the capital during a diplomatic visit by U.S. envoys over the weekend.
"It's like The Hunger Games, it's just about survival," Dariia Kolisnyk, a resident of a building damaged by a missile in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, told the Kyiv Independent.
"You just go to bed, wondering whether you'll wake up or not. That's life in Kyiv."
The strike follows Russia and Ukraine's agreement to pause aerial attacks on each other's capitals for three days. While the precise expiration time of the truce was hazy, there is no doubt about its end.
Liudmyla Akhremenko, also a resident in Kyiv's Solomianskyi district, said her home has been damaged for the second time in an attack in the area.
"The blast wave blew out the windows, and stones flew into the house. People’s furniture was damaged," Akhremenko told the Kyiv Independent.
According to Akhremenko, no shelter has yet been built nearby, so she was at home when the attack occurred.
"It was very scary," she said. "I was sleeping and woke up to the explosion. I saw that the windows had opened, the glass had shattered, and the flowers had fallen. Everything jumped up to the ceiling."
Explosions rang out in the capital at around 3:30 a.m. local time, according to Kyiv Independent journalists on the ground. Another loud blast occurred about 10 minutes later.
At around 4:14 a.m. local time, Kyiv Independent journalist Yevgeniya Doluda reported a series of up to six explosions in rapid succession.
"There was a very strong bang," Kolisnyk said. "I opened my eyes and saw the window flying, and big flashes. I ran to the second room, where my child and my husband were sleeping and climbed through the broken door and windows."
"I got the child, thank God, sat him up, everything is fine. My husband was cut a little by the glass. But, thank God, everything is fine," she added.
The blasts followed warnings from Ukraine's Air Force that Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered strike drones were bound for Kyiv. Monitoring channels reported that at least 12 ballistic missiles have targeted the city in the span of about an hour.
The Air Force later reported that Russian forces launched 32 cruise missiles, 166 Shahed-type drones of which "more than half" were jet-powered, and an unspecified number of ballistic missiles. Two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones were intercepted, it said.
It added that missile and drone strikes were recorded at 29 locations.
As of 6:20 p.m. local time, three people had been killed and another 29 injured in Russian attacks, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported.
Meanwhile, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said that as of 5 p.m. local time, 23 people had been injured, 14 of whom were hospitalized. Three people are in serious condition.
The death toll had also risen from three to five, the mayor added.
"The Russians tried to deliberately cause as much harm to life as possible — ballistics, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered 'shaheds,'" President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a post on social media.
Speaking to reporters later in the morning, Zelensky described the interception of almost all Russian cruise missiles as "a good result."
"Is it enough? No. We need (interceptor) missiles," he added. "We need a package of ballistic missiles from the Americans. They heard in detail what we need, when we need it."
"I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic. And, God willing, we will get a result."
At least two multistory residential buildings in the capital were damaged by drones, the Kyiv City Military Administration reported. Fires also broke out in warehouses, and garages and vehicles were reported damaged.
Rescuers evacuated two people from a 16-story apartment building that was damaged in the attack, Ukraine's State Emergency Service said. Another 10 people were rescued after being trapped in a five-story building during the strike.
A drone attacked the building of the We-Ukraine TV channel, which is part of Ukraine's national telethon, which has been broadcasting since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion. The attack occurred during a live broadcast, injuring at least five people, Zelensky said.
"‘Shaheds’ against the media is a new chapter in Russia's degradation, and there must certainly be a response from Europe and the world to this," Zelensky said.
The TV channel reported its newsroom and offices were struck during the attack.
Yevhen Panchenko, one of the residents in the Solomianskyi district whose homes were damaged, said he was initially in his apartment on the ninth floor during the attack but ran down to the first floor as the explosions intensified.
"I already call this street a 'training ground' because these attacks are not happening for the first time," he said.
"These attacks destroy people’s lives and livelihoods. They have nowhere to live or work. It’s horrible."
The State Emergency Service reported fires and damage in several neighborhoods, including Kyiv's Holosiivskyi, Solomianskyi, Darnytskyi, Podilskyi, and Dniprovskyi districts.
The attack comes after sustained Russian drone attacks against Kyiv that, before the weekend's truce, targeted the capital around-the-clock for nine consecutive days.
In an apparent sign of their resumption, air raid sirens sounded throughout the morning with the Air Force reporting several jet-powered drones in the airspace above Kyiv. Air defense fire and explosions were heard throughout the day and into the evening as Russian jet-powered drones continued to target the capital.
read also
The assault also affected communities in the surrounding region, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration. Russian forces attacked the area from the evening of Sept. 7 into the morning of Sept. 8, hitting residential areas and civilian infrastructure.
Three people were injured in the region, Tkachenko said. One of those injured was a 2-year-old girl who suffered a shrapnel wound to the eye and was hospitalized, according to Tkachenko.
Two apartment buildings, a house, a warehouse, and a production facility in the town were also damaged in the city of Bila Tserkva. Damage to homes, warehouses, businesses, and vehicles occurred in the Kyiv Oblast districts of Brovary, Boryspil, Fastiv, and Obukhiv, Tkachenko added.
Air raid alarms also sounded overnight in other regions of Ukraine, including Rivne Oblast in the northwest and other areas far from the front lines. The Air Force warned less than an hour earlier that Russia had likely launched cruise missiles from its Tu-95 and Tu-160 strategic bombers.
Moscow on Sept. 6 announced a three-day pause on attacks against Kyiv while U.S. Special Envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the city for peace talks. The Kremlin declared the truce would "begin at midnight today," without specifying if that meant Sept. 5 or 6.
While Witkoff and Kushner's visit passed without an aerial attack against Kyiv, Russia immediately began firing drones at the capital after their departure on Sept. 7.

articles.title: European NATO members may be the second target of Russia’s winter missile buildup—Ukraine’s foreign intelligence
articles.body:
Russia is accumulating missiles for autumn and winter strikes on Ukraine's critical infrastructure as well as for possible provocations against European NATO members, Ukraine's Foreign Intelligence Service (SZR) reported. Major General Oleh Luhovskyi, the service's first deputy head, gave the assessment to the national security advisors of European leaders, SZR said on 6 September. SZR did not say how they responded.
Russia has repeatedly tested NATO's eastern flank through drone incursions, airspace violations, and military activity, increasing pressure on the alliance's eastern members. But no Russian missile strike on NATO territory has been established as deliberate, so SZR's warning points to a potential new form of escalation rather than an established pattern.
Russia's missile buildup
SZR said Russia has accumulated about 400 hypersonic missiles of various types, without specifying which systems are included, and could produce up to 300 ballistic missiles by the end of 2026.
Russia has also deployed additional launchers in the Bryansk, Kursk, and Voronezh oblasts bordering Ukraine, according to the service.
About 60% of the enterprises involved in missile production are still not under international sanctions, SZR said, presenting that as a gap allowing the Kremlin to sustain production. The service called for urgent sanctions on at least 55 more companies still supplying Russia's military-industrial chain with electronic components and machine tools, or handling its payments.
Ukraine's Defense Intelligence (HUR) has estimated that Russia can produce 60–70 Iskander-M missiles per month. In August, HUR said Kinzhal mass production had been suspended in April and that about 50 Kinzhals remained in reserve. Kinzhal is one hypersonic type among several that SZR's undivided figure of 400 may include.
Pressure on NATO's eastern flank
- Russia's military aircraft repeatedly approached NATO airspace in July, and allied fighter scrambles along the eastern flank jumped by more than 250% compared with July 2025.
- Russian drones have also approached Romania's airspace and entered Latvia's.
- A Russian Kh-101 cruise missile landed in a field in Poland during a strike on Ukraine in July, putting a Russian missile on NATO territory.

articles.title: 175 Targets Down, But Ballistic Missiles Still Get Through
articles.body:
Ukraine’s air defenses intercepted 175 Russian aerial targets overnight, but President Volodymyr Zelensky said ballistic missiles remain a major challenge as Kyiv steps up efforts to secure additional interceptors and develop its FREYJA anti-ballistic system.
In a Telegram post on Tuesday, Sept. 8, Zelensky said the overnight Russian attack combined ballistic and cruise missiles, anti-ship missiles and Shahed drones, in what he described as a complex assault designed to inflict maximum damage.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
“Despite very good results with cruise missiles, it is especially difficult with ballistics,” Zelensky said, adding that Ukraine continues to need additional interceptors.
He said Ukraine had already raised the issue with its US and European partners.
“We have already talked about this with the Americans and Europeans, and there will be more meetings, in particular today, with representatives of states and companies that can help with supplies and with our FREYJA anti-ballistic system,” Zelensky said.
“Thank you to all our partners who make air defense assistance to Ukraine a priority. This directly means saving people’s lives,” he added.
Russian attack causes damage across Ukraine
The overnight attack targeted Kyiv and several other Ukrainian regions.
In Kyiv and the surrounding region, emergency crews continued working on Tuesday to clear the aftermath. Zelensky said residential buildings and other civilian infrastructure sustained significant damage.
A Tale Of Two Cities
Thirteen people were rescued by State Emergency Service (DSNS) workers, while 10 people in Kyiv were reported injured. Two people were killed, Zelensky said.
Critical infrastructure was also targeted in the Kyiv region.
In the Odesa region, a regular market was struck. Additionally, two people were wounded in Kharkiv, where an apartment building was damaged.
In the Sumy region, Russian forces attacked a diesel locomotive of the Kyiv-Sumy train at a railway station. No one was injured, but an evacuation was underway, Zelensky said.
Strikes were also reported in Zaporizhzhia and the Dnipropetrovsk regions.
Failed pause
Russia’s three-day pause on strikes against Kyiv appeared to unravel hours before its stated deadline on Monday, as Russian drones were detected over the capital while US envoys were still in Kyiv seeking to revive peace talks.
On Monday, at 8:45 p.m, Ukraine’s Air Force warned of a Russian jet-powered drone over Kyiv and several others approaching the capital – more than three hours before Moscow’s stated 11:59 p.m. deadline.
The attacks intensified overnight, with explosions heard across Kyiv at around 3:30 a.m. on Tuesday after authorities issued an air raid alert and warned of a missile threat.
Russian drones also struck the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of the Kyiv region. Fires broke out at industrial facilities in Boryspil, seven trucks were destroyed, and a logistics complex was hit twice, according to Ukraine’s DSNS.
Limited ceasefire
Russian state news agency TASS reported that the three-day suspension ordered by President Vladimir Putin had expired. Russian accounts said the pause began at midnight between Friday and Saturday and was to last until 11:59 p.m. on Monday.
The halt was limited largely to Kyiv and Moscow rather than being a broader ceasefire. Russian attacks elsewhere in Ukraine continued throughout the weekend.
Putin announced the pause as US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv as part of Washington’s latest push to revive negotiations aimed at ending Russia’s war against Ukraine.
The temporary lull followed more than eight consecutive days of Russian drone and missile attacks on Kyiv and the surrounding region, putting further strain on Ukraine’s air defenses.
During their meeting in Kyiv, President Volodymyr Zelensky joked about the apparent effect of the envoys’ visit on the capital’s security.
“Today, you worked even better than the Patriot systems for our citizens here in the capital,” Zelensky told Witkoff and Kushner, urging them to visit more often.

articles.title: A US-Russia deal won’t end the war. It will start the next one
articles.body:
After talks between President Putin and President Trump's representatives Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner ended, the White House called them "substantive." Putin's aide Yuri Ushakov called the meeting "substantive, constructive and exceptionally frank," adding that the US representatives "formulated a number of considerations on ways to reach a settlement."
According to Bloomberg, Putin is prepared to end the war only on Moscow's terms, and Russian demands have hardened because the Kremlin believes it holds a military advantage. Putin expects to seize the rest of Donetsk Oblast by the end of 2026, Reuters reported, citing a person close to the Kremlin: "There is no chance of reaching an agreement on the front line until Putin finishes taking the rest of Donetsk Oblast."
Witkoff has made many trips to Moscow. He arrived in Kyiv for the first time only the day after. That speaks volumes about where America's focus lies: Russia, not Ukraine.
The danger, though, is not the deal alone. Two American processes are running at once—a peace negotiated on Moscow's terms and a review that would pull US forces from Europe—and together they lower both the political and the military cost of a Russian attack on NATO. Everything below is why that convergence, not the handshake in Moscow, is the thing to watch.
Negotiating a Russian lie, not its strategic demand
Russia has long used disinformation to create strategic ambiguity, offering the West four different tales—all unpleasant, one designed to look like an "easy way out."
The first—give up Crimea, Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhzhia, and Kherson—is what Trump's plan offers. But Putin's demands transcend Donbas, as both his 2024 speech and Russia's military operations show. His stated prerequisites require Ukrainian withdrawal from territory Russian forces do not even occupy, the "demilitarisation" and "denazification" of the Ukrainian government—meaning its replacement with a pro-Russian one—and Ukrainian neutrality excluding NATO.
The second: Foreign Minister Lavrov said in January that "nothing will work without settling the issue of Novorossiya"—which adds Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa.
The third, "one people, one nation," claims all of Ukraine. And the fourth—"the Russian World," the only one formalised in Russian strategic documents—encompasses the "former territories of Kyivan Rus, the Kingdom of Muscovy, the Russian Empire, the Soviet Union, and the contemporary Russian Federation." Its ultimatum of 17 December 2021 demanded that the US leave the European continent entirely.
This is what Russia is fighting for, and why the Kremlin sees an existential war: Russia becomes a Great Power or remains a pariah state. Trump is negotiating the first lie. If he intended a just and lasting peace, he would be addressing the fourth—Russia's actual strategic aim—not the one designed to look easy.
The so-called peace plan
Six months before Trump took office, I concluded his "peace plan" was a blueprint for Russian victory over Ukraine and the West. The 28-point plan published by Axios in November 2025—which alarmed European leaders, excluded NATO, and imposed demands on the EU beyond America's authority—proved the point.
The transactional logic is explicit. On 2 September, Trump said: "We want to have good relations with Russia, Ukraine, with everybody. Be great for business. Russia's got great land and very valuable land."
Asked whether Washington would pressure Russia if talks stalled, Kushner sidestepped and applied a corporate frame to the war: "In the business world, you think in terms of win-win." Of Putin, he added: "he has certain objectives... but there are different aspirations he has for his country that can also be achieved once this is concluded."
The administration does not care about peace or war, international law or the security architecture—only trade. And it has signalled that the aggressor should be rewarded, implying might makes right. This is why Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently blamed Ukraine—not Russia—for high fuel prices: "Ukraine has decided that they want to blow up Russian energy assets." He said it after a meeting with Russia's finance minister.
The sequence of talks
The US representatives went to Moscow first, Kyiv second—carrying the aggressor's terms to the victim, not the other way around. Since they are effectively negotiating European security, an objective team would have consulted US allies in Europe first. According to the EU Ambassador to Washington, Jovita Neliupšienė, Moscow has not abandoned its military objectives, and "the top priority remains unchanged: to provide Ukraine with everything it needs to defend itself"—implying US and European strategy are no longer aligned. We already know the US is not planning to provide Ukraine any defence aid. French, British and German security advisers were allowed to join only the final Kyiv session—informed, but not allowed to influence their own security.
It is strategically absurd to let Europe's two strategic adversaries negotiate European security—which is what happens when we insist on solving the war from within NATO and the EU rather than through a coalition of like-minded countries able to stand up to both Russia and Washington.
The military half
For Europe, the ongoing US review of its troop levels and basing matters as much as the peace process—and it is equally transactional. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the review at NATO on 18 June, framing it as a transition to "NATO 3.0," with Europeans taking on conventional defence and the US concentrating on strategic and nuclear priorities.
The Pentagon's Terms of Reference reportedly examine troop levels, basing, overflight rights, capability gaps Europeans would have to fill—and, tellingly, "the degree to which individual allies support broader US strategic priorities." The Pentagon expects four options ready by 6 November, with a decision in December. There is no reason for optimism.
There are roughly 80,000 US personnel in Europe. At the June meeting, Washington indicated it would immediately reduce the aircraft, reconnaissance drones and naval assets it would activate for Europe in a crisis. Defenders note that Congress set a floor of 76,000 and that European allies have largely filled earlier gaps. But the floor guards the headcount, not the cavalry. The assets that decide a European war—the aircraft, drones and naval power surged in a crisis—are exactly what Washington signalled it would hold back.
More troubling is a Pentagon questionnaire—sent partly in response to Europe's unwillingness to back Trump's war on Iran—asking whether governments have been "publicly supportive of US foreign policy priorities," whether they restrict US basing and overflight, and whether those restrictions could be removed. It reads as a loyalty test: the US making the size and location of its commitment conditional not on military utility but on political alignment—turning the alliance into a competition for American favour and gutting any European strategic autonomy.
Be afraid
If the USA and Russia reach an agreement, be afraid. It would mean the Kremlin has convinced the White House to give it what it wants—and that Russia is positioned to do what a growing number of European intelligence services warn of: war against NATO by 2029.
The US will want its forces out of Europe before Russia moves. Russia will await the outcome of both processes before it strikes, to reduce the risk of a US response. On my read of both timelines, the assault comes while Trump is still in office—and Russia may attack within three years. Europe will not be ready until 2035.
The two processes are not coordinated. They do not need to be. Both flow from the same transactional instinct, and both land on the same variable: Russia's calculation of whether it can attack NATO and survive the response. A deal on Moscow's terms removes the political cost of aggression—it tells the Kremlin that force sets borders and the West will ratify what the battlefield delivers. The force-posture review removes the military cost, cutting the reinforcement flow that makes an assault on NATO expensive. Lower the political cost through the "peace" and the military cost through the withdrawal, and both sides of Moscow's equation fall at once. That is the link: not a plan, but a convergence—two American processes that together make a Russian war on NATO cheaper to start.

articles.title: UK commits £100m to bolster Ukraine’s air defences over winter
articles.body:
The US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby, told European countries they “must not slacken” in their remilitarisation and their backing for Ukraine in a virtual meeting aimed at securing 300 Patriot interceptors for Kyiv.
The influential Pentagon official praised Ukraine’s recent “stout defence”, which he said proved that Europe was capable of leading the defence of its own continent from Russian aggression rather than relying on the US.
“Support for Ukraine contributes to Europe’s security,” Colby said at the start of a 50-country virtual meeting of the Ukraine contact group, reflecting what appears to be a warmer tone from the US on Ukraine.
It helped, he continued, “to rebuild Europe’s military strength and industrial capacity. But words are not enough. Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work. Again, I underline that this is happening, but we must not slacken.”
Led by its president, Donald Trump, the US has been pushing for Europe to dramatically increase defence spending and pay to supply American weapons, such as Patriot interceptors, to Kyiv, via a scheme set up by Nato.
The UK announced it had committed £100m to boost Ukraine’s air defences over winter by buying a package of US military equipment that will include urgently needed Patriot missiles, before the meeting had started.
Boris Pistorius, the German defence minister, pledged in his opening remarks that Berlin would donate a number of older Patriot Pac-2 interceptors from army stocks, and urged other allies of Ukraine to follow suit.
Ukraine is currently unable to prevent Russian ballistic missile attacks because of a shortage of Patriot interceptors, leading to attacks that have killed civilians and destroyed food and logistics warehouses over the summer.
Wes Streeting, the UK defence secretary, said that Ukraine had been “pretty clear” about what it needed: “Three hundred Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability, $2bn for drones,” and continued contributions to other schemes.
The UK did not say how many Patriots it would be able to buy, but the number is likely to be only a fraction of the number sought, given the cost of each interceptor is estimated at about $3m.
Yehven Khamarra, Ukraine’s newly appointed defence minister, acknowledged that Ukraine’s “situation with ballistics is much more difficult” and which was “precisely down to a lack of Patriot missiles”. It was a situation, he added, that the Kremlin was aware of, and trying to exploit.
The Ukrainian minister also said that Ukraine faced a defence budget gap of €23bn this year, and he hoped that countries would bring forward more funding so that its drone investment programme could continue uninterrupted. Kyiv hopes that the EU will bring forward some of a €90bn two-year loan to help plug the shortfall.
An escalation of the long-range war has meant that the harm to civilians is increasing as Ukraine targets Russian oil refineries and warehouses, while Russian bombing has meant that civilian casualties in Ukraine are at their highest level since May 2022 amid near constant attacks on the country’s cities.
On Sunday, US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time, to discuss peace proposals, though no breakthrough was made. A day earlier they had visited the Kremlin, which is still pressing for Ukraine to give up territory and make a string of concessions for ending the war.
The prime minister, Andy Burnham, spoke to tTrump about the war on Monday, with the two agreeing on the need to “continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life”.

articles.title: Russian air defenses down 12 smart bombs, 713 Ukrainian drones over past day
articles.body:
MOSCOW, September 8. /TASS/. Russian air defense systems have shot down 12 guided aerial bombs, a rocket from a US-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket system, and 713 fixed-wing drones of the Ukrainian armed forces over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Air defense systems shot down 12 enemy guided aerial bombs, a US-made HIMARS rocket, and 713 fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles," the statement reads.
Ukraine loses nearly 1,285 troops in special op zone over past 24 hours
Ukraine has lost approximately 1,285 troops in the special military operation zone over the past 24 hours, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
According to its statement, Russia’s battlegroup North wiped out up to 180 Ukrainian servicemen, the battlegroup West eliminated up over 190 enemy troops, the battlegroup South wiped out over 190 military, the battlegroup Center eliminated up to 380, the battlegroup East destroyed up to 300 troops, and the battlegroup Dnepr wiped out over 45.
Russian forces strike Ukraine’s UAV production facility in Belaya Tserkov
Russian forces have struck the Warbirds of Ukraine facility in Belaya Tserkov, manufacturing TRX drones with a range of 450 km, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, the following targets in the Kiev Region were struck: an industrial facility (Warbirds of Ukraine LLC) in Belaya Tserkov, which manufactured unmanned aerial vehicles for various purposes. At this facility, the company [Warbirds of Ukraine] was developing and testing TRX UAVs with a striking range of 450 km," the statement reads.
Russian forces strike encircled Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
The Russian Armed Forces have struck encircled Ukrainian troops in the Kharkov Region, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"Inside the ‘cauldron, ’ enemy units were defeated in the area of the settlements of Malaya Volchya, Varvarovka, Buzovo, and Nefedovka in the Kharkov Region," the ministry said in a statement.
Battlegroup North continues to encircle Ukrainian troops in Kharkov Region
Russia’s battlegroup North is expanding the outer ring of encirclement around Ukrainian troops, the Defense Ministry reported.
"The battlegroup North continues to expand the outer ring of encirclement around enemy formations in the Kharkov Region," the statement said.
Russian forces take control of Dolgenkoye, Berezniki in the Kharkov region
Units of Russia’s Battlegroup North have established control over the settlements of Dolgenkoye and Berezniki in the Kharkov region, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"Control has been established over the settlement of Dolgenkoye in the Kharkov region. The inner ring [in the Kharkov region] continues to narrow, and the settlement of Berezniki in the Kharkov region has come under the control of Russian troops," the ministry stated.
Russian Armed Forces strike Khimtransagro logistics center in Kiev Region
The Russian Armed Forces have struck the Khimtransagro logistics center in the Kiev Region overnight, which was being used for military logistics, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, the following targets were hit: the Khimtransagro logistics center in the Shkarovka settlement, Kiev Region, which was used for the delivery and distribution of military cargo, including components for unmanned aerial vehicles of various types," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike missile plant in Kiev that produced UAV components
Russian forces struck a Kiev-based missile assembly and component plant overnight that was manufacturing unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) components, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"In the city of Kiev, a missile assembly and component plant (Kiev Radio Plant JSC, Trimen-Ukraine LLC), which manufactured components for reconnaissance and strike UAVs, including long-range ones, used to strike civilian targets on Russian territory, was hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Shark, Hornet drone assembly sites in Kiev
Russian forces have struck assembly sites of the Ukrainian armed forces’ Shark and Hornet reconnaissance and strike drones in Kiev, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"An industrial enterprise (Element UA LLC), manufacturing and storing components for Hornet-type medium-range strike unmanned aerial vehicle (UAVs), a retail and warehouse complex belonging to the Ukrspetsystems company, on the premises of which Shark fixed-wing reconnaissance UAVs and medium-range strike UAVs were assembled and stored, were hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Ukrainian Vasilkov airbase, fuel, lubricants depot in Borispol
Russian forces have struck Ukraine’s Vasilkov airbase, a fuel and lubricants depot in Borispol, and the electronic intelligence center of the Security Service of Ukraine (SBU) in Markhalevka, the Russian Defense Ministry reported. According to the ministry, the strikes were carried out overnight.
"In addition, in the Kiev region, the Ukrainian armed forces’ Vasilkov airbase, a fuel and lubricants depot in Borispol, and the SBU’s electronic intelligence center in the Markhalevka settlement were hit," the ministry said in a statement.
Russian forces strike Smart Ammunition logistics center
The Russian military has struck a major logistics center of the Smart Ammunition company in Belaya Tserkov, Russia’s Defense Ministry reported.
"As a result, <…> the R-Plast logistics center in Belaya Tserkov, which manufactured and stored ammunition for medium-and long-range unmanned aerial vehicles, was hit. It was a major logistics center of the Smart Ammunition company," the ministry stated.
At least 384 Ukrainian UAVs downed over Russian regions overnight
Russian air defense forces intercepted and destroyed 384 Ukrainian UAVs over Russian regions and the Black Sea over the past night, the Russian Defense Ministry reported.
"During the past night, from 8:00 p.m. Moscow time [5 p.m. GMT] on September 7 to 8:00 a.m. [5 a.m. GMT] Moscow time on September 8, air defense forces on duty intercepted and destroyed 384 Ukrainian fixed-wing unmanned aerial vehicles over the territories of the Belgorod, Bryansk, Voronezh, Volgograd, Kaluga, Kursk, Lipetsk, Tambov, Oryol, Rostov, Saratov, Smolensk, Moscow and Krasnodar regions, the Republic of Crimea, and over the Black Sea," the ministry said.

articles.title: Germany sending ‘urgently needed’ Patriot air-defence missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
Germany sending ‘urgently needed’ Patriot air-defence missiles to Ukraine
- Germany is sending urgently needed Patriot interceptor missiles from its military stockpiles to Ukraine amid increased Russian missile attacks.
- The UK announced £100 million to supply interceptors, ammunition, and drones to support Ukraine's air defence.
- Ukraine seeks about 1,000 Patriot missiles but most deliveries will only start in coming years, urging allies to provide current stockpile missiles now.
AI generated
BERLIN – Germany is sending Ukraine further “urgently needed” interceptor missiles for Patriot air-defence systems from its own military stockpiles, German Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on Sept 8.
“I have decided... to deliver urgently needed PAK-2 interceptor missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to Ukraine,” Pistorius said, during an online meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
He also appealed to other supporters of Ukraine “to look into their own stocks and make similar deliveries”.
However, Pistorius did not specify the number of interceptors or mention a timeline.
Faced with Moscow’s intensified ballistic missile strikes on the capital, Ukraine has warned of its urgent need for US-made Patriots amid dwindling supplies.
Patriot interceptors are among the few air-defence weapons in Kyiv’s arsenal that are capable of shooting down ballistic missiles, which fly at high speeds on steep trajectories.
However, the United States is conserving its stocks after having used a large number of Patriot interceptors during the war with Iran.
US deliveries of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine have been drastically reduced, and other countries are also clamouring for the weapons.
“I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
“But please, if in doubt, decide in favour for Ukraine.”
The United Kingdom announced earlier on Sept 8 that it was releasing £100 million (S$170 million) for interceptors, large-calibre ammunition, and drones for Kyiv.
Ukraine’s new acting defence minister, Yevgeniy Khmara, underscored the importance of air-defence weaponry as the country tries to fend off increased Russian drone and missile strikes.
“Just last night, the enemy has resorted to another mass air attack,” Khmara said at the meeting.
Ukraine is currently placing orders for roughly 1,000 Patriot interceptors with help from supporters and a loan from the European Union, Khmara said.
“However, the majority of these missiles will only start to be shipped in the coming years, which is why we ask that you supply us the missiles from your stockpiles today,” Khmara told Pistorius and other officials from countries supporting Ukraine. AFP

articles.title: Ukraine says TV channel building in capital Kyiv hit during Russian airstrike
articles.body:
Burc Eruygur
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
Ukraine said Tuesday that a daytime drone attack in the country’s capital Kyiv hit the building of a local TV channel, injuring at least five people.
In a statement on US social media company X, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the drone strike partially destroyed the building of the My-Ukraina TV channel, part of the country’s United News telethon.
All necessary services are working, Zelenskyy said, adding that State Emergency Service personnel have already extinguished the fire that occurred at the site.
“As of now, five people have been reported injured. Unfortunately, that number may still rise,” Zelenskyy said, adding: “Not a single strike against Ukraine and Ukrainians – against life itself – can be left unpunished. Russia must be stopped, and this is possible only through joint efforts.”
The statement comes just hours after local authorities in Kyiv said that at least three people were killed and 19 others injured in overnight Russian drone attacks on the Ukrainian capital.
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said on Telegram that the overnight strikes caused damage in the city's Darnytskyi, Holosiivskyi, Podilskyi, Shevchenkivskyi, and Solomianskyi districts, as well as in the Boryspil and Fastiv districts of the wider Kyiv region.
The strikes extended far beyond the capital, hitting key regions such as Dnipropetrovsk, Sumy, Odesa, and Kharkiv.
Ukraine's Air Force claimed that the country's air defenses shot down 142 out of 166 drones, as well as 33 missiles, launched by Russia overnight.
For its part, the Russian Defense Ministry claimed it launched overnight strikes on "Ukrainian military-industrial facilities, logistics and warehouse centers, and military installations" in Kyiv and the Kyiv region, among other targets in Ukraine.
Independent verification of the claims remains difficult due to the ongoing war.
The strikes mark a continuation of hostilities amid the Russia-Ukraine war. A three-day pause in strikes on Moscow and Kyiv until Monday evening had been declared while US envoys visited both countries' capitals over the weekend for peace talks.
Russia and Ukraine have increasingly targeted each other's logistics centers, as well as port and energy infrastructure, in recent months.
Both sides deny deliberately targeting civilian infrastructure, maintaining their strikes are directed at military targets or facilities linked to military activities.

articles.title: Nearly Half of Russia’s 155 Ruselectronics Facilities Remain Unsanctioned — DIU
articles.body:
Defense Intelligence of Ukraine (DIU) has published data on 155 enterprises that are part of or managed by the Russian JSC Roselektronics.
The information appears in the Aggressor’s Military-Industrial Complex section of the War & Sanctions portal.
The holding is part of Russia’s state-owned Rostec corporation. It brings together specialized enterprises and research organizations across Russia.
These entities develop and manufacture radio-electronic components, communications equipment, and automated control systems. They also produce robotic systems, microwave electronics, and computing equipment.
The holding’s products are used in most types of Russian weaponry, particularly in ballistic and cruise missiles, UAVs, and electronic warfare systems.
These components are also installed on military equipment, radar systems, and aviation communication systems.
Roselektronics includes enterprises involved in the joint production of 9M723 missiles for the Iskander-M system and 3M22 Zircon missiles. Among them is JSC Scientific Research Institute GIRICOND, which manufactures precision potentiometers for Zircons.
Another entity, JSC Scientific Research Center of Electronic Computing Technology (NICEVT), supplies flight data processing units for Iskander ballistic missiles. The list also includes JSC Scientific and Production enterprise INTEGRAL-V, which manufactures pulse and heating transformers for 9M723 missiles.
JSC INTEGRAL-V is currently not subject to sanctions imposed by any country in the sanctions coalition. Overall, restrictions have yet to be imposed on nearly half of the enterprises in the published list of holding company entities.
At the same time, the inclusion of GIRICOND and NICEVT on most countries’ sanctions lists has had little impact on overall missile production volumes. DIU notes that this highlights the need to improve mechanisms for monitoring compliance with restrictions.
Ukraine’s intelligence service stresses the necessity to strengthen accountability for sanctions violations. Partner countries should review their approaches to verifying product end users.
Components, equipment, software, and critical raw materials must not reach foreign intermediaries. Buyers must verify that the end recipient has no ties to Russia’s defense industry.
Ukrainian specialists had previously identified an NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module in Russia’s new S-71M Monochrom air-launched cruise missile.

articles.title: USA Simulated Russian Nuclear Explosion in Space and Its Impact on Satellites
articles.body:
U.S. analysts conducted a simulation of a nuclear explosion in space triggered by Russia, which would cause significant damage to satellite infrastructure.
The results of the study are outlined in a report by the American Foreign Policy Council (AFPC).
In the simulation, a fictional Russian satellite, Kosmos-2567, carries out a nuclear detonation with a yield ranging from 500 kilotons to 2 megatons at an altitude of about 400 km, causing widespread destruction of U.S. satellite infrastructure.
Separately, the authors suggest that Moscow could use a space-based nuclear threat against Starlink to force Washington or SpaceX to limit their support for Ukraine.
The simulation shows that the radiation belt created by the explosion could cause 11,000 satellites to fail within a week.
According to the report, the U.S. lacks the means to mitigate the consequences of a nuclear explosion in orbit.
The proposed concept explicitly outlines a task for U.S. Space Command, in coordination with the Department of Defense: to launch a program to counter space-based nuclear threats within a year.
Options for neutralizing a Russian nuclear device include cyber capabilities, lasers, electronic warfare, jamming, and kinetic interception. The AFPC also proposes considering the adaptation of the Golden Dome architecture to detect and neutralize nuclear space threats.
Among the document’s practical recommendations is to create a plan in advance for deorbiting large commercial satellite constellations in the event of a nuclear detonation threat.
The possibility that Russia could launch a nuclear device into orbit was confirmed by the Pentagon as early as 2024.
In the Decree on Space Superiority of December 2025, the country’s relevant agencies were tasked with developing “a space security strategy that takes into account the interests of the United States in space, from space, and into space,” as well as “a technology plan to detect, characterize, and counter an adversary’s potential deployment of nuclear weapons in space.”
At the same time, the U.S. is developing a new nuclear strategy that places significant emphasis on the possible use of tactical nuclear weapons.

articles.body:
