NATO-Ukraine Council Holds Extraordinary Meeting on Urgent Air Defense Needs
An extraordinary meeting of the NATO-Ukraine Council at the level of Permanent Representatives convened at NATO Headquarters in Brussels to address the urgent need to strengthen Ukraine’s air and missile defense capabilities.
Chaired by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, the session was initiated by Ukraine ahead of the upcoming Ramstein-format meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group on September 8, according to the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The NATO meeting comes against the backdrop of revelations that Moscow spent years digitally rehearsing a war with the Alliance. Russia’s General Staff had conducted extensive computer simulations modeling full-scale wars against NATO, the U.S., and Ukraine.
This includes scenarios like seizing Sweden’s Gotland island—and has since updated these virtual war games with real-world battlefield data from Ukraine.
During the meeting, Deputy Minister of Defence of Ukraine for European Integration Sergiy Boyev and Deputy Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of Ukraine Brigadier General Serhii Sobko presented allied representatives with a detailed assessment of current air threats and submitted a priority list of urgent requirements for air and missile defense systems.
“It is important to focus on helping Ukraine here and now. Right now, timeliness is more important than volume. Drones and air defense systems will determine the course of this winter and whether Ukraine emerges from it weaker or stronger,” Boyev stated in comments published by the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine.
Following the presentation, Ukrainian officials called on NATO allies to transition from what is politically possible to what is operationally necessary by rapidly providing defense capabilities directly linked to protecting Ukrainian lives.
The delegation also urged partners to mobilize the resources required to meet NATO’s stated level of €70 billion ($81.2 billion) in military support for Ukraine by the end of the year.
The Ukrainian Ministry of Defense noted that the delegation emphasized how reinforcing the country’s air defenses serves security interests of the Alliance.
“A russian drone or missile destroyed over Ukraine will never reach a NATO country. Likewise, a russian service member killed in Ukraine will never reach Alliance territory,” said Alyona Getmanchuk, Head of the Mission of Ukraine to NATO.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air and missile defense remains the central focus for allies heading into the September 8 Ramstein-format meeting, the Ministry of Defense of Ukraine reported.
The British government had also recently announced a £100 million ($135.1 million) military aid package to supply Patriot missiles, air defense interceptors, artillery rounds, and drones. Funded through NATO’s Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List (PURL) , the equipment is designated to protect critical infrastructure ahead of expected Russian winter strikes against Ukrainian civilian and energy infrastructure targets.

articles.title: Russia pounds Kiev, ending halt for US talks
articles.body:
Firefighters push out a fire following Russian missiles strikes in Kyiv early on September 8, 2026, amid the Russian invasion in Ukraine. (AFP Photo)
Russian missiles and drones pounded Kiev on Sept. 8, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as U.S. President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
“The moment the U.S. president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kiev, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”
Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s reengagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko said people were trapped in a residential building after the strikes.
Russia’s army said it had a carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial sites, logistics hubs and storage centers in Kiev and its suburbs.
Civilian deaths in Ukraine are running at their highest rate since the first months of Russia’s invasion, according to statistics verified by the United Nations.
In the Moscow-annexed Crimean peninsula, Russian-installed officials said a Ukrainian attack killed two people.
The strikes came hours after Witkoff touted “substantive progress” in the discussions with Ukraine and Russia, raising the prospect of reviving three-way peace talks to end Europe’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace,” he said on X.
Witkoff and Kushner met Putin in Moscow on Sept. 5, before holding separate talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky in their first official trip to Kiev.
The Kremlin announced on Sept. 7 that it did not rule out three-way talks, with spokesman Dmitry Peskov telling reporters “it is too early to say anything about the venue or the exact dates at this stage.”
Zelensky told U.S. news outlet Axios that the U.S. was pushing to deescalate the conflict ahead of the long winter.
Russia has struck Ukraine’s energy grid each winter since invading in February 2022, cutting power and heating to millions in temperatures as low as -20 degrees Celsius.
Zelensky has said the weekend talks included U.S. proposals around energy facilities, grain shipments and oil and gas exports, but declined to give further details.
Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov on Sept. 5 appeared to rule out a Turkish proposal for a truce on strikes in the Black Sea, saying it was “unrealistic” and “impossible to monitor.”
The two sides appear no close to agreeing on how the war should end.
Moscow is demanding Ukraine cede territory in its eastern Donetsk region that it still controls and renounce Western military support.
Kiev has said such terms amount to capitulation and would only allow Russia to prepare a fresh attack in its bid to install a Moscow-friendly puppet government.

articles.title: Russians Brought Su-57E Jets to Egypt Equipped with Monochrome, Kover, and Dan-T Missiles
articles.body:
The Russians have delivered a Su-57E fighter jet to Egypt along with the latest high-precision munitions for it.
Rostec reported that it will publicly showcase the weapons at the El Alamein International Airshow 2026, taking place from September 8 to 10.
A Chinese military observer took photos in which Russian high-precision munitions are visible, specifically the S-71M Monochrome, S-71K Kover, and Dan-T.
During the exhibition, the company will showcase the Su-57E equipped with short-range RVV-MD2 air-to-air missiles, long-range RVV-BD air-to-air missiles, the Kh-38MLE air-to-ground missile, and the Kh-69 and Kh-58USHKE cruise missiles.
The S-71K Kover is a Russian aviation cruise missile developed by the United Aircraft Corporation (UAC) for use on Su-57 fighters; its integration onto the S-70 Okhotnik heavy UAV is being considered for the future.
The S-71K saw its first combat use in late 2025. According to the Defense Intelligence of the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense, its estimated range is up to 300 km.
The S-71K also served as the basis for the S-71M Monochrome missile version, adapted for the internal compartments of the Su-57 and S-70 and equipped with autonomous target-seeking systems.
In August 2026, Defense Intelligence reported discovering an American NVIDIA Jetson Orin computing module in the S-71M. Its presence indicates the use of AI for data processing and guidance without a constant external connection.
The missile’s warhead is an OFAB-250-270 high-explosive fragmentation warhead weighing approximately 250 kg.
The Dan-T is a cruise missile that Russia plans to produce in about 10,000 units per year.
As of August, the Dan-T cruise missile can be launched from both ground-based and airborne platforms. Launches can be carried out from Su-25SM3, Su-30SM, Su-34, and Su-57 aircraft, as well as the Mi-28 helicopter.
The Su-57 is a Russian fifth-generation multi-role fighter developed by Sukhoi (part of the United Aircraft Corporation, UAC) as the successor to the Su-27 family. In the war against Ukraine, the Su-57 is used, in particular, as a carrier for X-69 cruise missiles.

The President noted that the Defense Forces had shot down a total of 175 aerial targets overnight, but not all of them.
“Despite very good results against cruise missiles, ballistic missiles are particularly difficult, and every day we are proving to our partners that we need interceptors. We have already discussed this with the Americans and Europeans, and there will be more meetings, including today, with representatives of states and companies that can help with supplies and with our FREYJA anti-ballistic system,” Zelensky reported.
He thanked the partners who have made assistance to Ukraine with air defense a priority.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, overnight on September 8, Russia carried out another combined attack on the capital, with destruction and fires reported in at least five districts .

articles.title: Allies consider rapidly supplying Ukraine with Patriot systems - media
articles.body:
Allies consider rapidly supplying Ukraine with Patriot systems - media
Kyiv • UNN
The countries that manufacture Patriot systems are seeking ways to quickly strengthen Ukraine’s air defense before winter. France and Italy are preparing to transfer SAMP/T systems and Aster missiles.
Countries that have Patriot air defense systems are considering several options for their rapid delivery to Ukraine ahead of winter. Ukrinform reports this, citing sources at the Élysée Palace, as reported by UNN.
Details

This issue is currently being discussed. Countries that produce or have already purchased Patriot systems are considering several options. ... We have already announced that, in coordination with Italy, we will transfer not only the SAMP/T systems at our disposal, but also Aster missiles. They will effectively strengthen the protection of Ukrainian cities
France understands that the coming winter will be difficult for Ukraine due to Russian strikes on civilian infrastructure facilities.

Their strikes on cities cause great damage and have a dramatic impact on the civilian population, but on the battlefield the Russians are not making a breakthrough
According to them, under these circumstances, it is necessary to continue providing military and financial support to Ukraine while simultaneously increasing pressure on Russia.
We remind you

articles.title: U.S. negotiators think Russia may return to peace talks after its parliamentary elections. Zelensky expects Moscow’s rhetoric to change then, too.
articles.body:
U.S. negotiators think Russia may return to peace talks after its parliamentary elections. Zelensky expects Moscow’s rhetoric to change then, too.
Russia has shown a new willingness to resume peace talks, according to the French newspaper Le Figaro and the German broadcaster Deutsche Welle, citing sources in French President Emmanuel Macron’s administration. American negotiators conveyed that assessment to Paris.
A source in Macron’s administration told Deutsche Welle: “The main thing the Americans told us is that Russia has shown a new willingness to negotiate after the State Duma elections and that, in this context, we need to prepare for a fresh round of talks.”
The sources also said Russian President Vladimir Putin’s position on a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky remains unchanged: It could take place only at the final stage of negotiations. “Putin is setting conditions that are unacceptable today and will probably remain so, because he is effectively demanding that Ukraine accept all of them before he meets with President Zelensky,” a source told Deutsche Welle.
The source also said he was confident European countries would remain involved in the talks: “As you could see, we were there [in Kyiv, at the talks between Zelensky and the Americans] yesterday, and we are confident that we will continue to be involved.”
Zelensky said today that the parties are moving toward resuming three-way talks between Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, which were suspended in early spring. He gave no details, saying only that Kyiv and Washington had agreed to coordinate preparations before discussing them publicly. The trilateral meetings could take place in Turkey, Switzerland, or the United Arab Emirates, he said.
Zelensky said Ukraine is ready for a “compromise on energy” — referring to strikes on infrastructure — and that Moscow as well as Kyiv must take steps toward compromise.
The Ukrainian president said he believes Russia will “demonstrate strength” with constant air attacks on Ukraine until the State Duma elections on September 18–20. He expects Moscow’s rhetoric to change afterward.
Russian officials have also said they are willing to resume talks following Putin’s meeting with U.S. presidential envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said yesterday that the Americans’ visit was “one small step toward peace” and that Moscow does not rule out resuming the three-way talks. However, Peskov said it was “too early to talk about the location or exact timing.”
The war in photos: Kyiv
Russian forces resumed airstrikes on Kyiv this morning after a three-day “period of calm” prompted by U.S. presidential envoys’ visits to Moscow and Kyiv. The attack with missiles and jet-powered drones killed two people and injured 10 others. Damage was reported in six districts of the city.

articles.title: Yemen truce unravels as Houthis attack Saudi Arabia and ground fighting intensifies
articles.body:
After four years of a truce in Yemen that largely held despite occasional flare-ups, the country’s civil war appears to be resuming, while Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia are also expanding.
The Houthis said Tuesday that they had launched a large-scale missile and drone attack against oil facilities in southern Saudi Arabia, claiming it was retaliation for Saudi attacks against them. Riyadh reported at least 73 people wounded and several energy facilities shut down after being damaged, and vowed revenge that came within hours: By midday, Saudi airstrikes were reported in Marib province in central Yemen, followed later by strikes in Taiz and Al-Wazi’iyah in the southwest.
The escalation comes as fighting on the ground in Yemen also has widened in recent days between the Houthis and forces loyal to the internationally recognized government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia. By midday, the Yemeni government said it had captured new territory from the Houthis in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen.
The latest escalation in Yemen began in July, when the Iran-backed rebels tried to break the air and sea blockade imposed on them for about a decade by the Saudi-led Arab coalition, using an Iranian aircraft that attempted to land in the capital Sanaa, which has been under Houthi control since the civil war began in 2014. Saudi Arabia struck the airport to prevent the landing, and the Houthis subsequently retaliated with several attacks of their own on Saudi airports and oil facilities. They also declared a “naval blockade” of Saudi Arabia, attacking Saudi tankers and ships attempting to cross the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a strategic waterway linking the Indian Ocean with the Red Sea and, from there, the Suez Canal.
That escalation came alongside tensions between Iran and the United States, and in recent days it has expanded from airstrikes into actual ground fighting between Houthi forces, which control large parts of northwestern Yemen, and forces of the government based in the southern city of Aden, which also controls broad areas in the country’s east.
The Houthi attack overnight, first reported at around 3:30 a.m., targeted the cities of Abha, Khamis Mushait, Jazan and Najran, all in southern Saudi Arabia. The Energy Ministry in Riyadh said several energy facilities were damaged.
“The attacks caused fires, leading to the temporary shutdown of some activity. The relevant authorities are continuing to deal with the consequences of the attacks,” the ministry said.
Turki al-Maliki, spokesman for the Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis, said 73 civilians were wounded in the attacks, including women and children.
“The Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia constitute a dangerous escalation,” he said, stressing that the assault targeted “civilian and economic sites.”
The statement added that the attack was a “blatant violation of Saudi sovereignty and a direct threat to the security and safety of its citizens and residents. The coalition forces command will take all necessary operational measures to deter the Houthis, respond to the sources of the threat and neutralize the danger posed.”
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said Tuesday morning that the attack included “dozens” of ballistic missiles and drones, and claimed it caused “significant damage” to the energy facilities that were struck.
He said the targets included facilities in Abha belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco, the world’s largest oil company, as well as an air base in Khamis Mushait. Saree said the attack was the rebels’ response to “escalatory measures” by Riyadh and warned that “any aggression against our country will be met with a decisive response.”
He added: “We will not hesitate to launch even stronger and broader attacks against the Saudi enemy. We will be even more determined to confront any aggression and any attack. We will continue our operations deep inside Saudi Arabia and maintain the equation of ‘blockade for blockade’ until the aggression ends and the siege on our country is lifted.”
The strikes came hours after the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of bombing a prison in Al-Jawf province in northern Yemen, saying at least seven people, including one child, were killed.
At the same time, ground fighting against Yemeni government forces also appeared to be intensifying. By midday, government forces, backed by Saudi Arabia, said they had taken control of new areas in Al-Jawf.
“The Al-Yatmah area in Al-Jawf province has been liberated from the Houthis. The advance of the forces on the ground is continuing,” government forces said in a statement, after claiming in recent days to have captured territory from the rebels in the Hodeidah and Taiz areas of southwestern Yemen.
Fighting between government forces and the Houthis was also reported in Marib and Al-Bayda provinces in central Yemen, as well as Al-Jawf in the north.
As part of the escalation, the Houthis themselves have also launched missile and drone attacks on government forces. On Monday, they published footage that they said showed a large fire at the Al-Wadi’ah camp in northern Yemen, near the Saudi border, following a missile attack they had launched on the site.
In a statement, they claimed that trucks “loaded” with military equipment allegedly transferred from Saudi Arabia had caught fire there.
The renewed civil war in Yemen, which in the previous decade caused one of the world’s largest humanitarian crises and left more than 150,000 people dead, is now creating a new wave of displacement. According to the United Nations, the latest flare-up has forced at least 18,500 people to flee their homes in the Taiz and Hodeidah areas.
“Families are arriving with nothing: no shelter, no food and no way of knowing whether it is safe to return,” said Abdusattor Esoev, head of the U.N. International Organization for Migration mission in Yemen. “Many of them are people who have already been displaced from their homes once, twice and even four times before.”
Yemen’s civil war began in 2014 against the backdrop of the Arab Spring protests earlier in the decade, which led in 2011 to the ouster of longtime ruler Ali Abdullah Saleh after decades in power. Three years later, taking advantage of the weakness of Yemen’s new government, Houthi rebels launched a broad offensive and seized the capital Sanaa.
Saudi Arabia viewed the takeover as a direct threat to its security and regional influence, and in 2015 formed a military coalition of Arab states and launched a major campaign that included thousands of airstrikes, an air and sea blockade and support for Yemeni government forces, with the aim of halting the Houthi advance and restoring the government to power.
Although the coalition prevented the Houthis from taking control of all of Yemen, it failed to defeat them. The Houthis continued to control the country’s northwest and over the years launched missiles and drones at Saudi cities, airports and oil facilities.
At the same time, the war led to one of the world’s worst humanitarian crises, and the Saudi-led coalition faced sharp international criticism over civilian casualties and damage to infrastructure. Against that backdrop, Saudi Arabia changed course and in 2022 reached a truce with the Houthis, a shift that a year later was also reflected in the restoration of diplomatic relations with Iran, until then Saudi Arabia’s bitter rival.
Now, after four years of a truce that largely held despite occasional attacks, and against the backdrop of the parallel escalation with Iran, the civil war appears to be resuming.
Still, Saudi Foreign Minister Faisal bin Farhan stressed Tuesday afternoon that Riyadh continues to hope the current round can be brought to an end through negotiations.
“The Houthis prioritize their own interests over the interests of the Yemeni people. The latest Houthi escalation is part of their approach. The path to diplomacy with the Houthis remains open,” he said.
But he added: “Saudi Arabia will not hesitate to defend itself against attacks. We will not hesitate to support what serves the interests of Yemen and the region.”
Bin Farhan spoke during a visit to Moscow, where Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov criticized the Houthis, despite previous reports that Russia had assisted the rebels in attacks on ships in the Red Sea.
Lavrov said the overnight attack on Saudi Arabia would have “negative” consequences for the global economy and added that it was “unacceptable” to resolve issues through military means.

articles.title: 'As much harm as possible' — 5 killed, 63 injured as Russia resumes mass attacks across Ukraine
articles.body:
'As much harm as possible' — 5 killed, 70 injured as Russia resumes mass attacks across Ukraine
Editor's note: The story was updated with the latest reports on casualties from Russian attacks overnight on Sept. 8 in Kyiv and the surrounding region.
At least five people were killed and 70 others injured in Russian attacks across Ukraine over the past day, local authorities said on Sept. 8.
The mass attacks marked the end of a brief pause in strikes that was in place during a weekend visit by U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner to Moscow and Kyiv. The talks failed to produce a major breakthrough, with President Volodymyr Zelensky saying afterward that he expected the war to continue into the winter.
The overnight attack underscored that reports, as Russia launched a large-scale missile and drone attack across Ukraine, with Kyiv and Odesa Oblast among the main targets, according to Ukraine's Air Force.
"It was a difficult attack, which the Russians deliberately tried to calculate to cause as much harm to life as possible: ballistic missiles, cruise and anti-ship missiles, jet-powered Shaheds," Zelensky said.
As of 8:30 a.m., with the attack still ongoing, air defenses had downed or suppressed two ballistic missiles, 31 cruise missiles, and 142 drones. Strikes were recorded at 29 locations, while debris from intercepted drones and missiles fell at nine additional sites, the Air Force said.
"Despite very good results against cruise missiles, ballistic missiles remain particularly difficult, and every day we make clear to our partners our need for interceptors," Zelensky added.
In Kyiv, at least three people were killed and 25 others were injured in a mass Russian missile and drone attack, city authorities said. Residential buildings, a school, and warehouses were damaged, while several large fires broke out across the capital.
As the attack continued, at nearly 12:00 p.m., Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said drone debris had fallen on a four-story office building in Solomianskyi district, causing a fire and structural damage. People were being evacuated from the upper floors, with preliminary reports indicating that there were casualties.
The assault also targeted communities in the surrounding region, injuring two men, according to Tymur Tkachenko, head of the Kyiv Oblast Administration.
In Donetsk Oblast, two people were killed and 10 others were injured by Russian attacks, Governor Vadym Filashkin said.
Two people were killed in Kramatorsk, where six others were wounded. The security situation in the city has deteriorated as Russian forces continue their gradual advance toward it. Three people were also injured in Sloviansk and one in Raihorodok.
One person was killed and 13 others were injured by Russian attacks in Kherson Oblast, Governor Oleksandr Prokudin said.
In Zaporizhzhia Oblast, 12 people were injured in Russian attacks, Governor Ivan Fedorov said.
In Kharkiv Oblast, three people, including a 17-year-old boy, were injured by Russian attacks, Governor Oleh Syniehubov said. The attacks continued into the morning, with Syniehubov reporting at 9:41 a.m. that a Russian drone had preliminarily struck central Kharkiv.
Three men aged 58, 54, and 48 were injured in a Russian attack on a market in the suburbs of Odesa, with the 58-year-old hospitalized in moderate condition, Governor Oleh Kiper said.
In Sumy Oblast, a 65-year-old man was injured in a Russian drone strike, local authorities said.
On the morning of Sept. 8, Russian drones struck a Kyiv-Sumy passenger train twice, but no one was injured after the train was stopped during an air raid alert and all 90 passengers and crew members were evacuated, Governor Oleh Hryhorov said.
In Chernihiv Oblast, a 40-year-old woman was injured in a Russian drone attack on the village of Pryluky, Governor Viacheslav Chaus said.
One person was injured by Russian attacks in Dnipropetrovsk Oblast, local authorities said.

articles.title: Germany 'ready to provide missiles for Patriots,' Zelensky says
articles.body:
Germany is 'ready to provide' additional supplies of Patriot interceptors to Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Sept. 8.
"These are exactly the kinds of decisions that bring peace closer: when you reduce the aggressor’s ability to destroy lives," Zelensky said in a post on social media. No timescale was given for the arrival of the additional interceptors.
"Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority and it requires us to act resolutely and immediately," German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said in comments at the Sept. 8 meeting of the Ramstein Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further step up its continuous provision of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide greater quantities to Ukraine," Pistorius said, also committing to deliver additional IRIS-T air defense systems to Ukraine.
Ukraine relies on the American-made Patriot air defense system for its defense against Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has been increasingly using to pound Ukrainian cities.
Ukraine's stocks have dwindled as supplies have been diverted to the Persian Gulf due to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.
Ukraine's new Defense Minister Yevheniy Khmara urged Ukraine's foreign partners to secure funding for additional Patriot interceptors before winter at the meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group.
"To ensure Ukraine's resilience, we need solutions in the field of air defense," Khmara said. "We are concluding contracts for the supply of about 1,000 missiles for Patriot systems with our partners and through an EU loan," he said.
Khmara noted that long lead times for the manufacture of Patriot interceptors meant such missiles "will be supplied only in the coming years, so Ukraine is asking partners to provide missiles from their stocks today."
The announcement of the additional German support came after Kyiv suffered another overnight Russian drone and missile assault. Five people were killed in the Ukrainian capital and 25 were injured.
An additional £100 million package of British support was also announced on Sept. 8, with the funding also being directed toward additional Patriot interceptors.

articles.title: Iran Threatens to Target U.S. Energy Assets in Gulf If U.S. Strikes Again
articles.body:
Iran warned on Monday that it could target U.S. oil and gas interests in the Gulf if the U.S. launches any new attacks on its assets.
Responding to U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s warning that “if Iran shoots at U.S. ships, we will destroy (and sink) their oil tankers,” Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said: “It’s simple: the oil and gas production chain here is sprawling, accessible, and exposed. American oil and gas companies across these waters and facilities share that exposure. Strike our assets and you get struck."
Ghalibaf’s warning comes as Tehran seeks greater leverage amid Washington’s ongoing economic pressure campaign and stalled efforts to negotiate an end to the war that the U.S. and Israel launched on Feb. 28.
Mohsen Rezaei, Iran’s Supreme National Security Council Secretary, said Monday that "economic warfare will be met by a maritime exclusion zone across the Persian Gulf to the blockade perimeter." The "exclusion zone” in the Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman would begin at the blockade line, extend through the Strait of Hormuz, and continue into the Persian Gulf, Rezaei said. Vessels entering the zone to transit the Strait would be placed on an Iranian sanctions list.
The latest flare-up began Saturday, when Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) attacked U.S. warships in the region. The U.S. responded by striking three Iranian oil tankers, including one near Kharg Island, Iran’s main oil export hub. The U.S. and Iran have for the past week exchanged a flurry of attacks, ending a brief respite in active hostilities. Oil prices reached near six-week highs on Monday as commercial traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, a narrow waterway through which a fifth of global oil and liquefied natural gas shipments flowed before the war, has fallen sharply.
Negotiations remain at a standstill
Diplomatic efforts between the U.S. and Iran have stalled. The two countries signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) on June 17, agreeing to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and engage in technical talks to end the war. But the truce was short-lived.
After a commercial vessel was struck in the Strait in late June, the U.S. attacked Iranian missile storage and radar sites, prompting Iran to retaliate against U.S. military installations in the region. Intermittent attacks continued in July, and fighting resumed in late August after a brief, informal pause.
The Trump Administration has said it is investigating a U.S. strike last week on a family compound in southern Iran where a wedding celebration was underway, killing at least five people and wounding more than 60, according to Iranian state media.
No new formal negotiations have been announced since the MOU’s 60-day deadline expired on Aug. 17. Although some of Iran’s top officials, including President Masoud Pezeshkian, have signaled a willingness to return to the MOU and resume talks with the U.S., the two countries’ positions remain far apart. The U.S. wants to significantly restrict or dismantle Iran’s nuclear program and guarantee unrestricted commercial passage through the Strait of Hormuz. Iran has called for broad sanctions relief, access to frozen assets, an end to the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports, and a role in managing the Strait.
Hard-liners in Iran have shown little appetite for compromise on those red lines, and analysts previously told TIME that Iranian leaders may believe time is on their side, with Tehran prepared to absorb further economic and military pressure in hopes that rising energy prices will eventually prove too politically costly to U.S. President Donald Trump.
“The Iranian nation accepts neither threats nor coercion, nor negotiations whose outcome would be the weakening of the country’s rights,” Hossein Taeb, head of the IRGC’s Basij paramilitary force, said on Monday. “Negotiations are for securing the nation’s rights, not surrendering them.”
While Trump faces domestic pressure to rein in gas prices and avoid an open-ended war in the Middle East ahead of the November midterms, he has also appeared determined to secure an outcome he can present as a victory.
“I’m not trying to force Iran to the bargaining table,” Trump posted on Truth Social last week. “I like our position now much better, with almost total control of the Hormuz Strait, and their economy totally collapsing. They are just playing out the inevitable.”
Iran considers new tactics
Iran is planning to establish a new restricted zone to amp up global economic pressure and force an end to the U.S. blockade. At the same time, Iran and Oman have agreed on a temporary shipping corridor through the Strait of Hormuz and are in talks on its future administration—an arrangement that could formalize Tehran’s role in managing the waterway against U.S. opposition.
But Ghalibaf acknowledged in parliament on Sunday that Iran is struggling with sharp inflation, a collapsing rial, and high unemployment.
Washington’s economic pressure campaign, which includes the naval blockade, sanctions on Iran, and the threat of secondary sanctions on Iran’s trading partners, has squeezed Tehran. The International Monetary Fund estimates that inflation in Iran is near 70%.
The Strait of Hormuz, which Iran began restricting at the start of the war, has been the country’s most important bargaining chip. But that leverage may be weakening as Gulf states turn to routes that bypass the Strait and the U.S. escorts shipments through the corridor. The conflict has also inflicted mounting costs on Iran’s own economy by trapping tens of millions of barrels of Iranian crude inside the Gulf.
Oil prices near $100 as hostilities flare
Brent Crude oil prices approached the $100 per barrel benchmark on Tuesday, reaching near six-week highs of $98.51, after the Iran-backed Houthis attacked multiple Saudi energy facilities in the early hours.
The strikes represented a significant regional escalation, adding further pressure to crude prices.
Meanwhile, traffic via the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted.
Kpler, a commodities data and analytics firm, shared data with TIME that shows only 12 ships crossed the Strait on Monday, significantly lower than the 138 vessels that typically passed through the vital trade waterway during a 24-hour period before the war.
Meanwhile, President Donald Trump on Monday said that “oil prices will drop precipitously" when the U.S. "win[s] the war," but he did not provide a timeline or address the likelihood of energy markets remaining volatile even after the conflict is said to have ended.
Iran faces mounting international pressure
The U.K. is reimposing major economic sanctions against Iran in line with the European Union and the United States, it was announced Tuesday.
The legislation expands trade prohibitions against Iran to additional goods, technology, and services.
Financial measures will "further reduce the government of Iran’s ability to access the U.K. financial system and raise funds in support of its nuclear programme," according to Minister for the Middle East Stephen Doughty.
Additionally, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband announced the U.K. will take action this week to "report Iran to the U.N. Security Council for its nuclear violations, alongside our allies."

articles.title: Russia prepared first Avangard hypersonic missile test in nearly eight years but canceled the launch, says expert Pavel Podvig
articles.body:
Russia appears to have been preparing to conduct its first test of the Avangard hypersonic system since 2018, but the launch was canceled for unknown reasons, writes Pavel Podvig, an expert on Russia’s strategic nuclear forces. Podvig, who has spent years observing Russia’s protocols for conducting such tests, reached that conclusion after analyzing aviation warnings issued ahead of the apparent launch and notices distributed by local authorities.
According to Podvig, the test was planned for Sept. 3-5. A UR-100N UTTKh intercontinental ballistic missile carrying an Avangard hypersonic glide vehicle was expected to launch from the Dombarovsky/Yasny area in Russia’s Orenburg region and to fly toward the Kura missile test range on the Kamchatka Peninsula.
Ahead of the expected test, Russia issued NOTAMs, or Notices to Air Missions, temporarily closing sections of airspace. The restricted areas covered Dombarovsky along with expected rocket-stage impact zones in the Tyumen Region and the Khanty-Mansi Autonomous Region and the area around the Kura test range.
Residents of the Vikulovsky, Vagaysky and Sorokinsky districts of the Tyumen Region were also warned about an upcoming launch. Sept. 3 was listed as the primary date and Sept. 4 as a backup date.
Podvig said the locations of the restricted areas indicate that the planned test involved Avangard rather than Russia’s Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missile. In particular, the NOTAM around Dombarovsky covered the missile silo used for previous Avangard tests but did not include the silo from which Sarmat had previously been launched.
Another indication that an Avangard test was planned, Podvig said, was the fact that an area near the village of Vikulovo in the Tyumen Region was designated in the September notices as an expected rocket-stage impact zone. The same area was used during previous Avangard tests in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2018.
Avangard is a Russian strategic missile system equipped with a hypersonic glide vehicle capable of carrying a nuclear warhead. Unlike a conventional intercontinental ballistic missile warhead, the glide vehicle travels toward its target through the atmosphere at hypersonic speed and can maneuver both laterally and vertically. The capability is intended to make its trajectory harder to predict and more difficult for missile defense systems to intercept.
Vladimir Putin first publicly unveiled Avangard in 2018 and the system’s last known test took place in December 2018.If a fresh test had been successful, Russian authorities almost certainly would have publicly reported it due to Avangard’s symbolic importance to the country’s missile program, Podvig explained.
Notably, there were also no signs that an accident occurred during a Russian launch attempt. If a launch failure had occurred, Podvig said, the NOTAMs could have been expected to be canceled early. Instead, they remained in effect and simply expired after Sept. 5.
“The bottom line is that Russia apparently planned to launch Avangard from Dombarovskiy to Kura, but had to scrub the test for some reason. We should expect another attempt at some point,” Podvig concluded.
The Russian authorities have not publicly commented on preparations for such a test, nor about its cancellation.

articles.title: Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
articles.body:
Zelensky gives cautious backing to Trump envoys' 'good' ideas to end Russia's war
U.S. President Donald Trump's envoys, Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, brought Kyiv some "pretty good, decent" ideas on how to end Russia's war against Ukraine, President Volodymyr Zelensky told reporters on Sept. 8.
Zelensky said it remains unclear whether the proposals can actually work.
"We need to understand whether we can implement them and make them effective," the Ukrainian president said. "I don't know yet if it will work out."
His comments came days after Witkoff and Kushner traveled to Moscow and Kyiv with revised peace proposals in an apparent attempt to restart negotiations that have been deadlocked for months.
Zelensky stopped short of disclosing the details of the U.S. proposals but pointed to two issues that could play an important role in any potential agreement: grain and energy.
"Grain and energy are sensitive issues for Ukraine and Russia," he said.
Grain, energy
One new proposal discussed during the talks involved a potential truce in the air, either focused on energy infrastructure or halting aerial strikes altogether, one person familiar with the negotiations previously told the Kyiv Independent.
Russia has not agreed to the proposal so far.
Both Ukraine and Russia have repeatedly targeted each other's energy infrastructure throughout the war. While Ukraine has targeted Russia's energy exports to cut off a key source of funding for the war, Moscow has focused on destroying Ukrainian power plants and substations in an effort to trigger blackouts across the country.
The issue has become particularly urgent for Kyiv ahead of another winter, when Ukrainian officials expect Russia to intensify attacks on the country's energy grid.
Last winter, Kyiv faced a major Russian campaign against its energy infrastructure, causing mass blackouts amid freezing temperatures.
Grain has also emerged as another sensitive issue.
Russia has intensified attacks on shipping corridors in the Black Sea, including deadly strikes on civilian grain ships. The campaign has contributed to declining exports, rising costs, and a shrinking number of vessels willing to dock at Ukrainian ports.
Zelensky said the consequences extend far beyond Ukraine and Russia.
"These are pressing issues for the entire world," he said. "And these are pressing issues for India today, for the Emirates, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Asia, and many other countries. We are ready to find a compromise here."
read also
Meeting with Trump
Zelensky said he hopes to meet Trump around Sept. 20 and plans to raise Ukraine's need for additional anti-ballistic missiles.
"We need a package of anti-ballistic missiles from the U.S. They heard in detail what we need," Zelensky said. "I count on meeting with President Trump to raise this topic."
Ukraine faces a shortage of missiles capable of intercepting Russian ballistic missiles, which Moscow has increasingly used against Ukrainian cities.
Zelensky did not disclose the details of the proposed support package.
"I cannot disclose all the details here," he said. "We have agreed with the American side that we will prepare everything and then communicate with the Europeans."
Moscow's demands remain
Despite the renewed U.S. push, the central obstacles to a peace deal remain unchanged.
The negotiations have been effectively deadlocked since earlier this year as Moscow continues to reject a ceasefire along the current front lines and demands that Ukraine cede Donbas — the strategically important, partially occupied region in eastern Ukraine — and abandon its NATO membership aspirations.
The Kremlin has not signaled that it is prepared to compromise on its territorial demands.
At the same time, Ukrainian officials warn that Russia is preparing to escalate attacks on Ukrainian cities and the country's energy infrastructure over the winter.
"Putin still hopes to break us this winter and isn't willing to agree to anything," one Ukrainian official previously told the Kyiv Independent.

articles.title: Russian strikes on Kyiv resume after pause for Witkoff and Kushner visit
articles.body:
At least 12 people were killed overnight Monday into Tuesday in the first Russian airstrikes on Kyiv since the three-day ceasefire prompted by the visit of U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, authorities in the capital said.
Administrative buildings, warehouses, schools and residential buildings were damaged in six districts of Kyiv, Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported. At least 10 people were injured.
The overnight attack extended beyond the Ukrainian capital to the Odesa region. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it "a complex strike" that "tried to plan to cause as much harm to life as possible."

Both Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered a pause on attacks on Moscow and Kyiv as Witkoff and Kushner traveled to both capitals for talks over the weekend.
"Please come more often, so that our people have the chance to live normally," the Ukrainian leader joked at a press conference with the U.S. envoys in Kyiv on Sunday.
"As soon as the U.S. presidential peace envoys left the city, Putin launched another massive and horrific attack on Kyiv," Minister of Foreign Affairs of Ukraine Andrii Sybiha said on Tuesday. "[Putin's] ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," the minister added.
On September 6, U.S. special envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Kyiv for the first time as Washington renewed its peace efforts, following talks with Vladimir Putin in Moscow. Witkoff said "substantive progress was made" during the visits, "including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks".

articles.title: Korea’s Hanwha brings lasers and drones to Poland’s biggest defense show
articles.body:
- Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems are showcasing air defense, laser weapons, unmanned systems and artillery at MSPO 2026 in Poland, building on a partnership dating to 2014.
- Hanwha is pursuing a third K9 howitzer contract with Poland while already building Chunmoo missiles at a new Polish facility under a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December.
South Korea’s Hanwha Aerospace and Hanwha Systems opened a joint exhibit at MSPO 2026 in Kielce, Poland, on September 8, presenting an expanded lineup of air defense, unmanned and artillery systems built around the company’s decade-long defense partnership with Warsaw.
The two companies are sharing a stand at the exhibition, which runs through September 11, under the slogan “Proven Partnership. Strategic Capabilities. Sovereign Defence.” Hanwha’s relationship with Poland dates back to 2014, when its K9 chassis was selected for the Polish Krab self-propelled howitzer, and has since expanded through the K9 howitzer program and the Chunmoo rocket launcher system, known in Poland as Homar-K.
The company’s newest offerings center on layered air defense. Hanwha is showing its L-SAM long-range surface-to-air missile launcher, the H-SHORAD short-range air defense system, the H-Shield counter-drone system, and a 40mm wheeled counter-UAS vehicle, all designed to link into Hanwha Systems’ command-and-control network alongside interceptor drones. Hanwha Systems is also displaying Cheon gwang, South Korea’s first operational laser weapon system, along with a 50-kilowatt laser mounted on an armored vehicle and a smaller 20-kilowatt tactical laser vehicle. The company says each laser shot costs roughly 2,000 South Korean won, or about $1.50, and can down a small drone within seconds.
On the ground, Hanwha is presenting its manned-unmanned teaming concept through a display combining the K9A1 howitzer with an unmanned rocket launcher and its H-UGV ground vehicle, an arrangement where the crewed howitzer provides firepower while unmanned systems handle reconnaissance and maneuver, keeping soldiers farther from direct fire. The stand also includes the export version of the K-NIFV infantry fighting vehicle and an active protection system meant to improve vehicle survivability. In the naval domain, Hanwha is showing unmanned surface vessels built for Baltic Sea operations, including the Striker-S, which pairs an unmanned boat with a Chunmoo rocket launcher.
Hanwha is also exhibiting the upgraded K9A2 howitzer alongside a new 155mm ammunition package that includes a trajectory-correcting fuze and a modular propellant charge system intended to improve accuracy. The company is pursuing a third execution contract with Poland for K9 howitzers, a follow-on to earlier deals that have made Poland one of the largest operators of the K9 family. Hanwha’s existing Homar-K contracts with Poland include a roughly $4 billion deal signed in December, covering Chunmoo CGR-080 guided missiles to be built at a dedicated production facility inside Poland, with deliveries beginning in 2030, part of a broader push to localize Korean weapons manufacturing on Polish soil. Hanwha is displaying four Chunmoo guided rocket variants at MSPO alongside maintenance tools including a predictive health-monitoring system and a K9 turret simulator.
On September 9, Hanwha Systems plans to publicly demonstrate a satellite-imagery analysis system for the first time, using artificial intelligence to process electro-optical, infrared and synthetic aperture radar imagery from satellites currently in operation, aiming to automate object detection and flag unusual activity for military analysts.
“Hanwha is proud to be a trusted defense and industrial partner in Poland,” said Jacek Cyrek, CEO of Hanwha Aerospace Europe. “At MSPO 2026, we are expanding our local footprint into air defense, MUM-T, and space AI, building true defense sovereignty and industrial capability together on Polish soil.”

articles.title: Ukrainian AI company after NATO competition: effectiveness of strikes on Russian airfields could increase tenfold
articles.body:
Ukrainian AI company after NATO competition: effectiveness of strikes on Russian airfields could increase tenfold
In a comment to Ukrinform, the company’s head, who uses the call sign Wild Cat, said the solution presented at the NATO competition would make strikes on enemy airfields many times more effective, as it represents an entirely new technological level.
“In short, our development is artificial intelligence for making the destruction of enemy airfields ten times more effective. It involves precision targeting of airfields, and the solution can be used both on UAVs and missiles,” the company head said.
He explained that Russia should not be underestimated, as it has one of the world’s best air defense systems, combined with one of the world’s best electronic warfare systems, which makes it considerably more difficult for Ukrainian forces to strike its airfields.
“Essentially, we are dealing with the protection of military airfields at a level that may not exist anywhere else in the world. Despite this, Ukraine is managing to effectively ‘reach’ Russian aircraft and helicopters at their airfields, both in Crimea and deep inside their territory,” Wild Cat said. At the same time, he believes that introducing the new development “will fundamentally change this situation.”
Read also: Ukrainian Forces Test New Robotic Turrets with Machine Guns on the Front Line
“This will help Ukraine significantly improve the effectiveness of strikes on enemy airfields,” the head of the Ukrainian company emphasized.
He noted that he had expected to win NATO’s Innovation Competition because he benchmarks his company against its main competitors in Ukraine and around the world, including the U.S. company Palantir Technologies, which develops artificial intelligence, including for Hornet “middle-strike” drones, “with which the Ukrainian side is currently wreaking havoc on the enemy’s logistics.”
According to him, Palantir remains stronger in the logistics sector, but the Ukrainian development has an advantage in airspace protection and operations against enemy airfields.
The company head said that winning the NATO competition represents recognition of the Ukrainian company’s solutions at the Alliance level.
“We are the only Ukrainian company to have won this competition. This means that our solution has been recognized as the best in this field across the Alliance. We are being invited to take part in further testing and trials, with the prospect of implementing our solutions at the NATO level. This is a huge boost for the company’s development and integration into the Alliance’s defense system,” he emphasized.
The head added that the company had been developing its technology since 2022 and had since collected, in his assessment, globally unique databases for training its artificial intelligence.
“No one else in the Western world has anything like this. And training data accounts for more than half of success,” the head of the Ukrainian AI company said.
Read also: Ukraine and Britain Sign Historic Artificial Intelligence Agreement
Wild Cat said that during the event, the company had also reached cooperation agreements with several other partners, including an agreement on joint production with a foreign company, as well as cooperation with a Ukrainian manufacturer. He added that since the company develops exclusively software modules, practical implementation of the solution requires cooperation with manufacturers of drones or missile systems.
The company head also said that a presentation of the solution at a training range was scheduled to take place within several weeks as part of an exercise. The next steps will include flight and combat trials, followed by the production of a small batch to identify shortcomings under real operating conditions, and only later full-scale production. According to the company head’s preliminary estimates, it should take between six and eighteen months for the development to enter combat use.
Regarding the financial prize in NATO’s Innovation Competition—the three winning companies will receive a total of €250,000—Wild Cat said it amounts to approximately 5–7% of the project’s current costs. However, he said the main value of the victory was not financial but reputational, providing an argument for potential investors and partners.
Assessing the development’s potential impact on the course of hostilities, the company head described it as “an ongoing confrontation between means and countermeasures.”
“We are now considering what the war will look like in two or three years. To some extent, we are already anticipating how the Russians will protect their airfields in the future—for example, they are already actively building bunkers for aircraft. We are developing the solution so that even these bunkers will not help them,” he emphasized.
The head of the AI company added that it had been working on strikes against enemy airfields since 2022, and that the current development takes into account its previous experience and the countermeasures Russia has attempted to use to reduce the effectiveness of Ukrainian attacks.
As previously reported by Ukrinform, NATO’s 19th Innovation Competition, organized by NATO’s Allied Command Transformation (ACT) and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC), focused on persistent airfield denial . The Persistent Airfield Denial competition sought innovative technologies capable not only of damaging a military airfield but also of making it difficult for the enemy to restore its operations for an extended period.
The Ukrainian company took third place with an artificial intelligence-based solution for autonomous control of unmanned aerial vehicles. The technology enables operation without a constant connection to an operator, as well as the use of autonomous navigation and target recognition.
First place in the competition went to Czech company LPP Holding, which presented an autonomous long-range unmanned system capable of operating in conditions of active electronic warfare and without GPS navigation.
Second place went to Polish company Supercluster with its StratoAIM concept. The development involves using high-altitude balloons to launch autonomous gliding systems.

articles.title: Defense Forces neutralize 175 targets overnight, including 2 ballistic, 31 cruise missiles
articles.body:
Ukraine's Defense Forces overnight into Tuesday, from 18:00 to 08:30, neutralized 175 enemy targets, including two ballistic missiles and 31 out of 32 cruise missiles; however, following the results of the night, missile and strike UAV impacts were recorded at 29 locations, the press service of the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine reported.
"According to preliminary data, as of 08:30, air defense shot down/suppressed 175 targets: 2 Iskander-M/KN-23/S-400/Onyx ballistic missiles; 31 Kh-101/Iskander-K cruise missiles; 142 enemy UAVs of the Shahed, Gerbera, and other drone types," reads the report by the Air Force of the Armed Forces of Ukraine on Telegram on Tuesday.
It is noted that the main directions of the attack were Odesa and Kyiv regions. Impacts of Russian missiles and strike UAVs were recorded at 29 locations, with falling debris from intercepted targets recorded at 9 locations.
The Air Force reported that the enemy attacked Ukraine with Onyx anti-ship missiles (from Bryansk, Kursk regions of Russia and occupied Crimea) and Iskander-M/S-400/KN-23 ballistic missiles (from Bryansk, Voronezh regions of Russia). The exact number of missiles for these types was not specified.
According to the Air Force, Ukraine was also attacked by 32 air-launched Kh-101 cruise missiles from Vologda region of Russia; 166 strike UAVs of the Shahed type (more than half of them jet-powered) and "Parodiya" decoy drones launched from Orel, Primorsko-Akhtarsk (Russia), occupied Donetsk, and Hvardiyske (occupied Crimea).
The air attack was repelled by aviation, anti-aircraft missile units, EW and unmanned systems units, and mobile fire groups of the Defense Forces of Ukraine.

articles.title: Russian ballistic missiles hit Kyiv as US envoys leave
articles.body:
Russia hits Kyiv after brief pause for US envoys' visit, killing two
Sept 8 - Russia pummelled Kyiv with drones and missiles early on Tuesday, resuming its air attacks after a brief halt for the visit of U.S. peace negotiators, killing two people and triggering fires across the Ukrainian capital.
Mayor Vitali Klitschko said 10 more had been injured in the city, while falling debris in one district caused fires at a five-storey apartment building and a three-storey residential block.
The attack damaged at least 14 high-rise buildings, a dorm, a school, a clinic, warehouses and other sites, officials said.
BRIEF RESPITE IN ATTACKS
Russia resumed its attacks after U.S. peace envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff left Kyiv following a meeting with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy on Sunday, as the Trump administration renewed its push to end Russia's 4-1/2-year war in Ukraine.
They arrived from talks in Moscow, after which the Kremlin said it did not rule out the resumption of the three-way negotiations.
"The moment the U.S. president's peace envoys left, (Russian President Vladimir) Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv," Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on X.
"His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy," Sybiha said, urging allies to ramp up pressure on Moscow, as well as to provide interceptors to down ballistic missiles, since Kyiv's stocks of these run critically low.
Prior to the talks, Russia stepped up air attacks on Kyiv and nearby areas to nearly round-the-clock for several days, rather than mainly at night, using faster jet-propelled drones that killed residents and disrupted activities.
The Russian defence ministry said Moscow hit military and logistic targets in Kyiv and the surrounding region, as well as in the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk, Russian newswires said.
POLAND ACTIVATES AIRCRAFT
Amid explosions heard in Kyiv, neighbouring Poland, a NATO and European Union member, launched preventive operations against Russian missile attacks on Ukraine, the Polish army said.
Poland's Lublin airport has temporarily suspended flights because of the military operations.
In Russia, Ukrainian drones damaged civilian infrastructure and injured people in the Volga river city of Saratov, some 730 km (450 miles) southeast of Moscow, the regional governor said.
The area is home to a large oil refinery run by state oil company Rosneft, as well as other industrial and military facilities. REUTERS

articles.title: Ukraine shows a home-built missile designed to hit ballistic targets for the first time, the Koral, at Poland’s MSPO
articles.body:
Ukraine has shown off, for the first time, a home-built missile designed to shoot down ballistic targets. The Koral surface-to-air missile appeared at the MSPO defense expo in Poland, in an Ukroboronprom image showing a launch from a self-propelled launcher on a Czech Tatra truck chassis, Militarnyi reports.
It is unclear what is meant by “ballistic targets.” Russia has a wide range of ballistic weapons, from Iskander ballistic missiles to Kinzhal air-launched ballistic missiles.
More broadly, the term “ballistic target” can refer to an object following a ballistic trajectory after the powered phase of its flight has ended, with its subsequent motion governed primarily by gravity and aerodynamic drag. This category can also include rockets fired by multiple-launch rocket systems (MLRS), such as the Grad and Smerch.
Evolution of the Koral
The missile weighs 450 kg, including a 36-kg warhead. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, radio correction, and an active radar homing seeker. The missile is 4.8 meters long and has a diameter of 230/300 mm.
At the initial stage, the “Koral” was advertised with significantly more modest specifications: an engagement range of up to 30 km, an engagement altitude of up to 10 km, a weight of around 300 kg, and a 25-kg warhead. The missile was 4.33 meters long and had a diameter of 230/260 mm. At the same time, the designers emphasized that the specific specifications could vary depending on the customer’s requirements.
History of the developement
Development of the “Koral” began as early as 2016. Initially, the project was conceived as part of a ship-based surface-to-air missile system. In 2021, the Luch State Design Bureau unveiled a full-scale mock-up of the missile for the first time at the “Arms and Security” exhibition.
At the time, the “Koral” was presented as a unified, modular missile for both land-based and shipborne SAM systems, with potential applications as an air-to-air missile as well.

articles.title: The least free place on earth: Occupied Ukraine
articles.body:
People play chess in a park in front of a sculpture reading "Russian Spring" in the Russian-occupied Crimean city of Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | AFP via Getty Images
No political rights. No freedom of expression. No protection from secret detention without access to family, an attorney or a physician. No protection from deportation.
Welcome to Russia-occupied Ukraine.
For the second year running, U.S.-based democracy tracker Freedom House has listed Ukraine’s occupied eastern and southern territories as the most unfree places in the world — outranking South Sudan, North Korea and the Gaza Strip.
Advertisement
Inhabitants here are subject to repressive Russian legislation, including forcibly imposed citizenship and the use of antiterrorism laws against political dissidents and religious minority groups, Freedom House says. And it is this system of surveillance, repression, indoctrination and statetheft that pushes occupied Ukraine to the top of the list.
Discriminatory policies publicly encoded in Russian law permeate every aspect of residents’ lives — measures that appear to be changing the region’s demographics. Russia is “deliberately changing the ethnic composition so as to destroy a culture or tip the political balance in favor of another group,” the report notes.
International humanitarian law forbids any occupying power from introducing permanent changes to territories it occupies, particularly in demographic, social and economic domains. But Moscow claims these areas are not occupied — they are simply a part of Russia, and therefore subject to Russian law.
“This occupation is one of the most well-documented systems of repression, oppression and human rights violations because so much is put on the public record,” said Danielle Bell, head of the U.N. Human Rights Monitoring Mission to Ukraine. “This is a systemic approach to restricting people’s rights and fundamental freedoms.”
The regime has “all the signs of cultural genocide,” said journalist Andrii Dikhtiarenko, a native of now-occupied eastern Ukraine.
Advertisement
From passportization to deportation
Starting from 2014, Russia has occupied about 20 percent of Ukraine in the country’s south and east — land Moscow calls “new historical territories.” And one of the processes aiding the Russification of these areas is passportization.
By officially designating Ukrainians living in Russia-occupied territories as “foreigners,” occupation authorities compel them to obtain Russian citizenship — which they can do through simplified procedures — in order to access essential rights, such as health care, social services, employment or property ownership.
For Liudmila Chub, it all began with her job. Speaking to POLITICO, Chub said that in 2023, she was told by her employer in Melitopol — located in the occupied Kherson region — that she had to obtain a Russian passport to keep working in his shop, or he would be fined. Chub went to the passport office, where she recorded an angry video about being forced to get a “chicken passport” — a dig at the two-headed Russian eagle emblem. The office’s security guard marched her straight to the occupation police.
A man waits for documentation to apply for a new Russian passport at a center in Melitopol in the Zaporizhzhia region in August 2022. | AFP via Getty Images
Chub spent the next eight months in detention in Kherson, with the courts regularly extending her arrest, alleging she was breaking military curfew. She was eventually given a statement to read out on camera, saying she did not want to live in Russia, then was allowed 15 minutes to collect items from her apartment and transported under armed guard to Russia’s border with Georgia.
Deported from the home she lived in her whole life, Chub still considers herself fortunate. She said others she encountered in prison had gone through the process of obtaining Russian citizenship only to be charged with spying or treason under Russian law, which carries huge sentences.
“They tie this passport to you, and then with it, they make you traitors to their country,” she said. “Everything in me was opposed to getting that passport, and it’s lucky I didn’t get it. That saved me.”
Advertisement
HRMMU has so far documented over 400 such detentions involving treason- and espionage-related charges in Russia-occupied territories, but it’s impossible to track numbers for incommunicado detention.
That is what happened to 59-year-old IT specialist Serhii Gryshchenkov from Sevastopol in occupied Crimea. After Russian security forces took him from his home in May 2025, Gryshchenkov’s family was unable to find out where he was, his daughter Darina told POLITICO. Her father, who did not hide his pro-Ukraine position, was held incommunicado and tortured for a year before eventually being charged with treason in June 2026, she said. The family does not know the details of the charges.
According to Darina, when her father reappeared in pretrial prison, he spoke of fellow prisoners who were still being secretly held after three or four years. “Their relatives don’t even know whether they are alive.”
One strategy encouraging demographic change in Ukraine’s occupied territories is the official confiscation of homes belonging to residents who fled the war, ensuring they cannot return.
Ukrainians who try to comply with this new rule and travel back home have fallen afoul of Russian “filtration,” faced with arrests and entry bans at Moscow’s Sheremetevo airport — the only possible entry point to get to occupied territories, as land borders are closed to them.
Journalist Olena — who was granted anonymity over security concerns regarding her relatives living under occupation — told POLITICO she had fled occupied Donetsk with her family in 2014. Helped by a sympathetic condominium manager, she had paid the utility bills for her own and her parents’ apartments for the next 12 years, hoping one day they could come home.
Later, Olena found out via occupation media that she had been publicly blacklisted as an “enemy.” Meanwhile, an acquaintance of hers was served a 50-year entry ban at Sheremetevo when trying to get back to her home in occupied Ukraine.
People dance at an outdoor bar in Sevastopol on July 22, 2026. | Igor Ivanko/AFP via Getty Images
With this new law, “nothing can help us,” said Olena.
According to HRMMU monitoring, more than 60,000 private properties in occupied Ukraine have been identified as “ownerless” as of July this year. At least 6,500 of those properties have been expropriated, often given to veterans of Russia’s “special military operation” or sold to immigrants from Russia under preferential terms.
The effect of this has heavily impacted education in the region, with the introduction of a militarized Russian curriculum in schools. New textbooks teach the Kremlin’s official narrative that the occupied regions never supported Ukrainian independence and were always Russian. Parents who refuse to enroll their children in these schools, or enroll them in online Ukrainian education, are fined and threatened with losing parental rights.
These educational institutions can sometimes funnel students straight into the Russian armed forces. Once an individual holds a Russian passport — which the enforced system makes almost impossible to survive without — they can be drafted to fight against Ukraine. A practice that, like deportation, is explicitly prohibited by the Geneva Conventions.
The cumulative effect of all these measures has been the eradication of visible expressions of Ukrainian identity and wider dissent, said journalist Dikhtiarenko. “People who want to survive have to accept the rules of the game.”
Over at HRMMU, Bell’s worst fear is that the world will stop hearing about or noticing these violations. “When the climate becomes that coercive and that restrictive, and people are that silenced, that’s when we stop seeing the reports because people stop daring to speak out,” she said.
As more time passes, some inhabitants wonder whether there will be anything Ukrainian left, even if their home ever comes back under Kyiv’s control. However, despite their enforced Russian citizenship, Dikhtiarenko said the majority of residents still hold on to their Ukrainian passports, hiding them under floorboards or buried in the garden.

articles.title: Ukraine Unveils Koral Air Defense Missile Launcher for First Time
articles.body:
Ukraine unveiled a self-propelled launcher for its Koral surface-to-air missile for the first time Tuesday at the MSPO international defense exhibition in Poland.
An image released by Ukraine’s state-owned defense conglomerate Ukroboronprom showed a missile being launched from a mobile system mounted on the chassis of a Czech-made Tatra truck.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
According to Ukrainian military news outlet Militarnyi, the Koral missile which is reportedly compatible with launchers used by the S-300 and Patriot missile system, is designed to intercept aerial and ballistic targets as part of an air defense system, according to information presented by the developer.
In exceptional circumstances, it could also be used against radar-visible targets on land or at sea. The missile weighs 450 kilograms (992 pounds), including a 36-kilogram (79-pound) warhead. Its guidance system combines inertial navigation, radio-command updates and an active radar-homing seeker.
The missile is 4.8 meters (15.7 feet) long and has a diameter of 230-300 millimeters (9-12 inches). Its wingspan is 835 millimeters (33 inches), while its control surfaces span 685 millimeters (27 inches).
Development work on the Koral project began in 2016. Documents from that period described the missile as part of a planned ship-based surface-to-air missile system.
The project became more widely known in 2021, when Ukraine’s Luch Design Bureau presented a full-size model of the missile at the Arms and Security defense exhibition.
Zelensky Offers Presidential Plane for Witkoff and Kushner’s Next Kyiv Visit
At the time, Koral was described as a modular missile that could potentially be used with both land- and ship-based air defense systems. Developers also considered adapting it for use as an air-to-air missile.
The initial version had more limited stated specifications. It was expected to have a range of up to 30 kilometers (19 miles), an interception altitude of up to 10 kilometers (6 miles), a total weight of about 300 kilograms (660 pounds) and a 25-kilogram (55-pound) warhead.
The earlier design was 4.33 meters (14 feet) long and had a diameter of 230-260 millimeters (9-10 inches). Developers said the specifications could change depending on customer requirements.

articles.title: Brussels cleared Ukraine to spend EU loan money on American Patriot missiles for the coming winter of Russian attacks
articles.body:
The European Commission has approved Ukraine's request to buy US-made Patriot interceptor missiles with money from the European Union's €90 billion ($105 billion) loan, an EU official told Suspilne. Kyiv filed the application four days earlier and asked for more than €2 billion ($2.3 billion). The decision settles who pays, not when the missiles arrive.
Brussels signed off four days after the request
Ukraine submitted the application on 3 September under the Ukraine Support Loan program. The Commission said at the time it was working to clear it in the shortest possible period.
Kyiv asked for the money to buy interceptors, and it falls under the EU credit line for 2026 and 2027. That sum can buy anywhere from about 190 to 580 interceptors, depending on the price Washington sets.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop
What the €90 billion covers
The European Council decided to create the loan in December 2025, and the Council of the EU finalized the financing mechanism in April 2026. Hungary's veto held the package up for months before it cleared, and Ukraine's parliament then accepted a wartime tax overhaul to unlock the first tranche.
About €30 billion ($35 billion) of the total goes to economic support and €60 billion ($70 billion) to military needs and defense capabilities. The EU raises the money by borrowing on international capital markets against guarantees from its own budget.
Why European money buys American missiles
The military half of the program funds arms purchases, Ukrainian and European defense industry in particular. It also allows purchases outside the bloc when European producers cannot supply enough of what Ukraine needs.
On 6 August the Commission confirmed Ukraine may use loan money for interceptors, noting that Kyiv defines its own requirements and files the applications. That opened the door to non-European weapons. Nothing in Ukraine's inventory stops Russian ballistic missiles without Patriot interceptors, as Russia showed in August by hitting Kyiv and the Boryspil airport hub twice inside a day.
Ukraine's interceptor arithmetic
Zelenskyy has said Ukraine agreed with the US on monthly interceptor deliveries, while calling the volumes short of what the country needs. He put the winter requirement at no less than about 5% of American output of these missiles.
A shortage of allied Patriot missiles, combined with heavier Russian strikes, made July the deadliest month for Ukrainian civilians since April 2022, according to UN figures.

articles.title: Ukrainian engine for “Bars” missile-drone passes final tests
articles.body:
Ukraine has developed its own jet-powered drone, as the arms race is pushing Kyiv to produce answers to Russia's new fast Banderol and Geran-3 drones. Ukraine's “Bars” missile-drones currently consist of more than 74% Ukrainian-made components, but their turbojet engines are still imported, the developer of the “Bars” missile-drones said in an interview with RBC-Ukraine on 7 September.
The “Bars” jet-powered drone can carry out strikes at a range of up to 1,000 km, and the team plans to increase its range in the future, the developer said in the interview. To speed up and increase production of such drones for the Ukrainian army, the team is trying to make the jet-powered drone consist of as many domestically produced parts as possible. This will remove the limitation on how many such jet-powered drones Ukraine can produce and deploy in response to Russia’s use of similar drones against Ukrainian cities.
“Without exaggeration, we source them from all over the world,” the Bars developer said in the interview about the imported engines.
The UAV strikes the Russian army both in occupied territories and deep inside Russia
The developer calls Bars a missile-drone: it resembles a missile because it has a jet engine, and a drone because it can be controlled by a pilot.
The basic characteristics of Bars include a warhead weighing up to 60 kilograms, a range of up to 1,000 kilometers, and a speed of more than 700 kilometers per hour, the developer added. He also explained that the UAV’s system is a modular platform that allows the drone to be used “in different planes.”
“Our basic modularity allowed ‘Bars’ to receive three main categories of use: DeepStrike, ‘middle-strike,’ and ‘front-strike,’” the developer said in the interview.
He also said that there have been more than 40 “engineering officially” modifications and iterations of the UAV alone.
A Bars production facility is already in Europe and will begin operating in early September
The first batch of Bars drones is planned to be delivered as early as 10 October, according to the interview.
“As of today, the only limitation to scaling up the production of ‘Bars’ is the so-called ‘bottleneck,’ and it is not so much the volumes as the delivery times of turbojet engines,” the developer said.
It was previously reported that Ukraine and Germany had signed an agreement on the joint production of Bars drones. Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said this on 8 July 2026. He said that at the first stage of the project, Germany would finance the production, while all manufactured UAVs would be transferred to the Armed Forces of Ukraine.
