articles.title: EU pursues closer Israel ties on air defense and space
articles.body:
BRUSSELS — The EU is looking to Israel to support its new push for high-tech air defense and space capabilities.
Israel Space Agency boss Shimrit Maman this week traveled to Brussels where she met Tuesday with Ekaterina Zaharieva, European commissioner for startups, research and innovation for talks on key areas like AI and robotics.
The visit comes before Commission President Ursula von der Leyen gives her first major speech on space at a summit in Paris on Thursday, where she is expected to warn of growing hostilities and the need for Europe to step up its presence in space.
Advertisement
"It's very hard to do things on your own," Maman told POLITICO, warning that the militarization of space "is already happening — we just don't realize how much" and that Israel is seeing more interest from allies in "dual-use" technology for both civilian and defense purposes.
"One of the things we are working on is early warning systems," she said. "We saw that very nicely in the last round [of missile strikes] we had with Iran, for example. How we are managing to get [warnings to] all the civilians in Israel and not have that many casualties. That's part of that system. We are working on that very wide look that you're able to warn in advance, have that system warn the citizens."
A string of recent deals have seen the EU pursue closer military and technological relations with Israel, after several years of effective disengagement as a result of political tensions that have followed the war in Gaza. However, competition from Washington and strategic rivalries with Moscow and Beijing have created a need for allies with advanced industrial capabilities.
In 2024, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen backed calls from Polish and Greek Prime Ministers Donald Tusk and Kyriakos Mitsotakis to create an EU-funded air defense shield.
However, three senior officials involved in the discussions told POLITICO the plans did not move ahead after the Commission and a handful of capitals concluded it would need to rely on Israeli air-defense technology, which they deemed too sensitive a year into the Gaza conflict.
Now though, in a major expansion of its operations in Europe, Israeli firm Rafael Advanced Defense Systems confirmed Monday that it will open a factory producing its Iron Dome air-defense system in a former Volkswagen factory in Germany. One week ago, Greece struck a €3 billion deal with Israel’s Defense Ministry to build a new multilayered air defense network designed to take down drones, hostile jets and rockets.
Advertisement
"We see that convergence of everything, of that multi-layer defense approach," said Maman, pointing to satellite imaging and AI modeling as a key focus for joint development.
"I don't treat only defense as ballistic missiles from Iran ... think about a fire or a flash flood or even a prolonged drought ... we have a proven track record and we do have very good results," she said.
Antoaneta Roussi, Jordyn Dahl, Chris Lunday and Romanus Otte contributed to this report.

articles.title: Russia is preparing to test ballistic missiles with a range of 800 km and may attack targets in western Ukraine — the HUR
articles.body:
Russia is preparing to test ballistic missiles with a range of 800 km and may attack targets in western Ukraine — the HUR
Kyiv • UNN
Russia plans to test new ballistic missiles with a range of up to 800 km by the end of the year. The HUR does not rule out strikes on western Ukraine.
Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers. This was stated by Deputy Chief of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine, Major General Vadym Skibitskyi, who added that the enemy may attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine, UNN reports, citing the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine.
Details
As Skibitskyi said at a meeting of the Ukraine-NATO Interparliamentary Council, the aggressor state of Russia is increasing the intensity of missile and drone strikes against Ukraine in order to provoke a socioeconomic crisis. To this end, Moscow seeks to increase ballistic missile production and extend the range of these weapons.
"According to our estimates, by the end of this year, Russia plans to conduct final tests of a new type of ballistic missile with a range of up to 800 kilometers," Skibitskyi said.
He clarified that during these ballistic missile tests, the Russians may attempt to strike targets in western Ukraine.
Russia's aggressive plans also include blockading the Black Sea and attempting to draw Belarus into the war against Ukraine and into hybrid operations against NATO.
"As of today, we do not see any real indicators of preparations for strike groupings, specifically, on the territory of Belarus, but we remember January-February 2022. [...] The key factor restraining Belarus is internal risks, limited military capabilities, and potential economic problems. At the same time, according to our estimates, we consider it quite likely that Belarus will continue to support [Russian] hybrid measures by providing its own territory to create pressure on the border with NATO states and increase the intensity of information and psychological operations," the major general noted.
Skibitskyi emphasized that Russia poses a threat both to Ukraine and to Europe, and also thanked the partners for their support in the war for freedom. The representative of the Defence Intelligence of Ukraine called for increased sanctions pressure on Moscow in order to finally deprive the aggressor of foreign components, particularly for long-range weapons with which the aggressor kills and terrorizes Ukrainians.

articles.title: Russia resumes deadly strikes on Kyiv after pause for Trump envoys’ visit
articles.body:
Russia resumes deadly strikes on Kyiv after pause for Trump envoys’ visit
Explosions rock Ukrainian capital after expiration of a three-day halt for Witkoff and Kushner visit
Russian missiles and drones pounded Kyiv overnight, killing two people and sending smoke billowing above the Ukrainian capital, ending Moscow’s temporary halt to strikes on the city.
Russian President Vladimir Putin had ordered the pause in attacks as US President Donald Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited the Russian and Ukrainian capitals at the weekend.
Fresh explosions early Tuesday triggered fires and sent locals down into basements and metro stations for shelter.
“The moment the US president’s peace envoys left, Putin launched another massive, horrific attack against Kyiv, damaging residential areas and killing at least two people,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andriy Sybiga said on social media.
“His ballistic missiles speak louder than his words on diplomacy.”
Witkoff and Kushner’s trips provided no immediate breakthrough in ending the four-and-a-half-year war, but represented Washington’s re-engagement with trying to broker a deal between the two sides, which had been on hold for months.

articles.title: Zelenskyy says US exploring steps to de-escalate Russia-Ukraine war as Russian attacks continue
articles.body:
The US is exploring possible steps for Ukraine and Russia to de-escalate the war during the winter while restarting negotiations toward a broader peace agreement, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy told the Axios news site, as Russia resumed strikes on Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said on Monday that the weeks ahead could provide an opportunity for diplomacy, arguing that Russian President Vladimir Putin may be seeking to avoid antagonising US President Donald Trump ahead of US midterm elections.
"My feeling (is) that Putin needs Trump," he said. "He doesn't want ... to upset him."
Asked whether Putin might seek to give Trump a diplomatic achievement before the elections, Zelenskyy replied: "Yeah."
Zelenskyy met on Sunday in Kiev with Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner following their three-hour meeting with Putin in Moscow.
He said they conveyed that "the Russians are ready to negotiate," while noting, however, that Russia's battlefield actions and intensified attacks do not indicate a willingness to compromise.
Still, he said his understanding was that Putin is "ready to discuss" ideas aimed at advancing negotiations.
New proposals
Zelenskyy said the US team travelled to Moscow and Kiev primarily to "unblock" the diplomatic process and brought new proposals, including possible measures to reduce tensions ahead of and during winter.
"There are ideas around energy (facilities) and around grain (shipments), around electricity (facilities) and around oil and gas (exports). We have different interests, Russia and we," Zelenskyy said.
He said the emerging US approach appeared to involve both restarting negotiations and finding arrangements that could prevent a major escalation during winter, calling that interpretation "very close to the reality of these conversations."
The aim, he said, would be to identify steps "which can bring (the) sides closer to peace."
Zelenskyy said Washington also supports a separate winter assistance package for Ukraine involving air defence and energy support.
"It's not only about missiles," he said. "It's also about LNG (liquefied natural gas) ... and it's also about steps of de-escalation."
Zelenskyy said Kiev wants to use September and October to revive diplomacy, with the UN General Assembly in New York later this month potentially providing an opportunity for further US-Ukraine discussions. He also said another trilateral US-Ukraine-Russia meeting remained possible.
"We have this September, October to find any way to speak," he said. "Without dialogue … we will not have (a) result."
Russian attacks continue
Meanwhile, a series of "strong" explosions rang out in Kiev, AFP news agency journalists said early on Tuesday, as Russia resumed strikes on the Ukrainian capital after a three-day halt.
The explosions triggered car alarms in the city centre, the journalists said, after the Kiev city military declared an air raid alert.
In the wider Kiev region, the State Emergency Service said Russian forces launched drone strikes targeting Boryspil and Fastiv districts.
The attacks ignited fires at industrial enterprises in the Boryspil area, where a blaze destroyed seven trucks. Rescuers also responded to a logistics complex that was struck twice, successfully extinguishing all fires at the scene.
Kiev Mayor Vitali Klitschko confirmed that the capital was under a ballistic attack, calling for medics to the city's Solomianskyi district, No official information is currently available regarding deaths or injuries resulting from the attacks.

articles.title: RAM-2X Strike Drones Surpass 450 Target Engagements
articles.body:
Ukrainian company Ukrspecsystems has first publicly presented its new RAM-2X strike UAV, featuring an X-shaped wing configuration.
The system was officially unveiled at the international MSPO defense exhibition in Poland, according to Militarnyi.
The RAM-2X loitering munition operates at the operational-tactical level and has a range of up to 180 km. The UAV is designed to engage enemy targets and has an endurance of more than two hours.
The UAV is equipped with a warhead featuring a 2.7 kg or 3.5 kg explosively formed penetrator and supports the integration of artificial intelligence systems. The system features high automation and a flexible communications architecture.
The UAV can operate via multiple radio-frequency communication channels across different bands, as well as through a Starlink terminal. RAM-2X also supports a communications relay function, enabling it to be used with reconnaissance UAVs, including the SHARK-M.
Ударний дрон RAM-2X на MSPO 2026 pic.twitter.com/AHAu70xhxJ
— Владислав (@Vladislav110528) September 8, 2026
In this configuration, the reconnaissance UAV provides target designation and helps the strike UAV more effectively overcome electronic warfare (EW) systems. In addition, the system is designed for interoperability with the company’s previous-generation platforms.
“Each type of equipment has its own role, and every target requires an appropriate means of engagement. Following a comprehensive approach, we develop strike systems across several subclasses, built around common components, a shared ground control station, and unified software,” the company stated.
This allows operators of Ukrspecsystems reconnaissance complexes to add a strike capability without replacing their existing ground control stations or antennas.
The RAM-2X UAV is actively employed by the Defense Forces of Ukraine; however, the developer had previously remained undisclosed due to security considerations.
According to the manufacturer, RAM-series loitering munitions have now been credited with more than 450 target engagements.
Alongside the unveiling, Ukrspecsystems launched its own public “X-Archive,” featuring declassified footage of Ukrainian forces conducting combat operations. The initial collection includes footage documenting strikes against Russian air defense assets and radar stations.
The company removed all sensitive information that could compromise ongoing combat operations from the released footage. The company plans to publish the declassified strike footage in batches. At the same time, information on current operational sorties and ongoing UAV modifications remains classified.

articles.title: Streeting says UK ‘won’t flinch’ in support for Ukraine
articles.body:
Britain will provide £100 million towards the rapid delivery of additional air defence interceptors to Ukraine this winter, Defence Secretary Wes Streeting has announced.
Speaking at his first Ukraine Defence Contact Group meeting as Defence Secretary, Streeting said Kyiv had identified 300 Patriot missiles from partner stocks, 500 air-to-air interceptors with counter-cruise missile capability and $2 billion for drones among its immediate requirements.
He announced a £100 million British contribution through NATO’s mechanism for financing priority Ukrainian requirements, intended to support the rapid provision of additional air defence equipment before winter. Streeting also said military assistance would continue alongside diplomatic efforts towards an eventual settlement.
He said: “We know that this will only end through a negotiated peace. It’s really important that Russia understands that we won’t flinch in terms of our support for Ukraine as they continue to fight for their freedom and, for that matter, for ours.”
The Defence Secretary also provided an update on Britain’s existing commitment to provide 120,000 drones to Ukrainian forces during the year. More than 25,000 have so far been delivered, according to Streeting, with thousands more expected to arrive before winter. The systems cover several roles, including drones intended to intercept Russian unmanned aircraft, reconnaissance systems used to observe the battlefield and areas behind Russian lines, and attack drones.
Streeting said: “Those cover a whole range of capabilities that will help Ukraine to take the fight directly to Russia, defend itself by taking out Russian drones, and also to see what’s happening both on the battlefield and behind enemy lines.”
Britain is also continuing deliveries of large-calibre artillery ammunition. Streeting said the UK delivered its millionth round in July, with tens of thousands more expected to follow.
The additional ammunition is being provided with funding involving Britain, Germany, Denmark, Lithuania, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden. Streeting said continued support was intended to demonstrate to Moscow that the countries backing Kyiv would not withdraw their assistance while fighting and diplomatic activity continued in parallel.
He described the Government’s commitment to Ukraine as unshakable and said supporting Kyiv would remain a central priority in Britain’s work with allied defence ministers.

articles.title: Germany pledges more air defense missiles to Ukraine
articles.body:
Ayhan Simsek
08 September 2026•Update: 08 September 2026
German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius on Tuesday pledged more Patriot interceptors, AIM-9 missiles and IRIS-T air defense systems for Ukraine.
Speaking at a video meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group, Pistorius said Russian hybrid attacks would not stop Berlin or its partners from backing Kyiv, and Berlin will increase its support.
“Winter is coming. Preparing Ukraine for winter is of the highest priority,” he said. “It requires us to act resolutely and immediately. Together, we must take the right measures to increase Ukraine's resilience.”
Pistorius said he decided to provide Ukraine with the urgently needed Patriot PAC-2 interceptor missiles from the German military (Bundeswehr) stocks. He urged other contact-group members to check their own inventories and do the same.
“I am aware that it is not easy to strike a balance between one’s own security requirements and urgently needed support to Ukraine, but please, if in doubt, decide in favor for Ukraine,” he said.
Germany will also step up the supply of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles to Ukraine from Bundeswehr stockpiles, Pistorius said.
“What is more, we are keeping up our continuous deliveries of IRST air defense systems, including guided missiles,” he said. ”I am pleased that Ukraine is going to order several thousand additional IRST-guided missiles that will be funded by the EU-Ukraine Defense Loan.”
Pistorius said Germany will keep up its continuous deliveries of drones and long-range ammunition to help stabilize the front. Beyond the ongoing support, he said Berlin will fund several tens of thousands of rounds of long-range artillery ammunition. The ammunition will be procured through the British Artillery and Air Defense Consortium and provided to Ukraine.

articles.title: Russia opened an ancient tomb – and found a message for today
articles.body:
Russia opened an ancient tomb – and found a message for today
In the dim interior of Moscow’s Cathedral of the Archangel, a candle softly flickered. Russian President Vladimir Putin stood by an open white stone sarcophagus, made the Sign of the Cross, and bowed his head. Only a few inches remained between the Kremlin of the 21st century and an ancient Russian ruler who died more than 600 years ago. The Russian president called the uncovering of the relics a “miraculous discovery.”
Several weeks earlier, restorers had removed the sagging floor near the cathedral’s southern wall. The old stone lid, which was in danger of collapsing inward, was carefully lifted. Beneath the burial cloth lay the remains of Prince Dmitry Donskoy, a warrior prince canonized by the Orthodox Church and venerated in Russia as the holy savior of Rus’.
On August 18, Patriarch of Moscow and All Rus’ Kirill held a prayer service at the sarcophagus. Particles of the relics were placed in reliquaries for veneration by the faithful; one of them may be delivered to Russian troops at the front. Thus, the warrior prince who once led a united Russian army against the nation’s fiercest enemy will once again stand alongside the nation’s army, in a completely different era and war.
On September 6, one of those reliquaries was carried at the head of a major religious procession through Moscow. Led by Patriarch Kirill, the procession drew around 100,000 people and followed a 6.5-kilometer route from the Cathedral of Christ the Savior to Novodevichy Convent. More than six centuries after his death, Dmitry Donskoy once again led a procession through the Russian capital.
Grand Prince Dmitry Ivanovich of Moscow, better known as Dmitry Donskoy, is a fairly common example of a historical figure remembered by virtually all his compatriots, but known only to specialists outside his country. This 14th-century prince played a huge role in the history of Russia, which was then still known as Rus’. His contributions to the fate of Russia as a warrior and statesman were recognized during his lifetime, but after his death, Dmitry gradually became a symbolic figure of the struggle for independence.
The uncovering of his relics could hardly have remained only an ecclesiastical or archaeological event. Modern Russia once again speaks the language of sovereignty, unity, and resistance to an external adversary – the same concepts which national memory associates Dmitry Donskoy.
To understand why Dmitry Donskoy is venerated by Russians centuries later, we must return to where his name became history – the field between the Don and Nepryadva rivers on the morning of September 8, 1380.
An existential enemy
Despite Russia’s long and dramatic military history, it didn’t have many long-standing adversaries with whom it was forced to fight again and again. The list of Russia’s historical adversaries isn’t topped by Poland, Germany, or Türkiye, as one might expect from a brief look at Russian history. The most formidable enemy, one that called into question the very existence of the Russian people, was a state that no longer exists on the world map – the Golden Horde, one of the major powers into which Genghis Khan’s empire was divided after his death.
In 1237, the still formally united Mongol state began its great march westward. Rus’ was one of the countries that fell prey to the Mongols. From this moment on, an epic struggle began, encompassing several dozen wars, not to mention isolated raids and minor border conflicts. Until the second half of the 15th century, Rus’ remained a vassal state to the steppe kingdom.
Regular and heavy tribute payments served as the basis of this dependence. If the people of Rus’ attempted to avoid them, a punitive expedition would arrive, destroying everything in its path, after which the survivors would go back to paying tribute. Horde officials known as the ‘baskaks’ were responsible for its collection. As is usually the case, the baskaks abused their power and engaged in extortion. Whenever they overstepped the boundaries, another rebellion would break out, followed by a new punitive campaign.
The Mongols also skillfully manipulated the Russian princes. There was no single leader in Rus’ at the time, so the princes traveled to the khan’s headquarters to intrigue against each other, turning to the Mongols as arbiters. The winners of this vile contest received a ‘yarlyk’ or charter to rule, along with the obligation to pay tribute and support the Mongols against those attempting to shake off their rule. This period in Russia is still called “the yoke,” calling to mind the yoke meant for draft animals. It aptly describes the severity and humiliation of the situation in which Rus’ found itself for many years.
Everything comes to an end, however; and by the 14th century, the Golden Horde had plunged into a protracted crisis. The khans were more likely to slaughter one another due to intrigues than to wage war on their neighbors. The nomadic empire was weakening.
The rise of Moscow
Some Russian principalities freed themselves from the yoke, falling under the control of other states, primarily the young and dynamic Grand Duchy of Lithuania. Lithuania’s time as a great Eastern European power was short but brilliant. The western principalities of Rus’ gravitated toward the Grand Duchy of Lithuania; this is how the future country of Belarus began to take shape. In the eastern part of Rus’, however, the control of the Horde was more strict, and events took a different course.
In 1325, Ivan Kalita became Prince of Moscow. ‘Kalita’ is a nickname meaning ‘money bag’ as he was indeed a sort of bagman, an unscrupulous schemer who based his power on the flow of money. He managed to ‘sell’ himself to the Horde as the most loyal of the princes and, most importantly, persuaded the khans to entrust him with collecting tribute from all of Rus’.
Baskaks and other options involving Horde officials were not very convenient for the khan: firstly, baskaks sought to pocket the money for themselves; secondly, dealing with one prince was easier: tribute collection proceeded more smoothly, a specific person could be held accountable, and naturally, the Russian prince had a better understanding of the country’s inner workings than the Mongols.
In this case, ‘Mongols’ is a very loose term. The rulers of the Golden Horde were the Chinggisids, descendants of Genghis Khan, and indeed Mongol by origin. However, the Horde’s majority at the time were descendants of numerous nomadic peoples who inhabited the steppe belt stretching from present-day Ukraine to present-day Kazakhstan. In Russian tradition, they were collectively called Tatars. Modern Tatars living in the Russian Republic of Tatarstan and the Crimean Tatars are descendants of some branches of the former Horde, but the historical meaning of this word is much broader, and at various stages included all Muslim peoples south and east of Russia, right up to the peoples of the Caucasus Mountains. In Russian, the name Tatar-Mongols is often used to refer to the entire group of peoples of the Golden Horde.
Ivan Kalita’s position as a go-between was disreputable but highly lucrative. He profited from the cash flow but managed to strike a fine balance, avoiding further rebellions within Rus’ while satisfying the khan’s demands. His accounting tricks still allowed him to keep some of the money for himself. He also used his position to quietly undermine his rivals, particularly the powerful prince of Tver. Now a smaller city northwest of the modern capital, at the time Tver was a serious rival of Moscow.
By 1340, when Ivan Kalita died, Moscow had become the richest and most powerful principality in Rus’.
Kalita’s successors – his elder son Simeon and later his younger son Ivan – were not as cunning as he, but managed to preserve their father’s gains. The principality was supposed to be headed by Simeon’s heirs, but both Simeon and his sons fell victim to the plague. The cause of death of his younger son Ivan is unknown, but he was 33 years old at the time and may have fallen victim to the same disease. Be that as it may, in 1359 rule over the principality was formally passed on to a nine-year-old boy named Dmitry Ivanovich.
The birth of a legend
Dmitry Donskoy’s personality is almost buried beneath the legend surrounding him. Generations of chroniclers and writers have described the prince as a chivalrous man and a patriot with deep convictions. Such a person was of course supposed to be ideal, and Dmitry was characterized as exceptionally virtuous and wise beyond his years.
More specifically, we may add the following about his character: Dmitry was certainly a religious man, and his faith was sincere. His guardian was Metropolitan Alexei, an authoritative figure and a shrewd politician who played a huge role in Dmitry’s development and the preservation of the principality. Dmitry always had a warm relationship with the Orthodox Church, not least because of the positive influence of Metropolitan Alexei, the most important Orthodox hierarch of his time.
The second important factor was that, after his father’s death, Dmitry was thrown headlong into the brutal maelstrom of politics. He had to learn self-control and military skills literally from childhood. Lithuania pressed in from the west, vying with Moscow as a rallying point for the Russian principalities; the Horde pressed from the south; and the independent principalities were in a state of constant feudal competition. In short, it was the ‘normal’ reality of medieval life. Thus, from childhood, Dmitry was exposed to the harsh school of politics, intrigue, and war. Young Dmitry had to endure short but intense wars with Lithuania. Moreover, Regent Alexei could not protect Dmitry forever, and the latter was forced to negotiate with the Horde and participate in campaigns against other princes. Dmitry besieged Tver, which had long been a thorn in Moscow’s side, and forced Prince Mikhail of Tver to pledge his loyalty to him.
In 1375, Prince Dmitry, who was then 25 years of age, concluded a treaty with Tver. Prince Mikhail of Tver called himself Dmitry’s “younger brother” (behind this elegant formula was actually a vassal treaty) but from a historical perspective, the key to the treaty was the phrase “If God changes the Horde”: if Moscow fought the Horde, Tver was obliged to join the fight. Apparently, Dmitry earnestly hated the Horde and wanted to fight it. Such an opportunity soon presented itself.
The rebellious prince
The Horde was rocked by coups. Its de facto ruler was the military commander Mamai. In Russian tradition, Mamai is often referred to as a khan, but this is incorrect. He was a ‘beklarbek’, i.e., one of the top-ranking officials. However, this position afforded him powers almost equal to those of a khan. Mamai ruled the Horde like an ‘eminence grise’, outliving a dozen khans while hiding behind the back of the nominal ruler Muhammad Bulak. Mamai maintained his rule by means of poison, dagger, and intrigue. In 1363, it was Mamai who granted the charter to young Dmitry. However, in the 1370s, Dmitry, feeling powerful enough, refused to pay tribute to the Horde.
This was a bold challenge. At that time, the Horde seemed almost invincible to the Russians. Psychologically, someone had to finally stand up and say “No”, and the most powerful prince of eastern Rus’ did so. Dmitry convened a congress of princes who expressed their support for him.
This certainly meant war, but this was no longer a rebellion of isolated outcasts. Dmitry spoke on behalf of all Rus’. Not everyone was ready to support him, but Moscow was not alone; it could count on the support of different corners of a country which, though humiliated, was still alive.
The war began dismally: a Horde detachment managed to surprise and defeat a small Russian force on the Pyana River. The river’s name in Russian sounds similar to the word ‘drunk’ [pianaya] and alas, in this case, “nomen est omen”: the Mongols took the Russians by surprise when they were relaxing in their camp. After the defeat in the field battle, Nizhny Novgorod, a large city approximately 400 km east of Moscow was devastated. However, during the very next skirmish, on the Vozha River, things took a different turn. This time, Dmitry, who personally led the army, surprised the Mongols at the crossing and pushed their detachment into the water.
Mamai faced a serious problem. Rus’, which was seemingly subjugated long ago, now rebelled. Moreover, Mamai was in serious trouble: Khan Tokhtamysh, a protégé of the mighty Tamerlane, rose up against him. Mamai needed to act quickly and brutally.
Another punitive expedition was organized against Rus’. This time, Mamai, a contender for power in the Horde, led it himself. It was late summer 1380.
Preparing for battle
Mamai saw that this time, he would meet with significant resistance and focused on the political preparations for the campaign. He negotiated with the Grand Duke of Lithuania Jagiello. As a rival of Moscow, Jagiello saw advantage in weakening Dmitry. Prince Oleg, the leader of Ryazan, which bordered the Horde, took an ambiguous stance. A century and a half earlier, in 1237, Ryazan had fiercely resisted the invasion, but the city had been completely devastated, and its inhabitants had almost entirely perished. Now, the descendants of the few survivors did not want to get involved.
Prince Oleg demonstrated exceptional political flexibility, expressing loyalty to both sides but refusing to lend troops to either. Meanwhile, Dmitry was gathering troops – his own and those of his allies – in Kolomna, a city southeast of Moscow. He did not have the full might of Rus’ at his disposal, but commanded a considerably large force assembled from various principalities: his own domain, which included the cities of Moscow and Vladimir; detachments from Novgorod and Pskov; and his cousin’s forces from Serpukhov. Moreover, individual detachments arrived from Ryazan, despite Prince Oleg’s ambiguous stance, and there were also troops from the Rostov Principality, Nizhny Novgorod, Yaroslavl, Bryansk, and Starodub. Small groups even came from the Lithuanian Principality – these were the detachments of the exiled princes, Jagiello’s half-brothers.
Admittedly, these troops likely numbered about 10,000 men – which is not a staggering number. However, we should remember that we’re talking about the 14th century, and at the time, Rus’, though large, was a sparsely populated country and could not assemble huge armies.
To dispel the fog of war, watchmen – i.e., reconnaissance detachments – were sent ahead to the steppe border. The first detachment went into the steppe and disappeared; a second detachment had already been dispatched from Moscow to search for it when a scout from the first group emerged from the steppe. This was Vasily Tupik, whose group managed to kidnap Mamai’s confidant. The scouts forced him to provide information about the enemy’s whereabouts and plans. This information was so vital that the name of the soldier who obtained it was written down in the chronicles, and thus remained in history.
Dmitry did not march directly towards Mamai. Instead, he first made a surprise dash west. This was done to accomplish two goals. Firstly, along the way, he ‘picked up’ several units that hadn’t made it to the general assembly. Secondly, he created a convincing illusion that he was busy attacking Jagiello’s Lithuanian army. Jagiello, unwilling to engage in a pitched battle with the strong Russian army, slowed his march. So, by the time Dmitry turned back and embarked on the campaign against Mamai, it was hard for the Lithuanian prince to catch up. By the morning of September 8, Dmitry had crossed the Don River which separated him from the army of the Horde.
This was a very risky maneuver. The Don is a large river. In case of defeat, the Russian army would have been pushed towards the river and easily annihilated. However, Dmitry wanted to avoid lengthy maneuvers. Time wasn’t on his side: the threat of Jagiello’s Lithuanians in the rear was still present, and no one knew what Oleg of Ryazan was up to. Therefore, he had to defeat Mamai in open battle, and do it quickly.
Dmitry employed a good deal of imagination in planning the battle. Historically, the Mongols possessed highly maneuverable cavalry. Dmitry occupied a battlefield bordered by forests, rivers, and ravines on the flanks; this protected his army from encirclement. But the Horde didn’t yet know the biggest surprise. The weakest link in the Russian position was the left flank, positioned next to a large oak forest. But it was precisely here that Dmitry had an ace up his sleeve – a powerful detachment of heavy cavalry led by the experienced commander Bobrok. Bobrok was an old, experienced warrior with strong nerves, and his task was to carry out a surprise attack when the situation became critical.
Before the battle began, Dmitry exchanged armor with boyar Mikhail Brenk. It was a cruel decision: both Dmitry and Mikhail Brenk knew that the enemy would try to kill the man wearing the prince’s armor. But Dmitry needed freedom to move around the battlefield and issue commands. However, he also took care to issue detailed instructions to the commanders.
The battle began on the morning of September 8.
Kulikovo Field
The chronicle states that the battle began with a duel between two fighters. A warrior monk, Alexander Peresvet, rode out from the Russian side. A former warrior from Bryansk, he had retired to a monastery some time earlier, but left for the campaign against Mamai, with the full understanding and approval of the abbot. Peresvet encountered a steppe warrior, known as Chelubey in the chronicles. The name sounds Turkic, which is logical: Mamai’s main forces were composed of various Turkic peoples. According to the chronicle, both warriors struck each other with spears and died. Apparently, they engaged in a head-on clash, and neither turned away.
Mamai seized the initiative in the battle. Apparently, the steppe army had a numerical advantage, as the Russians spent almost the entire battle on the defensive.
The size of the armies that fought at Kulikovo Field is a matter of debate. The biggest estimates place the number of participants at 100,000-150,000 men on each side. This is highly questionable. Firstly, such a number of men is dramatically at odds with the logistical capabilities of the time. Considering that both armies consisted almost entirely of cavalry, 150,000 warriors would have required forage for at least 300,000 horses (main + spare horse for each warrior), which is absurd. Not to mention that such numbers of men would require supply by rail. Later, when Russian military bureaucracy allowed for more precise troop estimates, 100,000-man armies ‘disappeared’ from the accounts and were replaced by armies of standard European size, i.e., 10,000-20,000 fighters. Considering that not all principalities of Rus’ took part in the battle of Kulikovo, one must agree with those researchers who limit the number of participants to 10,000-15,000 warriors on each side.
The Horde launched a series of attacks in various areas. They persistently sought out weak points and fought in waves for several hours. Of course, we’re not talking about hours of nonstop fighting. Cavalry armies fought on both sides and the battle resembled a series of skirmishes. The detachments charged at each other, fought for several minutes, then dispersed, making way for fresh reserves.
The Advance Regiment was positioned ahead of the main body of the Russian army. Under the Horde’s attacks, it retreated toward the Grand Regiment, the main line of the Russian army. The right flank repelled all attacks and was in least danger. The center fought very hard, but stood firm and did not crumble. The battle raged past midday. Mikhail Brenk, who had exchanged armor with Dmitry, was killed in battle. The prince himself not only commanded the battle, but actively participated in it and was wounded. This had no effect on morale; everyone knew Prince Dmitry was somewhere among the fighting ranks, but his simple, unadorned armor made it difficult to know his exact whereabouts.
The left flank of the Russian army was in danger, however. This regiment was retreating and the princes that commanded it had perished in battle. A small reserve detachment came to its aid, but stabilized the situation only briefly. The Horde forded the narrow Smolka River and pushed the Russians further and further back. The battle had reached its climax; both armies suffered heavy losses and were terribly tired. However, the Horde army had inflicted serious damage on the Russians’ left flank and was about to move into the rear of their center.
That’s when Bobrok’s Ambush Regiment struck the Horde army.
The old commander had calculated the moment with perfect precision. He arrived when the enemy was already exhausted by the long, hard battle, but the Russian line of defense had not yet crumbled.
Fresh cavalry reserves are a terrifying force at the end of a major battle. After several hours of heavy fighting, the Horde army was hit from the flank as if struck by a train. The balance of power didn’t just shift: the Horde panicked. Now, instead of the Russian left flank, the Horde’s right flank began to crumble. Mamai had no reinforcements left, as he had thrown all his forces into battle.
Some time after the attack by the Ambush Regiment, the enemy wavered and began to scatter.
The pursuit of the Horde was led by Dmitry’s cousin, Prince Vladimir of Serpukhov. Mamai fled, and most of his army followed on exhausted horses. The Russians relentlessly pursued the enemy for about 30 kilometers.
The Russians suffered heavy losses. For several more days, the army stood “on the bones,” picking up the dead, nursing the wounded, and gathering all the weapons and equipment they could find.
Prince Dmitry was found among a pile of corpses. He was alive, but gravely wounded; his armor was mangled, and he was unconscious. He fought the most important battle of his life at the forefront of his warriors, with a war club in hand, and nearly paid for the victory with his life. Unfortunately, the chroniclers did not specify in what circumstances he was wounded, but the location where he was found speaks for itself: it was, of course, the left flank.
From that moment on, Prince Dmitry of Moscow would be known by the name that would become part of history: Dmitry Donskoy, i.e., Dmitry of the Don.
On September 14, the army turned back.
Afterword
The Battle of Kulikovo had a huge psychological impact. The Russian army routed the Horde in a proper pitched battle – it didn’t hide behind fortified walls, and didn’t just defeat a single detachment; it utterly destroyed the enemy’s main field army. This was not accomplished by any single principality but by a broad alliance. Men who had seen the backs of the fleeing Horde army with their own eyes returned to Nizhny Novgorod, Pskov, Novgorod, and Yaroslavl.
After the battle, the Lithuanian army quietly retreated home.
The struggle for independence did not end there, of course. After this defeat, Mamai lost the internal struggle in the Golden Horde to Khan Tokhtamysh, fled to Crimea, and was killed there. Tokhtamysh set about restoring the Horde’s former glory. In 1382, he launched a new campaign against Rus’, and this time succeeded in taking Moscow while Dmitry was gathering a field army. Dmitry, through gritted teeth, paid tribute for the previous two years (but not for the earlier years). However, the Battle of Kulikovo marked a new style of relations between Rus’ and the Horde. Tokhtamysh made no attempt to install anyone else as ruler of Moscow. The idea of independence and political unity took hold in Rus’, and Moscow clearly headed this process. The Russians were still paying tribute, but they already saw that they could seize the opportunity to avoid it. The gaps between payments grew wider and successful battles with the Horde became more frequent.
In 1395, Khan Tokhtamysh suffered a terrible defeat at the hands of Tamerlane, with whom he had fallen out. The Horde was falling apart and the Russians accelerated this process as best they could.
In 1389, Dmitry Donskoy died before reaching the age of 40. The cause of his early death is unknown. However, he left behind a powerful legacy: a large principality that became the leader in the unification of Rus’; a son who continued his policies; and, finally, the idea of a unified state that would never again lose its independence.
At the end of the 14th century, ‘Zadonshchina’ – a literary monument about the Battle of Kulikovo – was published.
In 1480, Ivan III formalized the complete political independence of Rus’; By this point, its dependence was more of a formality and Ivan III sealed the recognition of the new reality.
In 1783, Empress Catherine II annexed Crimea – the last fragment of the Golden Horde to be incorporated into Russia. The great conflict thus ended, and all debts were settled.

articles.title: Ukraine is sending its winning brigades to where the fighting is worst. The 46th just turned up outside Kramatorsk
articles.body:
- Free to redeploy from the stabilized southeastern front, a key Ukrainian brigade has moved north to help defend Kramatorsk and Sloviansk
- It took two months, and almost nobody outside the Ukrainian army knew it was happening
- The 46th Airmobile Brigade's first task may be to cover a short retreat by an adjacent brigade
Kramatorsk and Sloviansk are the last two big cities in the Donbas that Russia does not hold, and taking them has been the main Russian objective in eastern Ukraine since 2022. Ukraine is now moving forces north from the southeast to defend them.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade began that move in July. The first outside confirmation came this week.
Shifting north to plug a gap between two Ukrainian corps, the brigade could protect adjacent units as they retreat a short distance from what's left of Chasiv Yar—a battleground since the spring of 2024—and straighten the Ukrainian line where the 11th and 19th Corps meet. Both corps now sit under Biletskyi's new force grouping, according to Unit Observer—a command relationship no Ukrainian outlet has reported and which open sources cannot independently confirm.
Zooming out, the reshuffle around Kostiantynivka runs alongside a wider effort to redistribute Ukrainian troops along the 1,200-km gray zone threading through southern, eastern, and northern Ukraine. Gen. Mykhailo Drapatyi took over as commander-in-chief on 22 July, arriving with a mandate to unwind the Soviet-inherited command model Ukraine has fought this war with, and a reputation for favoring decentralized command. The 46th began moving before he did, in early July, according to Unit Observer, so this redeployment is not his. But the 33rd Assault Regiment was partially reassigned to Biletskyi's corps after the handover.
The best-case scenario is that the redeployment helps stabilize the front 16 km south of Kramatorsk, delaying the Russian siege of that city and Sloviansk to the north. In the worst case, the 46th Airmobile Brigade and its thousands of troops are too few and too late to make much of a difference as the Center Group of Forces and its tens of thousands of troops grind through Ukrainian defenses on their slow march toward Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
The 46th Airmobile Brigade spent years fighting in southeastern Ukraine. But it's arguably no longer needed along the southern end of the gray zone after a Ukrainian counteroffensive that kicked off in February halted and then rolled back Russian forces, stabilizing what was once Ukraine's most vulnerable flank.
Free to fight elsewhere, the brigade began its move north toward Kostiantynivka and Chasiv Yar two months ago. The move happened almost entirely in secret. "Strict OPSEC measures have become the standard for the Ukrainian armed forces in 2026," mapper Unit Observer noted, "with units delaying posts up to several months to avoid giving away their relocation along the front line."
That discipline is now visible across the whole Ukrainian effort. The southeastern counteroffensive that freed up this brigade ran for six months with very few videos and small teams. Ukraine's Swedish radar planes flew combat sorties for half a year before the defense ministry said so. A brigade crossing the front unremarked for two months is the same practice, applied to ground forces.
Confirmed moves
Recent videos confirmed the deployment. The 46th Airmobile is now in position just north of the ruins of Kostiantynivka and just west of the ruins of Chasiv Yar, which lie 11 km northeast of Kostiantynivka. Sitting astride the juncture between two Ukrainian corps, the 11th and 19th, the brigade is set to play a crucial role in the ongoing Ukrainian defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk.
According to Unit Observer, the 46th Airmobile Brigade's move "will likely support the gradual retreat of elements of the 24th Mechanized Brigade remaining between Chasiv Yar and the village of Stinky," 6 km west of Chasiv Yar. The 24th Mechanized Brigade has fought long and hard in and around Chasiv Yar to hold back a much larger Russian force. But incremental Russian advances north and south of the 24th Mechanized Brigade's positions have put the brigade at risk of partial encirclement.
It's a dangerous position for the weary brigade. If it could fall back to the west a few kilometers, it could eliminate the risk to its flanks—and straighten and shorten the overall Ukrainian line. It's possible the 46th Airmobile Brigade's job is to safeguard the short retreat.
Desperate to save Sloviansk and Kramatorsk, Ukrainian forces counterattack and reinforce
The command and control process is deceptively complex, and the confusion is exactly the kind Drapatyi is trying to engineer out. Ukraine's new corps are supposed to be its highest front-line commands, coordinating the brigades, regiments, and battalions fighting in the same sectors. But in the areas where two corps meet, it may be unclear which corps is in charge.
Ukraine's answer has been to add a layer above the corps. On 26 August, Zelenskyy announced that two reinforced groupings would take over the defense of Donetsk Oblast, commanded by Denys Prokopenko of the 1st National Guard "Azov" Corps and Andrii Biletskyi of the 3rd Army Corps, both named Heroes of Ukraine.
The 3rd Corps' zone of responsibility has grown daily since the start of the year, its deputy commander Lt. Col. Rodion Kudriashov told NV, and he framed the new groupings as Ukraine scaling up what already works.
The grouping formalizes an arrangement that had already grown up in practice. The 46th Airmobile Brigade fits the same logic. It belongs to neither the 11th nor the 19th Corps—it is an 8th Air Assault Corps unit—but it is a brigade that works, freed by an offensive that worked, arriving in the sector that matters most. It is also arriving into a corps run by its own former commander: Brig. Gen. Valeriy Skred, recently given the 19th, led the 46th through 2022 and 2023.
Only time will tell whether the reshuffling of Ukrainian forces will bolster the defense of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. And even if the redeployments do stiffen the Ukrainian line south of Kramatorsk and Sloviansk, they do nothing to stiffen the line north of the twin cities.
Russian troops are closing in from that direction, too. Fortunately for the Ukrainians, there's a separate plan for that northern sector. A carefully planned series of Ukrainian counterattacks has quietly cut across a salient of Russian troops marching on Sloviansk.
The Ukrainian attacks may compel the Russians to pull back a short distance. That could give the defenders of Sloviansk more space and time to prepare for the coming siege.

articles.title: Confidence in imminent victory, Putin’s visit to India: statements by Kremlin spokesman
articles.body:
MOSCOW/NEW DELHI, September 8. /TASS/. Moscow is confident in an imminent victory, and combat operations are progressing very successfully for Russia, Kremlin Spokesman Dmitry Peskov stated during a briefing for Indian media ahead of the BRICS summit in New Delhi.
He also noted that Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries.
TASS has compiled the key statements by the Kremlin spokesman.
Conflict in Ukraine
Russia did not want and did not start the war in Ukraine but it is trying to stop it: "We actually never wanted this war. What we’re trying to do, we’re trying to stop the war that was launched before, and it was not launched by us. It was not started by us."
Russia remains open to the peaceful settlement of the Ukrainian conflict: "We do want the solution of the Ukrainian conflict by peaceful means, and Russia is open for this process."
India’s position regarding the Ukrainian conflict largely coincides with Russia’s: "We know the position of India on the Ukrainian conflict, and to great extent it corresponds with our own position".
Russia has to achieve its goals regarding Ukraine through a special military operation, although it would prefer to do so by peaceful means: "We have to reach our goals during the special military operation, but we would prefer to do it in a peaceful way."
Russian troops are advancing in the special military operation zone: ""The dynamics on the front is known to all the experts. We’re moving forward."
Russia is confident in an imminent victory: "We are sure that the victory is very near. We are very confident in our military potential, in our military. Our military actions are going on very successfully."
Russia welcomes any efforts by other countries to achieve a peaceful settlement of the conflict in Ukraine: "We welcome all the attempts to make any contribution in the sphere of the Ukraine settlement. We welcome the willingness of the Indian side to contribute. We welcome the efforts of American President President Trump."
Moscow expects the resumption of trilateral negotiations with Washington and Kiev to resolve the Ukrainian crisis: "We hope that there will be some movement in this respect. We hope to restart negotiations between three parties: Russian, Ukrainian, and American."
The conflict in Ukraine could have ended long ago, but Kiev, being incited by Europeans, does not want an end to it: "I wouldn’t say that Kiev is that flexible, and I wouldn’t say that Kiev is really willing to stop this war. Should they be willing to do that, the war [would have] been over for a long time, but they’re being provoked to great extent by some European countries."
Europeans are inciting Kiev to go to war and deluding themselves with the hope of achieving a "strategic defeat" of Russia: "They [the Kiev authorities] are still being provoked to a great extent by some European countries that cannot get rid of the idea of strategically defeating Russia. We will not let that happen, and we’re not letting that happen."
Indian citizens participating in the special military operation will be returned home as soon as their identities are established and a list of names is compiled: "Now the work is being done to make a list of those Indian citizens, who are now on the battlefield, and they will be sent back home as soon as they are determined. We are in very deep contact, profound contact with the Indian side on this issue."
Dangers of trying to preserve a unipolar world
Attempts to preserve a unipolar system in the world are very dangerous: "Unipolar system is actually collapsing, it is losing losing its competitiveness, and then at the same time, the unipolar system is trying to regain power, taking sometimes very harsh steps, injuring the global system, the global economy, the global environment and politics, the global system of international law. So this is a very dangerous process."
The global majority, represented by BRICS, is striving for a different world order: "Where every country is equal to another, where every country has a right to a say, where every country has the right to fair competition and trade, where every country is secured from any illegal sanctions or illegal pressure, where every country can secure its national interests without without experiencing somebody’s pressure and demands to do otherwise."
Sanctions and de-dollarization
Russia is not seeking de-dollarization: "It’s not because we are aiming for de-dollarization <…>. To the contrary, we’re open to every acceptable method of payment. But you know that certain countries are using some national currencies as a tool for political pressure."
Since some countries do not allow Russia to use their currency for trade, Russia must use rubles: "So, if they don’t let us use their money, we use our own money."
The United States itself is undermining confidence in the dollar as a reserve currency: "The more trust is ruined, the more trust goes in favor of national currencies. This is the process, and this is the nature of the process."
Russia considers Western sanctions unacceptable: "Of course, we do not accept, and we consider it to be definitely illegal in terms of international law, any attempts to introduce limitations on international trade and to threaten other countries' third parties for doing trade with others."
Russia intends to discuss this issue as part of settling the Ukrainian crisis, but the settlement itself is of paramount importance to Moscow: "[The] issue of sanctions is on the agenda. It is not in the front row because the settlement itself is the issue number one, but it’s an untakable part of the whole agenda of the peaceful settlement around Ukraine."
Putin’s visit to India and bilateral relations
Russian President Vladimir Putin’s visit to India, which will take place in a few days, will be significant for both countries: "In a couple of days he [Putin] will start his visit to India. <...> Jointly our two leaders are going to visit some forums."
Putin and Modi are also going to hold a mutually important bilateral meeting on the sidelines of the BRICS summit in New Delhi on September 11.
Putin and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi have a close yet pragmatic relationship: [They are] able to discuss in a very open and constructive way the most sensitive issues of the global agenda and our bilateral relations."
They will be discussing economic cooperation, although the specifics will remain confidential so that unfriendly countries cannot interfere: the conversation will proceed "discreetly, but in a very very constructive manner."
During the meeting, Putin will tell Modi about the current situation in the special military operation zone: "It will be another opportunity for President Putin to inform his Indian friend on the current situation on the fronts, on the war with Ukraine."
The leaders will also discuss the impact of US aggression against Iran on the global economy: "Negative consequences of all that are inevitable, unfortunately. And our two countries, they are also subject to those consequences."
India is Russia's strategic partner, and Moscow expects to develop relations with New Delhi across a wide range of issues: "We really consider it of extreme importance for our two countries that we continue to develop our cooperation in a very very wide scope of fields, we're quite successful in that."
Russia has excellent military equipment and is ready to continue supplying it to its Indian partners: "We have very good military equipment. Some of the equipment items are the best in the world, and we're ready to share them with our Indian partners."
Middle East
Russia believes that the situation around Iran is having a negative effect on the global economy: "The situation [surrounding Iran], unfortunately, is still very tense, and every day brings new turbulences. This is definitely not doing well for the global economy."
Russia would prefer that the United States and Iran return to the previously signed memorandum of understanding: "We prefer that countries involved return to the memorandum of understanding that was signed between Iran and the United States, or turn to something else that would bring peace to this region."
Trump's statement about the Moon
Space should be a space for interaction, not confrontation between countries, and cannot be subject to any "privatization": "I don't think that we can support the idea of privatization in space. It should be free of that. Space should be a ground for mutual cooperation and for mutual dialogue, not a ground for confrontation."
As for US President Donald Trump's publication, he hardly "declared" the Moon as belonging to the United States: "When [US] President [Donald] Trump said that 'the Moon is ours,' I think he meant that it wasn't their property, but he meant that very soon, hopefully, American astronauts will stand on the moon."

articles.title: Brazil’s cruise missile testing resumes after years of delay
articles.body:
- Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army successfully test-fired the MTC-300 cruise missile on August 26, resuming certification testing after a roughly four-year pause.
- The missile can strike targets up to 300 kilometers away, and Brazil's army has also revived plans for an upgraded Block II version with improved range and guidance.
Brazil’s Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army completed a successful test launch of the country’s first indigenous cruise missile on August 26, a milestone in a certification process that stalled for roughly four years while the missile’s manufacturer worked through a severe financial crisis.
The test took place at the Army Evaluation Centre’s Marambaia Test Range in Rio de Janeiro, according to a joint statement from Avibras Aeroco and the Brazilian Army. The missile, known as the Tactical Cruise Missile or MTC, is part of the ASTROS artillery system’s family of guided munitions and is designed to strike targets up to 300 kilometers (186 miles) away. The companies said the exercise met all objectives set for this phase of testing.
The MTC-300, also called the AV-MTC 300, has a range of 300 kilometers, a diameter of 450 millimeters and a length of 5.4 meters (17.7 feet). Each ASTROS launch unit currently in Brazilian Army service can carry two of the missiles. The system uses a combination of satellite and inertial navigation to hit within roughly 30 meters of its target, and Brazil has designed two warhead options for it: a high-explosive version and a cluster configuration carrying 66 submunitions. A turbojet engine built by Brazilian company Turbomachine, producing up to 499 kilograms-force (1,100 pounds-force) of thrust, propels the missile to high subsonic speeds of around 1,000 km/h (620 mph) at cruising altitudes between 200 and 800 meters.
Brazil’s army and Avibras began developing the missile in 2012 under the ASTROS Strategic Programme, intending to give the country’s rocket artillery system enough range to strike well beyond its immediate region. Testing stalled in 2022, when Avibras fell into a financial crisis tied to roughly 800 million reais ($133 million) in debt, triggering a prolonged strike involving around 900 employees and effectively freezing the company’s defense programs. The situation began to turn around in May, when Avibras reached an agreement to settle its outstanding labor debts, clearing the way for the company’s restructuring under the new name Avibras Aeroco and the resumption of missile testing.
According to the Brazilian Army, the August test served as part of the missile’s final flight-verification testing, ahead of a last remaining test that will use a live warhead, the final step required before the MTC-300 can be formally validated for service.
Brazil’s army has also revived plans for an upgraded version of the missile, known as MTC Block II, according to guidelines the army published in August for its broader ASTROS-FOGOS Strategic Programme. The Block II upgrade calls for adding an unspecified terminal guidance system, extending the missile’s range and improving its warhead, changes the army has linked to new requirements for coastal defense and for striking moving targets, a description that suggests the upgraded missile could eventually engage ships. The Block II project remains officially listed as “not started.”
Officials attending the August test included Brig. Gen. João Paulo Zago, head of the Army Evaluation Centre; Brig. Gen. Marcelo Gurgel do Amaral Silva, manager of the army’s FOGOS Strategic Programme; and Brig. Gen. Moisés da Paixão Junior, manager of the Field Artillery Sub-programme, alongside representatives from the Army Projects Office, the Manufacturing Directorate, the Military Institute of Engineering and the Army Technology Centre.
Avibras’s pause since 2022 gave rise to competition it did not previously face in Brazil’s missile industry. Other Brazilian firms have since disclosed their own cruise missile programs, including the AATD, reported to have a range of up to 2,000 kilometers (1,240 miles) using the same turbojet engine as the MTC-300, and the MCX, described as an export-friendly medium-range cruise missile with a satellite datalink. Separately, Brazilian company SIATT integrated Brazil’s MANSUP anti-ship missile onto Marine Corps ASTROS launchers in 2025, despite legal action from Avibras at the time, and is developing its own coastal defense missile system.

articles.title: UK Allocates £100 Million Package to Ukraine, Including Patriot Missiles
articles.body:
The UK has allocated £100 million for a new air defense package for Ukraine ahead of the winter season.
According to European Pravda, the package will include interceptor missiles for Patriot air defense systems, large-caliber artillery ammunition, and drones.
The weapons will be procured through the PURL (Prioritised Ukraine Requirements List) mechanism, under which partner countries fund the purchase of US-made weapons for Ukraine.
The British government plans to ensure Patriot missiles and other air defense equipment are delivered before winter begins. The weapons are intended to strengthen the protection of Ukrainian cities, critical infrastructure, and the Ukrainian Defense Forces against Russian air attacks.
“We promised to mobilise our allies and provide as much support as we can,” UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting stated.
According to Streeting, during a recent visit to Kyiv, the British side received information from the President of Ukraine about the country’s needs ahead of the winter.
London expects Russia to continue attacking civilian and energy infrastructure.
The package was announced ahead of the next meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, known as the “Ramstein” format, which will take place online on September 8.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting and German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius will co-chair the meeting.
Strengthening Ukraine’s air defenses will be one of the main topics of the Ramstein meeting, as Ukraine prepares for the coming winter.
Militarnyi previously reported that Spain will continue to supply Ukraine with Patriot missiles as part of its military aid.

articles.title: Iran conveys its ‘conditions’ to US – source
articles.body:
Iran conveys its ‘conditions’ to US – source
Iran has conveyed its conditions to the US through intermediaries after Washington recently sent new proposals to Tehran, a political source in the Iranian capital has told RT.
The reported contacts come amid renewed regional efforts to revive diplomacy after last week’s flare-up, when the US carried out several rounds of strikes on Iran and Tehran retaliated with missile and drone attacks on American military facilities in Jordan and Bahrain.
“Following the halt of negotiations resulting from US breaches of commitments and its repeated failures in military engagements, the US has recently conveyed proposals to Tehran through mediators,” the source said.
Given Washington’s “repeated violations” and “constant fluctuations in its positions,” Tehran responded by conveying its own conditions to the intermediaries, the source added.
The source did not disclose the details of either the American proposals or the Iranian conditions, but said mediators “continue to talk to both parties.”
Tehran has been pushing Washington to honor the commitments outlined in the June Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), but the US is now reportedly seeking a new, broader agreement covering both the Strait of Hormuz and Iran’s nuclear program, the Financial Times reported last week.
Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei said on Monday that US and Israeli attacks on Iranian nuclear facilities were themselves the main obstacle to inspections by the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), arguing that Washington was responsible for the resulting lack of access while simultaneously using the issue to increase pressure on Tehran.
“The ball has long been in the US court,” Baqaei said, adding that Washington must end its military attacks, economic sanctions and naval blockade if it wants to resolve the confrontation.
“Diplomacy is a dynamic and continuous process,” the spokesman said, noting that delegations from Oman and Pakistan have visited Iran in recent weeks, while Qatari representatives held talks with Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi in Tehran on Sunday.
Qatari Foreign Ministry spokesman Majed al-Ansari told CNN that Doha had put forward several ideas and was exploring different scenarios aimed at addressing the concerns of both sides.
Tehran and Muscat have meanwhile reported significant progress on a separate arrangement for a temporary safe shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian officials have stressed, however, that such an agreement would not amount to the full reopening of the strategic waterway, as Washington has claimed.

Ukraine asks partners for 300 Patriot missiles from existing stocks – DM Khmara
Ukrainian Defense Minister Yevhenii Khmara said this during the 36th meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format, according to an Ukrinform correspondent.
Khmara said that with the help of partners and funding from an EU loan, Ukraine is signing contracts for approximately 1,000 missiles for Patriot systems. However, most of these missiles will only begin to be delivered over the coming years.
“That is why we ask that you supply us with the missiles from your stocks today in exchange for future improved missiles from our contracts,” the minister said.
Khmara also emphasized the need to supply Ukraine with man-portable air defense systems and air-to-air missiles to counter jet-powered Shahed drones and cruise missiles.
According to him, dozens of Ukrainian companies are working on cheaper means of intercepting jet-powered attack drones, and some of the interceptors developed are already being tested in combat conditions.
The minister also urged partners to make decisions on financing Ukraine’s defense as soon as possible.
“70 billion euros for security assistance this year were promised in Ankara. So far, we see that our partners are already providing €62 billion, including bilateral assistance and the EU loan. Thank you for that. Thus, the additional €8 billion are still needed to fulfill the declaration. However, I want to stress that the overall defense deficit is €23 billion, or $27 billion,” Khmara stressed.
According to him, these funds would make it possible to finance drones and ensure their stable supply through the end of this year and into early next year.
“Up to 90% of our success on the battlefield is driven by drones,” he added.
The minister asked partners to make the necessary financial decisions by November so that their impact could be felt on the battlefield as early as winter. He also emphasized the need to maintain an adequate level of defense support for Ukraine in 2027.
“The support for Ukraine is not a subsidy. It is an investment. We are offering a mutually beneficial partnership,” the minister stressed.
As reported, the UDCG meeting is being held virtually. Opening remarks were delivered by NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius, UK Secretary of State for Defence Wes Streeting, and U.S. Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby.

Germany to send more Patriot missiles to Ukraine, warns of stepped-up Russian winter attacks
Sept 8 - Germany will send Patriot air defence missiles to Ukraine from its national stocks, Defence Minister Boris Pistorius said on Tuesday, warning that Russia was likely to intensify its air campaign against Ukrainian infrastructure as winter approaches.
Speaking at a videoconference of nations supporting Ukraine, Pistorius said he had decided to "deliver urgently" additional PAC-2 interceptor missiles.
Patriot missiles are currently the only effective defence against Russian ballistic missile attacks on Ukraine, officials say.
"Since Russia is only advancing very slowly at the front line, it is trying to destroy Ukraine's economic base and critical infrastructure by way of air raids on port installations, power plants, and other civilian targets," Pistorius said.
"Unfortunately, we can expect Russian air raids to increase again once temperatures drop, and then the damage will be even greater," he told the meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group.
Pistorius did not say how many missiles Germany would provide.
He said Germany would also expand deliveries of air-to-air missiles and continue supplying drones and long-range ammunition to Kyiv.
Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said Kyiv is contracting to buy around 1,000 Patriot missiles but most would only be shipped in the coming years. He urged allies to dig into their stocks for Ukraine now, on the basis that Kyiv would replace those missiles from future deliveries.
NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte also pressed allies to increase support, saying civilian casualties from the war were at their highest level since May 2022.
"Nations must dig deeper. We do not have a choice," he said.
Ahead of the meeting, Rutte and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said EU members states had agreed to use part of a €90-billion ($105 billion) EU loan to allow Ukraine to buy crucial supplies for Patriot systems. REUTERS

articles.title: Sweden to Buy U.S. HIMARS, Plans to Produce PrSM Missiles
articles.body:
Sweden will purchase U.S.-made HIMARS multiple launch rocket systems for approximately SEK 7 billion ($729 million) and will cooperate with Finland on their operation.
The Swedish government announced the deal on its official website.
The first HIMARS rocket systems, manufactured by Lockheed Martin, are expected to be delivered in 2027.
The Swedish Armed Forces will fund the purchase through its investment plan and the country’s 2025–2030 defense program.
The HIMARS rocket systems will expand the Swedish Army’s long-range strike capabilities and strengthen NATO’s defensive posture in Northern Europe.
They will complement existing Archer artillery systems and mortars while ensuring interoperability with weapons systems operated by other NATO countries.
According to Swedish broadcaster SVT, the deal involves more than ten HIMARS launchers and a large quantity of GMLRS guided rockets. The Swedish government’s official announcement did not specify the exact number of systems.
Meanwhile, Saab and Lockheed Martin have signed a letter of intent to potentially integrate GLSDB munitions into the new systems.
The companies are also considering producing PrSM precision-guided ballistic missiles in Sweden. HIMARS and other systems, including the Patriot air defense system, use the missiles.
However, the Swedish government’s official announcement does not yet specify which type of missile it plans to manufacture in Sweden.
HIMARS is a U.S.-made highly mobile wheeled multiple launch rocket system designed to conduct precision strikes and rapidly relocate to new firing positions. It can carry six GMLRS rockets, two PrSM missiles, or one ATACMS missile.
PrSM is a surface-to-surface ballistic missile with a range of 60 km to more than 500 km, developed to replace ATACMS. A single HIMARS launcher can carry two PrSM missiles instead of one ATACMS, or a pod containing six GMLRS rockets. The missile is also compatible with the tracked M270 launchers.
