articles.title: Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
articles.body:
Moscow vows ‘harsh and painful’ response to Hungarian expulsions
Moscow will deliver a “harsh and painful” response to Hungary’s expulsion of ten Russian diplomats, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova has warned.
The remarks were in response to Budapest’s decision to expel ten members of Russia’s diplomatic mission over alleged activities deemed “unacceptable for diplomats” under the Vienna Convention.
“The response to the Russophobic lobby in Budapest will be harsh and painful,” Zakharova said on Tuesday.
Hungarian Foreign Minister Anita Orban announced the decision on Tuesday. She said the Russian ambassador had been informed that, “according to the assessment of the Hungarian authorities,” the diplomats had engaged in activities incompatible with their status.
Orban did not specify the alleged activities or say how long the diplomats had been given to leave. She said the decision was intended to protect Hungary’s “security and sovereignty,” while stressing that Budapest was not severing diplomatic ties with Moscow and intended to maintain dialogue.
The expulsions come as Prime Minister Peter Magyar’s government has sharply reversed Hungary’s policy toward Russia since taking office in May. In a new foreign policy directive, Budapest designated Russia a “threat to Hungary, Europe, and the global order,” marking a dramatic break with the pragmatic relations pursued under former Prime Minister Viktor Orban.
Hungary had not formally designated Russia as a “threat” at any point since 1945. Under Orban, Budapest repeatedly opposed what the former prime minister called the West’s “war policies,” refused to supply weapons to Kiev, and argued that the conflict could not be settled through a Ukrainian military victory.
Orban also repeatedly delayed or watered down EU sanctions on Moscow and resisted major financial packages for Kiev, while seeking exemptions that allowed Hungary to continue importing Russian oil, gas, and nuclear fuel. He maintained that cutting Europe off from comparatively cheap Russian energy would damage the bloc’s industrial competitiveness.
Magyar’s new position closely mirrors that of the EU, which also advocates “sustainable peace and long-term security guarantees,” but only on terms that recognize Kiev’s maximalist demands – a return to Ukraine’s 1991 borders, freedom to pursue NATO and EU membership, and NATO-like security guarantees provided by European and American forces.
His government has also backed new sanctions on Russia and dropped Budapest’s objections to a €90 billion ($105 billion) EU package for Kiev, reversing policies that had previously set Hungary apart from most other EU members.

articles.title: Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Huawei heads to trial in US over its business dealings in Iran
Eight years after US prosecutors secretly charged China's Huawei Technologies with defrauding HSBC and other banks over its business with Iran, the case is finally heading for trial.
Huawei also faces charges for conspiring to steal trade secrets from five US technology companies, and is accused of lying about its dealings in North Korea and supplying surveillance equipment to Iran to track protesters during 2009 anti-government demonstrations in Tehran. Jury selection is expected to begin on Tuesday in federal court in Brooklyn, New York.
The trial will bring to a close one of the US government's earliest and most closely watched battles against a Chinese company, and will play out as tech competition heats up between the two countries and Washington seeks to prevent American technology from aiding Beijing's military. The US-China tech war has now spread across multiple technology sectors, including artificial intelligence.
The saga began in 2018 with the arrest of Huawei Chief Financial Officer Meng Wanzhou in Vancouver, which sparked a diplomatic crisis involving the United States, China and Canada.
Convictions on the Iran-related charges would bolster Washington's case for having placed Huawei, one of China's leading technology companies, on a US trade blacklist in 2019, citing alleged criminal conduct that threatened national security.
The trial before US District Judge Ann Donnelly is expected to last about three months and overlap with Chinese President Xi Jinping's September 24 meeting with President Donald Trump in Washington. Potential jurors have filled out 27-page questionnaires, including about their views on China's and Iran's governments.
Other charges include violating US sanctions against Iran, money laundering, racketeering, wire fraud and obstruction. Huawei has pleaded not guilty on all charges and denied any wrongdoing.
The criminal case is based in part on reporting by Reuters in 2012 and 2013 about close ties between Huawei and Skycom, a firm that operated in Iran.
Reuters reported that Skycom had offered to sell at least €1.3 million ($1.5 million) worth of embargoed Hewlett-Packard computer equipment to Iran's largest mobile-phone operator in 2010. Reuters also reported that Meng had served on Skycom's board of directors between February 2008 and April 2009. The coverage can be read here and here.
Beijing has long criticized the case, saying it was part of a bigger campaign against China's technological rise. A Huawei spokesperson said in a statement on Saturday, "The government's overarching narrative is demonstrably false."
Today Huawei is a centerpiece of China's AI chip ambitions, and has diversified beyond network gear and smartphones. It has described the criminal case as an effort to undermine its competitiveness and the theft accusations as a repackaging of long-resolved commercial disputes.
If Huawei is convicted, prosecutors will seek the forfeiture of property or proceeds obtained from its illegal activity.
The case against the company was brought during the first Trump administration, which also took actions to curb the use of Huawei equipment in the US and pressed other countries to drop Huawei from their telecommunications networks, saying China could use its equipment for espionage.
The indictment covers alleged wrongdoing between about 1999 and 2020.
It accuses Huawei of using Skycom to obtain embargoed US goods, technology and services for Huawei's Iran-based business, and to move money out of that country through the international banking system.
The US said one bank, which was not named in the indictment but which sources and documents reviewed by Reuters identified as HSBC, cleared more than $100 million worth of US-dollar transactions related to Skycom.
Prosecutors accused Meng of misrepresenting Huawei's ownership and control of Skycom in a presentation to an HSBC executive. She later admitted the statements were false, as part of an agreement with prosecutors to drop the charges against her.

articles.title: Inside Russia’s Secret War Games Where Generals Seized Gotland and Defeated NATO
articles.body:

Inside Russia’s Secret War Games Where Generals Seized Gotland and Defeated NATO
Russian military commanders spent years using large-scale computer simulations to rehearse potential wars with NATO, Sweden, Japan, the US, and Ukraine, including scenarios involving the seizure of Sweden’s Gotland island and operations in the Baltic region.
According to an investigation by the Dossier Center, a Russian investigative media outlet, published on September 8, Russia’s General Staff conducted the simulations at the Military Academy of the General Staff in Moscow, using specialized software to model terrain, military units, weapons, and the actions of opposing forces.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
The exercises involved senior Russian officers and, in some cases, more than 1,000 participants connected from military institutions across the country. Officers were divided into opposing teams, while instructors familiar with NATO doctrine frequently represented the adversary.
In one scenario conducted in 2017, Russian commanders modeled operations involving Gotland, a strategically located Swedish island in the Baltic Sea, with Russia’s Kaliningrad region playing an important role in the simulated campaign.
A year later, the Russian military reportedly conducted another simulation involving a fictional war against the US and Japan. More than 320,000 virtual troops were involved, with maps showing areas of northern Japan where key US and Japanese military facilities are located.
Simulating war with Ukraine
The investigation found that Ukraine increasingly became a focus of Russian military simulations ahead of the full-scale invasion. In 2021, Russian commanders reportedly conducted exercises related to a potential operation against Ukraine almost every month.
The simulations relied on a group of interconnected systems developed by Russian defense contractor RusBITech. One platform, Iris-T, generated three-dimensional battlefields using military maps, aerial photography, and satellite imagery. Another system, Spektr-7E, allowed commanders to develop operational plans, simulate their execution, calculate outcomes, and repeat scenarios with different decisions.
By 2021, Spektr-7E reportedly contained around 5,000 digital models representing weapons, military equipment, units, and other objects.
The effectiveness of such simulations, however, depends heavily on the assumptions and intelligence used to construct them. The Dossier Center investigation suggested that inaccurate assessments of Ukraine’s military capabilities and Russia’s own forces may have shaped the scenarios examined by Russian commanders before February 2022.
Russia’s initial attempt to rapidly seize Kyiv and force a political collapse failed after the launch of the full-scale invasion, forcing the Russian military to reconsider some of its operational assumptions.
Russia reworked its war games after 2022
The General Staff subsequently incorporated lessons from the actual fighting in Ukraine into new simulations.
In spring 2022, Russian military institutions held two major command-and-staff exercises. One, completed on April 4, involved nearly 1,300 students and instructors from 15 military educational institutions, according to the investigation.
Later simulations reflected battlefield conditions encountered in Ukraine, including fragmented front lines, special operations forces, foreign fighters, and cities that remained under Ukrainian control behind attempted Russian advances.
The investigation found that Russia continued updating its military gaming system as the war progressed, using battlefield experience to revise scenarios at the General Staff Academy’s military gaming center.
Ukraine and NATO have also expanded their use of war games since Russia’s full-scale invasion. Ukrainian and Western officers have used simulations to examine planned operations, including preparations related to Ukraine’s 2022 counteroffensive in the Kherson region and its 2023 southern offensive.
Ukraine’s battlefield experience is also being incorporated into NATO planning through joint initiatives, including the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Centre (JATEC) in Bydgoszcz, Poland, which studies lessons from Russia’s war and integrates them into allied training and planning.

articles.title: Ukrainian AI targeting module placed third among 60-plus entries in NATO contest
articles.body:
A Ukrainian company has placed third in a NATO contest to find ways of keeping an enemy's airfields shut down over time. Its artificial-intelligence targeting module finished among the top three of more than 60 entries in the Persistent Airfield Denial Innovation Challenge, Ukraine's Defense Ministry said.
The challenge was run jointly by NATO Allied Command Transformation and the NATO-Ukraine Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center, the first jointly staffed NATO-Ukraine body. The result shows NATO is building a direct channel for Ukraine's combat-tested technology into its own capability development.
On the NATO side, the finalists' proposals were evaluated by representatives of the Alliance's Commands, as well as the NATO Defense Innovation Accelerator DIANA.
An AI module lands third place
Organizers received more than 60 applications and brought nine finalists to Warsaw. The Ukrainian team took third place with a module designed to enhance the autonomy and accuracy of strike systems. The Ukrainian Defense Ministry did not name the developer.
A Czech firm, LPP Holding, won with a long-range system designed to work with minimal outside control, and a Polish team came second with a plan for the pre-planned destruction of key airfield infrastructure.
JATEC feeds Ukraine's lessons to NATO
Ukrainian experts helped define the problem and judge the entries, including officers from the Air Force Command, the Unmanned Systems Forces, and the National Guard's Omega unit.
The challenge, which carried up to €250,000 in prize funding, was the second of the two bodies to run together, after a 2025 round that fast-tracked European firms to counter Russian glide bombs.
In July 2026, Russian aviation used approximately 8,000 guided aerial bombs against Ukrainian cities.
The winning solutions now move to testing and combat validation, which the Defense Ministry said will show how well they work and whether they can scale.

articles.title: A Russian drone hit a Kyiv television newsroom in broad daylight while the channel was live on air
articles.body:
A Russian strike drone hit the Kyiv premises of the television channels My-Ukraina and My-Ukraina+ in the middle of the day on 8 September, the channel reported. The main blow landed on the newsroom and the working offices while My-Ukraina was live on the national newscast. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy urged a response from Europe and the world.
During its ongoing all-out war, Russia runs a parallel campaign against the people who document it, jailing reporters as terrorists in the territory it occupies, killing them with drones near the front, and accumulating hundreds of crimes against them that European bodies have counted.
The strike landed on the editorial floor
My-Ukraina was broadcasting the national United News telethon, the joint wartime newscast that Ukrainian channels share, at the moment of the attack. Rescuers and medics worked at the site and treated the injured, the channel said. The strike came in daylight, hours after a mass overnight assault on the capital.
Fire and structural destruction hit the business center in the Solomianskyi district, and rescuers evacuated two people from its upper floors, the State Emergency Service said. It put the number injured at five and called that figure preliminary, with the count of victims still being clarified.
"A new page of Russian degradation"
Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram that Russia had struck at media and at journalists with a Shahed, one of the Iranian-designed attack drones it launches at Ukrainian cities in mass waves.
"Right in the middle of the day. Exactly when the journalists were on air. The building is partly destroyed," he said.
Emergency workers had already put out the fire, and the number of injured could still grow, he added.
"Shaheds against media is a new page of Russian degradation, and there must certainly be a reaction from Europe and the world," Zelenskyy said.
Trump’s peace envoys left, and Russia hit Kyiv with ballistics—the one thing Ukraine still struggles to stop
Russia had already damaged the channel's office overnight on 20 August during a mass attack on Kyiv. That blast blew out the windows, badly damaged the newsroom, and tore down part of the ceiling in the corridors.
Three killed in the capital over the day
Kyiv Mayor Vitalii Klitschko said the number of people killed by Russian strikes in Kyiv since the start of 8 September had reached three. The city military administration put the number of injured across the capital at 19.
Explosions ran for almost five hours overnight and damaged more than 50 sites in Kyiv, the Interior Ministry reported. Russia fired ballistic, cruise, and anti-ship missiles along with jet-powered drones in that attack.

articles.title: Russia burns occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear plant’s last-resort generators as everyday power, Ukraine says
articles.body:
The Russian-occupied Zaporizhzhia Nuclear Power Plant lost the 330-kV Ferosplavna-1 line—which the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) called the plant's only remaining off-site power line—on 20 August and has since run on emergency diesel generators, Ukraine's state nuclear operator Energoatom said on 6 September. A day earlier, the IAEA said the plant's diesel reserves were under increasing strain and warned it could lose all power within days unless external power was restored or fuel deliveries continued.
The Zaporizhzhia plant has been under Russian control since March 2022, when Russian forces seized the facility during the invasion. The plant stopped generating electricity in September 2022, and all six reactors have been in cold shutdown since April 2024, leaving the plant dependent on external or backup power for cooling and other essential safety systems. Repeated damage to the plant's external power connections has forced it onto emergency diesel generators multiple times, including during a month-long loss of off-site power in 2025.
How much diesel the Zaporizhzhia plant has left
The plant's most recent delivery to its off-site fuel farm took place in March, and the next one, set for May, is still held up by military activity, the IAEA reported on 20 August. At that point, the plant reported having more than 10 days of diesel available for its emergency generators.
By 29 August, the plant was down to about 10 days of diesel—its minimum regulatory reserve—and IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said that was roughly how long it had left without restored power or more deliveries. Several dozen tons reached the plant on 27 and 28 August, but a week later the agency shortened the warning to within days, with the plant down to two generators and running its cooling pumps on and off to save fuel. No nuclear plant should have to throttle its essential cooling systems to conserve diesel, Grossi said.
How the plant lost its last external power line
Ferosplavna-1 is a backup line from the thermal plant next door, one of 10 the IAEA counted before the war. The main 750-kV Dniprovska line failed on 24 March. Technicians repaired it under a June ceasefire, but it has never been switched back on, because a substation more than 100 kilometers away was badly damaged. Ferosplavna-1 has carried the plant alone since. It went down on 26 April for the 15th time since 2022, by both counts, and cut out repeatedly around a June attack on the thermal plant. It went dead on 20 August—the 27th loss by Energoatom's count, the 26th by the IAEA's.
Ukrainian technicians began repairs on 5 September under a local ceasefire the IAEA brokered, with a few days' work expected. The line was still dead on 7 September, its 19th day without off-site power, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russian media. Fixing it may not bring the power back anyway, Rosatom chief Aleksei Likhachev claimed the same day, blaming Ukrainian inaction for the other line still sitting repaired and unconnected—which the IAEA puts down to the wrecked substation.
Energoatom's assessment of the generator risk and Russian claims
Russian forces run the plant's emergency generators as everyday power, outside the conditions they were built for, Energoatom said on 6 September. Weeks of continuous running raise the risk of several backups failing together, and constant starts under load make the systems that start them likelier to fail. Even in cold shutdown, a blackout would threaten control of the safety systems and the spent fuel pools, and the plant is already in gross violation of its safe-operation limits, it said. Only a Russian pullout, military and civilian, and a handover back to Energoatom would guarantee safe operation, the company said, which also wants both grid lines back.
The plant has enough fuel for its generators but cannot restock while the access roads are shelled, the plant's Russian-installed management claimed to Russia's state news agency TASS on 31 August. TASS blamed Ukrainian forces for the shelling, though the quoted remarks named no one.

articles.title: ‘God Willing, There Will Be a Result’: Zelensky Expects Trump Meeting in September
articles.body:
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky expects to meet US President Donald Trump in the second half of September, where he plans to press Washington for support for Ukraine’s new missile program and supplies of US ballistic missiles.
“I expect to meet with Trump in the second half of September. To raise this issue. And God willing, there will be a result,” Zelensky told journalists, including Kyiv Post, on Tuesday, Sept. 8.
JOIN US ON TELEGRAM
Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official.
Zelensky said Ukraine is developing its “Freya” missile program and hopes the US will support the initiative.
He said Kyiv expects to achieve its desired results with European partners but needs US ballistic missile packages to advance the program.
The meeting could take place on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York, where Zelensky has proposed holding a new round of talks involving the United States in late September.
The expected meeting comes amid an intensification of US diplomacy aimed at reviving peace talks. US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner traveled from Moscow to Kyiv over the weekend, meeting Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday before holding talks with Zelensky in Kyiv on Sunday.
Witkoff described the discussions with Putin as constructive and said Washington had heard “new ideas” from Moscow, while Kushner referred to a broader “peace package.”
Zelensky called his talks with the US envoys “very substantial” and said Kyiv was ready to move toward trilateral negotiations involving Ukraine, the US and Russia. National security advisers from Britain, France and Germany also joined part of the Kyiv discussions.
175 Targets Down, But Ballistic Missiles Still Get Through
Zelensky also said Kyiv and Washington are working toward a trilateral negotiating format.
“We agreed with the American side: let’s prepare all this among ourselves first, and then communicate it publicly,” he said.
The US is also reportedly examining the possibility of a winter de-escalation of the war between Russia and Ukraine alongside renewed negotiations on a broader peace agreement.
Ideas under discussion reportedly include measures involving energy infrastructure, grain supplies, and oil and gas exports.
Envoys say Russia willing to talk
The US delegation visiting Kyiv on Sunday reportedly conveyed to Zelensky that Moscow is prepared to engage in negotiations, even as Russia increases its aggression against Ukraine, casting heavy doubt on that possibility.
Regardless, the meetings appear to have moved forward, as demonstrated by all three sides on Monday.
Witkoff confirmed “substantive progress” had been made, “including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks.”
Zelensky echoed the development by saying that Ukraine was planning its “next steps” following three rounds of negotiations in Kyiv; and – though offering no timeline for the meetings – the Kremlin said that Moscow did not rule out resuming the trilateral format.

articles.title: Russia strikes Kyiv with missiles and drones, damaging residential buildings, injuring six
articles.body:
Russia strikes Kyiv with missiles and drones, damaging residential buildings, injuring six
An Ukrinform correspondent reported the explosions.
The Ukrainian Air Force warned of a ballistic missile threat and detected high-speed targets heading toward the capital. An air raid alert was declared in Kyiv and most regions of Ukraine.
The Kyiv City Military Administration (KCMA) and Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko reported the consequences of the attack.
At least six people were injured, three of whom were hospitalized. Residential buildings, vehicles, garages and warehouses were damaged, while fires broke out in several districts, including at an educational institution in the Holosiivskyi district. Debris fell onto a five-story apartment building in the Solomianskyi district, while another three-story residential building was damaged.
As Ukrinform previously reported, according to preliminary information from the Ukrainian Air Force, Russian forces launched cruise missiles from strategic aviation aircraft.

articles.title: Russia to build major battery plant for drones with up to $120 million in state support
articles.body:
The Russian government will provide up to 10.46 billion rubles ($120.8 million) in subsidies for the construction of a lithium-ion battery plant that is expected to produce components for drones. Details of the preferential loan for Innovative Energy Systems (INESIS), a company controlled by drone manufacturer Transport Budushchego (lit. “Transport of the Future”), was detailed in a government order dated Sept. 7.
The Insider analyzed the document, under which federal budget money will go to state-controlled Sberbank in order to compensate the lender for income it is expected to forgo as a result of the loan to INESIS, which was issued at well below market rate. The cost of the construction itself could not be determined.
The subsidies are spread over several years. Up to 491.9 million rubles is allocated for 2026, 1.78 billion rubles for 2027, 1.9 billion rubles for 2028, and nearly 2 billion rubles in 2029, while total subsidies through 2034 could reach 10.461 billion rubles. In practice, the funding is scheduled for 2026-2034, although the government’s budget commitment for the project can remain in force until Dec. 31, 2040.
INESIS manufactures batteries and is closely linked to Russia’s drone industry. According to Russia’s Unified State Register of Legal Entities, 85.81% of the company is owned by Transport of the Future LLC, which describes itself as one of Russia’s largest developers and manufacturers of unmanned aircraft systems.
In January 2025, Vladimir Putin took part in the opening of a research and production center for unmanned aircraft systems in Tolyatti, where Transport of the Future is the anchor resident. The company’s plant in the city already operates production lines for lithium-ion batteries used in drones, as well as electronic circuit boards, electric motors, propellers, and other components.
Transport of the Future has already received state support. The company participates in Russia’s national project for unmanned aircraft systems and is a resident of the National Technology Initiative, a state-backed program intended to develop emerging technologies. Over 20 billion rubles has been invested in the project, according to the company’s own data.
Notably, in May former Transport of the Future CEO Yuri Kozarenko was arrested on suspicion of large-scale fraud. Kozarenko led the company from 2022 until this past March and had previously served as an adviser to Samara Region governor Vyacheslav Fedorishchev. The investigation is being handled by the Interior Ministry branch in the Belgorod Region.
The Insider previously reported that the criminal case concerns the suspected theft of about 70 million rubles allocated under a state defense procurement contract for the production of drones. Investigators believe the money may have been diverted through friendly organizations that did not actually perform the work they were contracted to do. According to the same reporting, the company received a 4.5 billion-ruble state subsidy for the serial production of 750 vertical takeoff and landing UAVs.
Transport of the Future markets its products primarily as civilian equipment, including as agricultural drones. There is, however, evidence that technologies associated with the company are being used by the Russian military.
Novaya Gazeta Europe has reported that the Gektor drone, manufactured by Transport of the Future subsidiary Drone-Service and marketed as an agricultural aircraft, is being used by Russian forces in Ukraine. The outlet also reported that the company cooperates with the military training center at Tolyatti State University, where drone operators are trained.
The new plant, with an annual capacity of 4 gigawatt-hours, would become one of the largest projects in Russia’s emerging battery industry. INESIS has previously said the factory is intended to fully meet the battery needs of Russia’s unmanned aircraft sector.
A previous investigation by The Insider found that Russia is rapidly developing the domestic production of lithium-ion batteries, including those needed for the sorts of FPV drones commonly used on the battlefield.
In the first quarter of 2025, Russia imported more than 6.6 metric tons of electrolyte for lithium-ion batteries and lithium tetrafluoroborate (calculated in electrolyte equivalent). If that pace had continued for the full year, annual imports would have been more than three times the 2024 level. Imports of cobalt oxide for the battery industry increased by a factor of approximately 15 over the course of the year.
Chinese companies are the main suppliers of raw materials and production equipment. Russia remains dependent on imported components and raw materials, but the government has made localization of battery production a priority. State nuclear corporation Rosatom has said it intends to fully localize lithium-ion battery production by 2030. Its announcement, made in July 2025, followed the Russian military’s seizure of Shevchenko, a village in Ukraine’s eastern Donetsk Region that is home to one of the country’s largest lithium deposits.
Developing a domestic battery industry could reduce Russian FPV-drone manufacturers’ dependence on foreign supplies and, in turn, limit the ability of Western countries to disrupt production through export controls.

articles.title: FSB says it detained suspect in attempted murder of Russian general. Ukraine accuses the general of ordering the strike on Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt children’s hospital.
articles.body:
FSB says it detained suspect in attempted murder of Russian general. Ukraine accuses the general of ordering the strike on Kyiv’s Okhmatdyt children’s hospital.
Officers with Russia’s Federal Security Service (FSB) and the country’s federal investigative authority detained a 21-year-old Moldovan citizen, Nicolae Kochu, in the Astrakhan region on suspicion of attempting to murder a Russian serviceman in the Saratov region, the agencies reported.
According to official data, the suspect fired six shots at the serviceman on September 3 in the village of Probuzhdeniye, in the Saratov region’s Engels district. The serviceman was wounded but survived; his name has not been disclosed. The FSB specified only that he holds a high-ranking military position.
Unofficial reports identify him as Major General Nikolai Varpakhovich, commander of the 22nd Heavy Bomber Aviation Division in the long-range aviation branch of Russia’s Aerospace Forces. Ukraine considers him responsible for the missile strike that hit the children’s hospital Okhmatdyt in Kyiv on July 8, 2024, when the facility had more than 600 patients and roughly as many staff members on-site. Two people died in that strike.
The FSB claimed that a Ukrainian intelligence officer recruited Kochu through social media in 2025, while he was looking for work in Moldova. He underwent “mine-explosives and firearms training in Kyiv” in 2026 and traveled to Russia in June with the aim of killing the serviceman.
Kochu was supposed to return to Moldova after the attack, but he was detained while trying to leave Russia. Authorities opened criminal cases against him for attempted murder and illegal arms trafficking.
The FSB released video of Kochu’s detention and questioning, in which he says he saw a job ad on Instagram before Ukrainian representatives contacted him. It is unclear under what circumstances the footage was recorded, and Kochu does not always manage to get his words out on the first try.

articles.title: Foreign components manufactured in 2025-2026 found in Russian Geran drones, Iskander missiles – Vlasiuk
articles.body:
Foreign components manufactured in 2025-2026 found in Russian Geran drones, Iskander missiles – Vlasiuk
Vladyslav Vlasiuk, the President's Commissioner for Sanctions Policy, said this in a comment to Ukrinform.
"More strikes, Russian ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. Their electronic supply chain remains international, and components are still accessible. For example, 96 foreign components were identified in a Geran-4 drone shot down in the Kyiv region on August 12, 2026," he said.
According to the commissioner, these include components manufactured in the United States, China, Taiwan, Germany, Switzerland and Canada by companies including Texas Instruments, Amphenol, Diodes Incorporated, Kyocera AVX, Kemet, ON Semiconductor and Vishay Intertechnology. Seven of the components were manufactured in 2026 and another three in 2025.
"In the Iskander-M missile found at the site of a strike in the Kyiv region in early July, the picture is even broader. A total of 147 foreign-made components were identified. They came from the United States, Belarus, Switzerland, Germany, China and Japan. The manufacturers include Texas Instruments, Analog Devices, Maxim Integrated, Cypress, STMicroelectronics, Macronix, Integrated Silicon Solution, MaxLinear and others. At least 21 components were manufactured in 2025, and there are also components from 2026," he said.
At the same time, Vlasiuk said an examination of the Zarya-61 onboard computer in a Kinzhal missile showed that in 2023 Russia had been replacing U.S.-made Texas Instruments processors with domestically produced chips.
"But in a newer Zarya-61 unit recovered from a missile shot down in May this year, that replacement is no longer there. American processors are being used again. The examination directly indicates that the Russian substitutes did not deliver the required results," he said.
Vlasiuk also highlighted the composition of the computer. A circuit board assembled in May 2025 contains components manufactured in different years, from 2021 to 2024. Among them are a U.S.-made Texas Instruments DSP processor and memory manufactured by IDT, a company now owned by Japan's Renesas. Another board contains a Texas Instruments processor marked with the year 1986 and AMD chips manufactured in 1996.
According to him, this indicates that Russia may use older foreign electronics if they remain suitable for a particular weapons system, while simultaneously incorporating newer components.
"Therefore, the problem for Russia is not a complete lack of domestic electronic components. The same Iskander-M contains 36 Russian-made components and 11 from Belarus. But this is not enough for Russia's sophisticated weapons systems. It has to combine its domestic component base with foreign-made components, sourcing them through different markets and supply chains. Every manufacturer, law enforcement agency and export-control authority has enough information to stop such supplies to Russia," Vlasiuk added.

articles.title: Israel conducts wave of deadly strikes on Lebanon
articles.body:
Breadcrumb
Israel conducts wave of deadly strikes on Lebanon
Israel conducted a wave of airstrikes in south Lebanon, killing 13 people, including women and children, the Lebanese health ministry said on Monday, in an intensification of violence after a weeks-long lull.
Israel hit swathes of south Lebanon hard during the Middle East war that erupted with joint US-Israeli strikes on Iran, and its forces continue to occupy what it calls a "security zone".
One of the overnight strikes hit a building in the town of Kfar Rumman, killing 11 people, including two children and four women.
Another attack in the same town killed a rescuer and wounded another, according to the Lebanese health ministry.
A later strike on Rihan, also in the south but further from the border with Israel, killed one person, while a strike on the city of Nabatieh wounded nine, including two children and three women.
Israel has been intensifying strikes in the southern Nabatieh area after saying on Thursday that it had seized the strategic Ali al-Taher ridge from Hezbollah, a claim the group has not commented on.
The Israeli military in a statement said it had struck Hezbollah "infrastructure sites" across southern Lebanon after the launch of two explosive drones towards its troops, as well as "several terrorists" it said were transferring weapons.
The army said it "will continue to operate to remove threats while remaining committed to the ceasefire agreement".
In a separate statement, it said it killed a Hezbollah member in the area of the Beaufort fortress who opened fire on its troops from inside a building, and that "during the close-quarters encounter, two IDF soldiers were lightly injured".
School books in the rubble
Fighting in Lebanon, which erupted in March after Hezbollah targeted Israel in support of Iran, had decreased since a June memorandum of understanding between Washington and Tehran on the wider Middle East war and an Israel-Lebanon framework agreement later that month.
On Monday, Israel's foreign ministry accused Hezbollah of "repeated drone attacks" and "attempting to rebuild its military capabilities in southern Lebanon".
The ministry said Hezbollah had violated the ceasefire agreement between Lebanon and Israel that includes disarmament of the group.
The rescuer who was killed was just 18 years old, according to his civil defence organisation which is affiliated with the Amal movement, a political ally of Hezbollah.
An AFP photographer saw that the building that was hit in Kfar Rumman had been destroyed, with school books and remnants of furniture strewn across the rubble.
Rescue teams were searching the debris on Monday morning for other victims.
Villagers had returned home following the June truce after being displaced by the war.
"Since we returned here, we've lived in fear," Fouad Chakaron told AFP.
He insisted the targeted building was inhabited by "peaceful people with no connection to anyone".
Neighbours fled after the strike, which also damaged nearby buildings, AFP's photographer said.
The NNA later reported additional strikes on the Nabatieh area, and controlled detonations of unexploded munitions in at least two parts of the south.
'I couldn't believe it'
Israel issued no warning to Kfar Rumman before the strikes but released an evacuation order ahead of a separate attack in nearby Deir Zahrani.
The Israeli military said in an Arabic-language message that it was targeting a "Hezbollah terrorist facility", warning that those who remained in the area were at risk.
"They called me at 2:00 am and told me to get out of the house because it is being targeted," resident Abbas Toufeili told AFP, referring to the Israeli army.
"I said that's impossible, why is my house being targeted? There's nothing in it. I couldn't believe it."
He said he took his wife, children and elderly mother outside in their pyjamas and they stood on the street watching their house be destroyed.
On Sunday, Israeli strikes killed seven people. Attacks on Friday killed four.
The Israeli army has claimed it is responding to Hezbollah's launch of two drones towards its soldiers inside Lebanon, but did not specify whether any of its troops were wounded.
Hezbollah has not claimed any attack since 20 June.
Israeli airstrikes and a ground invasion of Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since March, Beirut says.
Israeli forces are operating inside a self-declared "security zone" around 10 kilometres (six miles) deep inside Lebanon along the border.
On Sunday, Lebanese President Joseph Aoun urged Washington and the international community to help stop Israeli attacks.

articles.title: Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats
articles.body:
Hungary expels 10 Russian diplomats
Hungary has ordered 10 Russian diplomats to leave the country, Foreign Minister Anita Orban announced.
According to Orban, Hungarian authorities determined that staff at the Russian diplomatic mission had been engaged in activity incompatible with their diplomatic status and in violation of the Vienna Convention. The Russian ambassador was notified of the decision on Tuesday.
“This decision protects Hungary’s security and sovereignty. It does not imply breaking off diplomatic relations with Russia. Hungary intends to continue the necessary dialogue, based on mutual respect and adherence to the rules,” Orban wrote on the social network X.
The expulsions come amid a marked cooling in relations between Hungary and Russia following a change of government in the spring of 2026. Under Prime Minister Viktor Orban, Budapest routinely opposed European Union sanctions against Russia and criticized military aid to Ukraine. His successor, Peter Magyar, is also reluctant to help Kyiv with weapons, but he has condemned Russian aggression and backs closer ties between Hungary and the EU and NATO.

Germany to Supply Ukraine With More AIM-9 and PAC-2 Missiles to Strengthen Air Defense
Germany will provide Ukraine with additional missiles for its air defense systems as Kyiv seeks to strengthen protection against Russian attacks ahead of winter, German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius announced on September 8, according to Ukrinform correspondent.
Speaking at the opening of a meeting of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group in the Ramstein format, Pistorius said Germany is expanding deliveries of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks alongside previously announced PAC-2 interceptors.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
“In addition to PAC-2 interceptor missiles, Germany will further increase the continuous supply of AIM-9 air-to-air missiles from Bundeswehr stocks to provide Ukraine with more of them. These missiles are being delivered right now and will strengthen Ukraine’s air defense before winter arrives,” Pistorius said.
The German defense minister recalled his decision at the NATO summit to urgently supply Ukraine with PAC-2 interceptors from Bundeswehr stocks, while calling on other members of the Ukraine Defense Contact Group to review their own inventories and consider similar contributions.
“From NATO’s perspective, further substantial deliveries of Patriot interceptor missiles by allies are acceptable,” Pistorius said.
Germany is also continuing regular deliveries of IRIS-T air defense systems and domestically produced guided missiles, Pistorius said, highlighting the effectiveness of the medium-range system in Ukraine.
Berlin’s support is expected to be complemented by additional Ukrainian orders for IRIS-T interceptors financed through the European Union’s defense loan for Ukraine.
“That is precisely why I am pleased that Ukraine intends to order several thousand additional IRIS-T guided missiles, which will be financed through the EU’s defense loan for Ukraine,” Pistorius said.
The additional German support comes as Ukraine works with its partners to expand its broader defenses against ballistic missile threats. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said on September 8 that Kyiv is seeking US backing for its FREYJA anti-ballistic missile program while also working with European partners on the initiative.
“We are preparing our own FREYJA program. We very much hope that the Americans will support this program as well. But, nevertheless, with the Europeans we will definitely achieve the desired result,” Zelenskyy said.

articles.title: Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
articles.body:
Syria’s Assad-era reactor configured for nuclear weapons: IAEA
UN watchdog says material now is under IAEA safeguards.
Syria’s Assad-era nuclear facility was configured to produce material for possible use in nuclear weapons, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency has reported.
The nuclear reactor, which the United Nations nuclear watchdog has been investigating with the cooperation of Syria’s new authorities, would have been able to produce fissile material that could be used for weapons, IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told a media conference in Vienna on Monday.
“This is a reactor that is very efficient in the production of fissile material that could be used directly for the fabrication of nuclear weapons,” he said.
Grossi’s comments came a week after the UN watchdog revealed in a confidential report that it had visited several sites in Syria in August and carried out verification work.
Based on observations at the Deir Az Zor site, the agency said it confirms “that the cooling infrastructure which has now been uncovered is consistent with that of a nuclear reactor”.
The agency added that it would continue to monitor the activities at the site “as the excavation work progresses”.
Syria was believed to have operated an extensive, undeclared nuclear programme under former President Bashar al-Assad that included a nuclear reactor built by North Korea in Deir Az Zor.
It only became public knowledge after Israeli air strikes in 2007 destroyed the facility. Syria later levelled the site and never responded fully to the IAEA’s questions about it.
Grossi said when the inspectors visited the site in August they had to “tear down walls” and go through “very difficult and narrow passages” to reach the nuclear material that had been hidden. The site had “boxes scattered all over the place,” he said.
Grossi said that “the important thing is that this material now is under safeguards” of the IAEA, adding that agency inspectors had managed to install cameras there.
Israel is believed to have its own undeclared atomic weapons programme, which makes it the only nuclear armed country in the Middle East. Israel neither confirms nor denies having nuclear weapons.
The IAEA has said that the former Syrian authorities had failed to report nuclear material, facilities and activities.
Besides the nuclear reactor at Deir Az Zor, the IAEA listed a fuel fabrication plant, where nuclear fuel for the reactor was manufactured and a store for the nuclear fuel, uranium scrap and waste.
During the visit to Syria last month, an IAEA team also visited a previously undeclared site.
The Syrian administration – made up of the group that overthrew Assad in 2024 – notified the agency of its existence in July and invited the nuclear inspectors to investigate.

articles.body:

How Qatar hopes to break the deadlock over the Strait of Hormuz
Qatar says "new ideas" are being discussed to end the US-Iran war and reopen the Strait of Hormuz, as Doha intensifies diplomacy with China and other regional and international partners.
The details have not been made public, and Qatar has not announced a formal new initiative.
But its latest diplomatic push comes as several proposals are already circulating over how to restore shipping through Hormuz without waiting for a comprehensive settlement to the wider US-Iran conflict.
Qatar's position is clear - the strait should be reopened immediately and without conditions, and should not be used as leverage in negotiations.
"It’s not acceptable at all to have this state of no war and no peace," Ibrahim Al Hashmi, director of the media department at Qatar's Foreign Ministry, said on Tuesday.
"Qatar is working hard with its partners, including China. Diplomatic efforts are being exerted and new ideas are being discussed," he added.
Al Hashmi said the most important requirement was "political will" from both Iran and the United States, while stressing that reopening Hormuz was a top priority for Qatar and other countries in the region.
Why is Qatar looking for a new approach?
The latest push follows the failure of an earlier agreement to produce a lasting settlement.
Washington and Tehran reached a memorandum of understanding in June with Qatari and Pakistani mediation, providing for a halt in military operations and arrangements to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
The agreement was meant to create space for further negotiations, including over Iran's nuclear programme and US sanctions, but implementation stalled and hostilities resumed.
The Hormuz dispute has since become one of the central obstacles to reviving negotiations.
Qatar has increasingly argued that the crisis cannot be allowed to settle into an indefinite state between war and peace, particularly because disruption to the strait has consequences far beyond Iran and the US.
Shipping through Hormuz has again slowed sharply amid the latest escalation, with only seven commodity vessels recorded passing through on Monday, according to Kpler data cited by Reuters.
Could Hormuz be dealt with separately?
One possibility emerging from the wider diplomatic activity is to find an interim solution for Hormuz before attempting to solve every dispute between Washington and Tehran.
Iran and Oman have been negotiating a temporary safe shipping route through the strait.
Iranian officials said this week that those talks had made "significant progress", with Tehran and Muscat working towards a temporary transit route while negotiations continue over a longer-term arrangement.
An earlier proposal envisaged inbound traffic passing through Iranian waters and outbound traffic using both Iranian and Omani territorial waters, followed by 30 to 60 days of talks on a more permanent route.
That plan is separate from Qatar's efforts, but it illustrates the type of narrower arrangement that could help break the deadlock.
Doha has previously argued that reaching an agreement on Hormuz could make it easier to restart wider US-Iran negotiations.
Where does China fit in?
China has now emerged more clearly in Qatar's diplomatic push.
Qatari Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani met Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi in Beijing on Tuesday, with Hormuz, regional security and possible solutions to the closure of the strait among the issues discussed.
Beijing has an obvious interest in restoring stable shipping through the Gulf because of its heavy reliance on energy imports from the region.
Its involvement also broadens the mediation effort beyond the countries that negotiated the June agreement.
Doha appears to be trying to assemble a wider diplomatic effort capable of addressing both the immediate shipping crisis and the larger political confrontation.
What might Qatar's "new ideas" involve?
Qatar has not disclosed them, so anything beyond its public statements remains interpretation.
But Ibrahim Freihat, professor of international conflict at the Doha Institute for Graduate Studies, has argued that an innovative approach could involve separating the different disputes instead of trying to resolve them through one comprehensive agreement.
"First, separating the issues instead of having all the files intertwined and interconnected. That makes a solution more difficult,” Freihat told Al Jazeera.
He argued that Hormuz itself could be treated as a separate negotiating track.
“Even the Hormuz issue itself could be addressed through a single track without requiring a comprehensive solution to the entire Hormuz question," he said.
Freihat also suggested replacing intermittent negotiating rounds with more permanent dialogue.
"Instead of negotiations taking place in separate rounds, they should become permanent negotiations,” he said. “In conflict terminology, they should become dialogue," he added.
He said a third element would be moving beyond purely bilateral US-Iran talks and giving Gulf countries a greater role in shaping a wider regional security arrangement.
Is there a new Qatari initiative?
Not formally, at least not yet. What Qatar has confirmed is that it is discussing new ideas with its partners, including China, and wants an unconditional reopening of Hormuz while wider diplomatic efforts continue.
The emerging approach therefore appears less like a single dramatic peace plan and more like an effort to break the crisis into manageable parts - reopen shipping, prevent further escalation and create enough political space for US-Iran negotiations to resume.

articles.title: Two Russian Su-35S fighter jets collide over Kursk Region, killing one pilot
articles.body:
Two Russian Su-35S multirole fighter jets collided over the Kursk Region on the evening of Sept. 7. The pro-war Telegram channel Fighterbomber was the first to report the incident, adding that the cause of the collision was still being investigated. Russian military blogger Yuri Kotenok confirmed the report in a now-deleted Telegram message, along with the fact that many key details of the incident remained unclear.
Additionally, the Telegram channel Voevoda Veshchayet (lit. “The Warlord Broadcasts”) which is run by Russian Aerospace Forces officer Alexei Zemtsov, said one of the pilots was killed and the other was evacuated. The Kursk-based outlet Pepel Kursk also reported that one pilot had died, saying the second managed to eject but was injured.
Voevoda Veshchayet also indirectly blamed outside forces, writing that the Ukrainians would “answer for this.” The channel provided no evidence that Ukraine was involved in the Russian plane crash.
Russia’s Defense Ministry had not commented on the collision at the time of publication. The Ukrainian authorities also had not officially claimed their involvement.
The Su-35S is a 4++ generation fighter — one of the most advanced combat aircraft in the Russian Aerospace Forces after the Su-57. It is equipped with the Irbis radar system and can carry R-37M air-to-air missiles with a range of up to 300 kilometers.
In July, Ukraine’s Air Force confirmed that it had shot down an Su-35 on the eastern front. Russian pro-war channels, including Fighterbomber and Voevoda Veshchayet, also acknowledged that loss at the time. The latter described it as an “ambush” and claimed a Patriot air defense system on the ground had illuminated the target for Ukrainian aircraft. The pilot survived.

articles.title: UK allocates over €100m winter air defence package for Ukraine, including Patriot missiles
articles.body:
UK allocates over €100m winter air defence package for Ukraine, including Patriot missiles
The United Kingdom is providing £100 million (around €116 million) for an air defence package for Ukraine ahead of winter, including Patriot missiles. The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, a US-NATO initiative under which European NATO allies purchase American weapons for Ukraine.
Source: European Pravda, citing the UK government
Details: As part of the new package, the UK will provide air defence interceptors, large-calibre artillery shells and drones to help Ukraine defend itself against Russian attacks this winter.
The weapons will be supplied through the PURL mechanism, under which Ukraine's allies purchase US weapons for its needs.
The Patriot missiles and other air defence equipment will be delivered to Ukraine before winter sets in, helping it protect critical national infrastructure, civilians and its armed forces from Russian attacks.
The aid announcement follows visits to Kyiv by the UK prime minister and defence secretary, who heard from the Ukrainian president about the importance of additional support ahead of winter.
"Both the Prime Minister and I heard loud and clear on our first visits to Kyiv the importance of supporting Ukraine through this winter, as Putin prepares to use winter as a weapon by continuing barbaric attacks against civilian and energy targets. We promised to mobilise allies and provide more support wherever we can," Defence Secretary Wes Streeting said.
Background:
- On 8 September, Streeting is chairing his first meeting of the Ukraine Defence Contact Group (also known as the Ramstein format), the 50-country alliance providing military equipment to Ukraine. The 36th Ramstein meeting is taking place remotely, co-chaired by the UK and German defence ministers.
- On 7 September, an extraordinary meeting of the NATO-Ukraine Council at the level of permanent representatives took place at NATO headquarters in Brussels, during which Ukraine presented a list of its priority and urgent needs for air and missile defence systems.

articles.title: Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
articles.body:
Europe’s biggest nuclear power plant back to normal after weeks in emergency mode
Power has been restored to the Zaporozhye Nuclear Power Plant (ZNPP) after more than two weeks in emergency mode, the CEO of the Russian state nuclear energy corporation Rosatom, Aleksey Likhachev, has said.
The main external power line to the plant was cut off in March following what the Ukrainian authorities described as “damage” to transmission towers. It has never been restored, with no explanations from Kiev.
Since then, the ZNPP has had to rely solely on the backup line – until August 20, when it was shut down by automatic control systems following an unspecified “incident” in territory controlled by Ukraine. That forced the power plant to fall back on emergency diesel-powered generators.
On Monday, Likhachev told journalists that the external power supply to the ZNPP had finally been restored, and the facility was now “operating as normal.” The Rosatom chief thanked all the parties involved in establishing a temporary local truce needed for the repair work, including the Russian defense and foreign ministries. He also praised the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) for its “mediation efforts.”
The ZNPP operator also confirmed that external power had been restored. No violations of safety limits were reported, and the radiation situation at the plant and in the surrounding area remained stable and did not exceed natural background levels, it said in a statement. The operator added that the second power supply line has yet to be restored and regular fuel supplies to the station need to be facilitated.
Diesel fuel deliveries to the station were “problematic” because of Ukrainian shelling targeting the roads in the area, ZNPP communications director Evgenia Yashina told Interfax earlier.
Europe’s largest nuclear power plant and the adjacent city of Energodar have been targeted by Ukraine on multiple occasions with artillery and drones since Russia took control of the facility in March 2022.
In July, a Ukrainian drone hit a ZNPP service vehicle on the edge of the plant’s industrial site, killing its chief engineer, Aleksandr Yakovlev, and his driver. At the time, Likhachev called the strike a “deliberate terrorist act.”
According to the Rosatom CEO, more than a dozen employees of the plant have been killed and many others wounded in Ukrainian attacks over the past three months. Kiev’s actions pose the “real danger of a massive nuclear incident” affecting parts of Russia, Ukraine, and the EU, he warned.
Several months ago, the Ukrainian military also started remotely mining the area near the ZNPP and Energodar, where plant employees reside, according to the nuclear chief. In early August, four ZNPP employees were injured by Ukrainian landmines dropped by drones.
Moscow has repeatedly criticized the IAEA, which has experts deployed at the ZNPP, for acknowledging the attacks on the facility but stopping short of blaming Ukraine for them.

More than 500 people were killed since Yemen's Houthi rebels launched an offensive last week to advance towards the Red Sea, most of them combattants, according to an AFP tally based on sources on both sides.
At least 216 government forces and 278 Houthi fighters were killed since the clashes began, according to sources from both sides who requested anonymity to discuss sensitive matters, in addition to at least 29 civilians.
Israel said Tuesday it would deny entry to 12 Britons if they wish to visit, including Jeremy Corbyn, former Labour Party leader and staunch advocate for Palestinians, in retaliation for UK sanctions targeting settlements.
Israel listed 11 members of parliament on the refuse-entry list. They also included Zarah Sultana, who joined Corbyn in breaking away from the Labour Party to form the left-wing Your Party.
Iran's Revolutionary Guards on Tuesday said they seized an unmanned American submarine in the strategic Strait of Hormuz, which Tehran has blockaded in the months-long Middle East war.
"The IRGC naval forces captured one of the most modern, unmanned, and smart submarines of the US terrorist army at the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz in a complex intelligence and operational action at dawn today," the Guards said in a statement carried by state TV.
The Palestinian Authority on Tuesday welcomed the announcement by 12 countries including France and the UK of trade sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank, calling it "an important step" to accountability.
"This as an important practical step toward holding the settlement system accountable and demonstrating non-recognition of the unlawful situation created by the occupation," Palestinian president Mahmoud Abbas's office said in a statement.
Israel's Foreign Minister Gideon Saar said Tuesday that the UK consulate in Jerusalem will be closed in response to Britain's sanctions on illegal settlements in the occupied West Bank.
He added that 12 British public officials and citizens will be barred from entering Israel, and that Britain was no longer permitted to participate in the US-led Gaza coordination mission based in Israel.
A local commander in Iran's paramilitary Basij force was killed on Tuesday in a "terrorist attack" in the country's restive southeast, local media reported.
Abdolraouf Eshaghi, a commander in the Parud district of Sistan-Baluchistan province, had been "martyred", Tasnim news agency said, without providing details.
It was not immediately clear who was behind the attack.
On Monday, Iranian authorities had said three people were killed and nine arrested during a raid in the province on hideouts of Islamist groups affiliated with Israel and the United States.

The US Treasury Department said its latest action takes aim at "36 targets for supporting Iran's aviation sector, which the regime uses to move weapons, personnel, and illicit cargo."

articles.title: US tells Europe to prepare for protracted Ukraine war
articles.body:
European countries should prepare for the possibility that the war in Ukraine continues for years while simultaneously rebuilding their own armed forces and defence industries, a senior US defence official has told allies.
US Under Secretary of War for Policy Elbridge Colby said Washington could not predict when the conflict would end and warned that Russia was rebuilding both its military forces and its defence industrial capacity.
Speaking at the Ukraine Defence Contact Group, Colby said: “From the standpoint of the Department of War, however, we cannot predict when this tragic war will end. As you all well know, Russia is reconstituting its forces and its defense industrial capacity.”
He continued: “We must be prepared for a protracted conflict and for Ukraine’s requirements to persist in the months and years ahead, and we must also be prepared for other plausible contingencies as well.”
Colby said European allies were increasingly taking the leading role in conventional defence and providing the bulk of military support for Ukraine, describing that transition as already producing tangible results. He said continued European funding of American-origin weapons was helping Ukrainian forces maintain their defence and deny further Russian advances. Colby argued that Europe now needed to prepare for sustained procurement rather than treating support for Ukraine as a short-term requirement. He said: “Europe must plan now for sustained procurement that supports both Ukraine’s long-term force reconstitution and Europe’s own defense requirements.”
The US official said European investment in defence industry should increase while remaining complementary to American production, and warned that political commitments alone would not provide the military capability required. Colby said: “Real money and industrial capacity must be put to work.”
He also said the United States would continue supporting allied procurement for Ukraine through the JumpStart mechanism, including the acquisition of air defence interceptors.
The shift was described by Colby as part of the US administration’s “NATO 3.0” approach, under which European allies assume greater responsibility for the conventional defence of the continent. In his closing remarks, Colby said the United States was seeking to “adapt America’s strategic posture in Europe and transition to a more durable and powerful European-led conventional defence”.

articles.title: Iran mass-producing home-grown weaponry: Air defense chief
articles.body:
Brigadier General Alireza Elhami, who serves as the commander of Iran’s Khatam al-Anbiya Joint Air Defense Headquarters, said on Monday that home-grown defense systems are being stationed at locations across Iranian territory, a report by Press TV said.
"The equipment produced [inside Iran] passed a successful test during that conflict, and now they are being rapidly mass-produced to be deployed across the entire expanse of the Islamic Republic of Iran," said Elhami, according to remarks published by Tasnim news agency.
Iran relied heavily on its home-grown weapons and ammunition during the 39-day US-Israeli aggression that ended as part of a ceasefire in mid-April.
Experts say Iranian-made missiles, drones, and interception systems were key to the country’s success in creating a robust deterrence against the US and the Israeli regime.
 
 Elhami said that Iran’s military forces have benefited massively from the use of their indigenous defense systems compared to the time when the country relied on imported military equipment.
He said home-grown defense systems do not need any upgrades from foreign suppliers, enabling the country to update its equipment and systems in line with new threats.
"This process is carried out much faster and more easily for systems whose software and hardware are completely under our own control than for foreign equipment," said the commander.
Elhami, who is also in charge of the Iranian army’s air defense force, said that Iranian-made weapons and defense systems are designed in a way that suits the country’s geography, climatic conditions, and the real needs of the battlefield.
"These characteristics have practically proven the superiority of Iranian equipment over foreign counterparts on the battlefield," he said.
The commander said Iran is increasingly relying on its domestic resources to boost the quality and quantity of its home-grown weapons while diversifying the applications of those weapons and the tactics needed to use them.

articles.title: Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
articles.body:
Ukrainian company unveils RAM-2X strike drone for first time, used to hit over 450 targets – photo, video
Ukrainian company Ukrspecsystems, which develops reconnaissance and strike drones, has publicly unveiled its RAM-2X strike UAV with an X-shaped wing for the first time. The drone was presented at the MSPO defence exhibition in Poland.
Source: Ukrainska Pravda
Details: The RAM-2X was designed to strike high-value targets at ranges of up to 180 km. The drone can remain airborne for more than two hours and has a high degree of automation. It can carry a 2.7 kg or 3.5 kg explosively formed penetrator warhead.
"Each type of equipment performs its own task, and every target requires an appropriate means of engagement. Following a comprehensive approach, we are developing strike systems in several subclasses at once, built around standardised components, a common ground station and unified software," Ukrspecsystems representatives said.
The RAM-2X can also use various AI assistant models to improve its effectiveness and operate with different communications systems. The drone can use several radio-frequency bands or Starlink.
In addition, the RAM-2X can operate together with a SHARK-M reconnaissance UAV acting as a communications relay. In this configuration, the reconnaissance drone provides targeting data and helps overcome enemy electronic warfare systems.
Ukrspecsystems says RAM loitering munitions have struck more than 450 targets. Although footage of these drones being used in combat has regularly appeared in the public domain, the company was unable for a long time to publicly confirm its connection to RAM due to security restrictions.
Ukrspecsystems has now decided to open its own "X-Files", a series of publications featuring footage of the drones being used in combat. The first compilation focuses on strikes against Russian air defence systems. Its publication was approved by the military.
RAM-2X drone strikes on targets. Video: Defence Intelligence of Ukraine
"These are targets that are themselves designed to hunt drones. There are simply no more difficult targets for a strike drone. Secondly, because of their value, they are better camouflaged and positioned further from the front line. That is why striking an air defence system or radar demonstrates the key capabilities: the system's ability to overcome electronic warfare and enemy defences and operate far beyond the line of contact," Ukrspecsystems representatives explained, describing why they chose to publish footage of strikes on air defence systems first.
Background: Ukrspecsystems previously announced that it had developed a ready-to-use medium-range strike drone similar to the US Hornet.

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across shared border, analysts warn it could become a key military supply route
articles.body:
Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge connecting the two countries across the Tumen River, according to a report by the Russian state-controlled news agency TASS. Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said the link would enhance cooperation in various fields. Analysts have previously noted, however, that the main purpose of the bridge likely involves the expansion of military cooperation between Moscow and Pyongyang.
Mishustin and North Korean PM Pak Thae Song took part in the opening ceremony by video link. During the festivities, Mishustin said:
“I am convinced that expanding cross-border transport infrastructure will give a powerful boost to the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation between the Russian Federation and the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea. The tourism industry will also gain good prospects.”
Primorsky Krai governor Oleg Kozhemyako, whose Far Eastern region borders North Korea, said the bridge “symbolizes the desire to strengthen friendly, good-neighborly relations and expand interregional cooperation,” adding that the bridge had been named after Soviet army officer Yakov Novichenko, who, according to the official Russian account, “saved the lives of participants of a peaceful demonstration in Pyongyang” on March 1, 1946.
As Kozhemyako also noted: “Today, the convoy of vehicles that crossed the bridge from the Russian side was led by a ZAZ-968M made in 1980. It belonged to Yakov Novichenko. At the wheel of the restored car was the grandson of the internationalist hero, Nikolai Shcherbitsky.”
TASS said the project was first conceived in 2018; however, the agreement to build the road bridge across the Tumen River was only signed on June 19, 2024 during Vladimir Putin’s state visit to North Korea. The opening of the bridge was been postponed several times —North Korea completed its required infrastructure on schedule, while Russia repeatedly missed construction deadlines.
Investigators with the Ukrainian organization Truth Hounds concluded that the real reason for building a road crossing over the Tumen River is not trade or cultural ties, but military cooperation, saying the bridge could become a key route for moving North Korean soldiers and weapons for use in Russia’s war against Ukraine. In the opposite direction, Russia could use the link to send North Korea various technologies and resources.
Until now, overland transport between Russia and North Korea had been limited to a single railway crossing, known as the Friendship Bridge. The investigators noted that road traffic is significantly harder to track by satellite than rail shipments because both countries have much more extensive road networks than rail networks. Loading and unloading trucks also takes less time than handling rail cars, reducing the window in which satellite imagery can capture such activity.
They also said analysts can often identify the category of goods being transported by rail based on the type of rail car visible in satellite imagery, while trucks generally look almost identical from space. Trucks can also be unloaded almost anywhere, whereas trains must use specific rail hubs.
More than 10,000 North Korean troops have taken part in Russia’s war against Ukraine, and at least 2,300 of them have been killed. North Korean authorities have described their troops’ participation in Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine as a “sacred mission.”
Pyongyang has also supported Moscow with weapons shipments, with North Korea’s military assistance to Russia estimated to be worth between $7.67 billion and $14.4 billion, according to South Korea’s state-funded Institute for National Security Strategy.
The independent Russian investigative outlet Important Stories and the UK-based non-profit Open Source Center also reported that during the war North Korea has supplied Russia with as many as 11 million artillery shells and rockets, accounting “for 75% to 100% of all daily artillery fire” by Russian forces at the front lines in Ukraine at various points in the fighting.
